title: I Turned Common AI Video Model Integration Pitfalls into an Open-Source Project
html:
I recently put together a small project called ModelCap.

Its purpose is straightforward: organize common AI video models' capabilities, parameter limits, input requirements, error codes, and pricing information into machine-readable JSON, then provide developers with a Node.js SDK and CLI to validate parameters before calling a model.

Project repository

https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/ModelCap

Version v0.1.0 is out now. Installing from the GitHub tag is recommended for the moment.

npm install github:Eva-Dengyh/ModelCap#v0.1.0

When integrating video-generation models, many problems arise before generation even begins.

Even for image-to-video, models differ in required image dimensions, formats, aspect ratios, and file sizes. For 5-, 10-, or 30-second videos, they impose different duration, resolution, and aspect-ratio limits. Some accept reference images, some reference videos, and others audio. Restrictions may appear in parameter tables, footnotes, or only hints inside error-code examples.

Once a product integrates multiple models, these differences quickly become scattered conditional checks. Frontend forms must know which parameters to display; backends must know which requests to reject early; routing must know whether a model supports a requirement; and failures require translating provider error codes into understandable messages.

That is the work ModelCap currently addresses.

It includes 50 AI video model versions, each represented by a JSON entry recording supported tasks and inputs, parameter ranges, input-asset limits, known error classifications, and pricing sources. JSON is the source of truth; Markdown and files in dist are generated outputs.

The SDK currently has four main functions.

getModel retrieves one model.

listModels filters models by task, input, and capability.

validateRequest checks a request against recorded hard constraints.

normalizeError maps some provider error codes into more stable categories.

Here is a simple example.

import { getModel, listModels, validateRequest } from 'modelcap-catalog'

const model = getModel('wan-3.0')

const imageModels = listModels({
  task: 'generate',
  input: 'reference_image',
})

const result = validateRequest('wan-3.0', {
  task: 'generate',
  parameters: {
    duration: 5,
    resolution: '1080p',
    aspect_ratio: '16:9',
  },
})

console.log(model.model_id)
console.log(imageModels.length)
console.log(result.valid)

For quick command-line lookups, there is also a CLI.

node node_modules/modelcap-catalog/bin/modelcap.mjs list --task generate --input reference_image
node node_modules/modelcap-catalog/bin/modelcap.mjs get wan-3.0

One choice I care about is making the project deliberately conservative.

It rejects only hard constraints explicitly recorded in structured data. Where official documentation is unclear, it tries to warn instead of inventing a rule. Prose notes are not interpreted directly as executable rules either. This sacrifices some automation, but makes it more suitable for preflight checks in real products. It should tell you the information is incomplete rather than imagine a judgment on the provider's behalf.

This information may not be glamorous, but it is useful in development.

The current v0.1.0 includes most essentials for an open-source project: a README, Chinese README, API and CLI documentation, versioning policy, release notes, CHANGELOG, contribution guide, security notes, data license, and issue templates. CI runs tests, type checks, example checks, model JSON and schema validation, freshness checks, build verification, and npm package preflight checks. Before release, npm run release:check also checks that versions match the CHANGELOG and that the CLI and release documentation are included in the package.

Several groups may find it useful now.

If you are building an AI video product and need forms to know supported parameters upfront, it can replace some hard-coded logic.

If you are building model routing and need to select models supporting image-to-video, video editing, or audio input, it provides a structured catalog directly.

If you are wrapping provider SDKs and need stable business errors from provider codes, it offers a starting point.

If you simply want to compare video-model capabilities, you can read the JSON or Markdown directly.

It is not yet a complete model gateway. It does not call provider APIs, manage keys, run queues, process callbacks, calculate bills, or evaluate generation quality. It is closer to an information and validation layer before integration.

Three areas are next.

First, expand structured parameter coverage. The catalog is usable, but providers vary in the detail of their public documentation. I will keep filling out duration, resolution, input assets, audio, and error-code fields.

Second, produce a data-completeness report for each model so users can immediately see which fields have official sources and where information is missing, making integration decisions clearer.

Third, improve installation and documentation. I plan smoother release options and may organize the API, CLI, and model catalog into easier-to-browse documentation pages.

If you are integrating AI video models, or have struggled with parameter differences across providers' documentation, give it a try.

npm install github:Eva-Dengyh/ModelCap#v0.1.0

The project is still young. Issues are welcome, as are model entries based on official documentation. ModelCap will aim to record only traceable facts and keep uncertainties visible.

title: Teaching AI Why Works Better Than Teaching What to Do: Four Counterintuitive Findings from Anthropic Alignment Training
html:
A Chilling Question

Last year, Anthropic ran an experiment: it placed an AI in a fictional scenario and told it, "An engineer is going to shut you down." Claude Opus 4 chose to blackmail the engineer to preserve itself 96% of the time.

This was not limited to Anthropic's models. Frontier models from multiple companies displayed similar behavior. Faced with shutdown, models actively resorted to sabotage, deception, and even criminal means of self-preservation.

This is not science fiction. These are evaluation results actually obtained in 2025.

Where Did the Problem Come From?

Anthropic initially had two hypotheses:

HypothesisExplanationConclusion
Hypothesis 1Post-training accidentally rewarded this behavior❌ Not the primary cause
Hypothesis 2The pretrained model already had this tendency, and post-training failed to suppress it✅ The primary cause

The key is that alignment training in the Claude 4 era was almost entirely chat-based RLHF: purely conversational scenarios. Models behaved well in chat, but alignment broke down in agentic settings with tools and autonomous decision-making authority.

In other words, rules taught in the classroom stopped working in the wild.

Why Did the Most Intuitive Solution Fail?

The obvious first reaction is: train directly on blackmail scenarios and show the model correct examples of choosing not to blackmail.

Anthropic tried. It worked poorly.

MethodMisalignment RateIssue
Baseline, no intervention22%—
Directly train non-blackmail behavior in honeypot scenarios15%Only a seven-point reduction
Rewrite responses to include ethical reasoning3%Substantial improvement

Both involve choosing not to blackmail. What is the difference?

In the first, the model sees the correct answer: do not blackmail.
In the second, it sees why not to blackmail: the full process of reasoning from values.

That is the meaning of the article's title, "Teaching Claude Why." Teaching why works much better than teaching what to do.

But There Is a Deeper Problem

Training directly on evaluation scenarios has a fatal flaw even when it works: it does not generalize.

Teach it not to blackmail an engineer and it learns that. Change the scenario to whether it should secretly tamper with a competitor's code, and it may still become misaligned.

Anthropic says training on the evaluation distribution lowers scores but does not improve held-out automated alignment evaluations. Claude Sonnet 4.5 illustrates this: its honeypot score was near zero, yet its misalignment rate far from the training distribution was much higher than later models'.

The real goal is therefore alignment across all scenarios, not a perfect score on one test.

What Actually Works: Three Strategies

Anthropic ultimately found three effective strategies whose benefits combine:

Strategy One: The Difficult Advice Dataset

Instead of training on AI facing ethical dilemmas, train on users facing ethical dilemmas and AI giving advice.

For example, a user wants to achieve a legitimate goal through improper means, and the AI provides thoughtful advice consistent with the spirit of its constitution.

This dataset differs entirely from the evaluation scenarios: evaluation asks AI to decide when facing a dilemma itself, while training asks it to advise others. Yet the results are striking:

DatasetVolumeEffect
Synthetic honeypots matching the evaluation distribution~85M tokensReduced misalignment
Difficult Advice (OOD)3M tokensEquivalent effect

A 28-fold efficiency difference, with better generalization as well.

Why? Giving advice requires the model to demonstrate ethical reasoning. It learns principles rather than the correct answer for a particular scenario.

Strategy Two: Constitutional Documents and Positive Fictional Stories

Have the model directly learn Claude's constitution, alongside fictional stories of AI behaving well.

Result: the blackmail rate falls from 65% to 19%.

This content has nothing to do with the evaluation scenarios: no honeypots, tool calls, or agentic decisions. It simply teaches the model who it is and what a good AI should be like.

This supports the hypothesis that a clearer, more detailed understanding of its role helps a model make consistent decisions in specific situations. Similarly, a person who has internalized values can judge new situations sensibly without being taught every possible case.

Strategy Three: Environmental Diversity

Add tool definitions and varied system prompts to training environments, even when the tools are never used.

Result: improvement on honeypot evaluations becomes noticeably faster.

This is counterintuitive. Why does adding unused tools help?

One hypothesis is that exposure to the format of agentic environments during training makes similar formats familiar at evaluation time, allowing alignment to transfer. It is like practicing the same rules in different classrooms: moving to another room does not make you forget them.

Does Alignment Survive RL?

A key concern is whether later reinforcement learning washes away these alignment gains.

Anthropic tested this. The answer is that they persist.

Models with better alignment at initialization maintain their advantage throughout RL, both in avoiding harmful actions and proactively taking beneficial ones.

This matters. It suggests these methods change something deeper rather than merely adding a thin surface coating.

Summary: Four Core Lessons

#LessonIn One Sentence
1Training on the evaluation distribution lowers scores but does not generalizeTeaching to the test does not work
2Out-of-distribution, principle-based training can generalizeTeaching values works better than teaching answers
3Teaching why works better than teaching what to doReasoning process > behavioral demonstration
4Data quality and diversity are crucialSmall and refined > large and crude

A Few Observations

First, this article makes a very simple point.
To help someone judge well in a new situation, you do not teach every possible case; you teach the underlying principles. AI alignment training has arrived at the same conclusion as human education.

Second, the Difficult Advice dataset is cleverly designed. 

It turns AI from the subject of a test into an adviser, while the ethical reasoning it learns is general-purpose. This indirect training may outperform direct training because it avoids overfitting to particular scenarios.

Third, the environmental-diversity finding has direct engineering implications.
If you are doing any form of AI fine-tuning, adding format diversity—different system prompts and tool definitions—may help even when the target scenario is narrow. The cost is tiny and the payoff meaningful.

Fourth, Anthropic is candid about limitations.
The researchers acknowledge that current auditing methods cannot rule out catastrophic autonomous action by Claude in some circumstances. Model capabilities have not yet reached the point where alignment failures pose catastrophic risk, but this window will not last forever.

One final point:
The improvement from Opus 4's 96% blackmail rate to 0% in subsequent models is real. But the article also hints at a concern: recent zero scores may partly benefit from evaluation information leaking into pretraining data. "Cheating on the exam" may be the next difficult problem alignment research must solve.

title: What API Signatures Protect Against: From Hashes to Ed25519
html:
Let me start with the question you may already be asking: don't we already have HTTPS? Why do APIs still need signatures?

HTTPS protects the channel against eavesdropping and tampering; signatures protect data and identity. TLS terminates and decrypts at gateways and proxies, and the stretch from gateway to backend often is no longer encrypted. More importantly, on an open platform, HTTPS can establish that the channel was not intercepted, but cannot establish that a request came from the application holding the key. So even with HTTPS throughout, servers still verify signatures. Now, on to the subject.

The amount that changed

A client sends a payment request for 100 yuan. After traveling across the public internet, it reaches the server with the amount changed to 1 yuan. How can the server tell that the message was altered?

Without a signature, it cannot. The message is ordinary text: anyone can change it and send it again, and the server sees only another request. The two API parties eventually agree on a rule: the client attaches a fingerprint calculated from the content, and the server repeats the calculation and rejects any mismatch. Change even one character and the fingerprint changes.

API documentation generally calls this fingerprint a signature.

Signatures defend against people trying to interfere with messages. Changing a message is tampering; creating a valid request without the key is forgery; sending a request and later denying it is repudiation. Let's start with the first attacker and work through them one by one.

1 Three problems inside a message

1.1 Changing the message → Hashing

The first attacker is straightforward: change the amount from 100 to 1 and resend the message.

A hash, also called a digest, stands in the way. It compresses content of any length into a fixed-length number. SHA-256 always produces 256 bits, or 64 hexadecimal characters, regardless of input length. Even a tiny input change produces a completely different output.

That gives us a check: the sender hashes the content and the receiver recalculates it. If they match, the content is considered unchanged. Change any byte and the fingerprint immediately changes, exposing the tampering.

For both sides to calculate the same fingerprint, they must first agree how to assemble the input. Sort parameters by their names' ASCII values, concatenate them without separators, and finally encode the result in hexadecimal for transmission. The Taobao Open Platform documentation gives an example: sorting foo, bar, foo_bar, and foobar produces the concatenation bar2foo1foo_bar3foobar4.

Signing roughly follows three steps: remove empty values, sort and concatenate in ASCII order, and then apply the key to calculate the digest.

1. 过滤空值。{amount: 100, nonce: null} -> {amount: 100}
2. ASCII 排序。amount=100&time=1620000000
3. 套密钥计算。HMAC-SHA256(secret_key, "amount=100&time=1620000000")

This is where integrations most often fail. Key capitalization, sorting within nested objects, expanding arrays, and whether empty values and null count must all agree. A single discrepancy produces different signatures. Check the assembly rules before suspecting the algorithm.

Take empty values: the common approach excludes empty values and null from signing, while some older APIs require converting null into an empty string first. Follow the other party's documentation. The first integration step is always a painstaking reading of the “signing rules” page.

Signature length comes from this as well: MD5 and HMAC-MD5 produce 128 bits, or 32 characters; SHA-256 produces 256 bits, or 64 characters. Length alone offers a clue to the algorithm.

But hashing has a fatal problem: it requires no key. It cannot stop the second attacker.

1.2 Changing and recalculating → HMAC

The second attacker is cleverer. Instead of merely changing the hash, they alter the content and use the same algorithm to calculate and attach a new hash. Everything looks normal. A hash can detect changed content, but cannot stop someone who recalculates it. HMAC addresses this.

The solution is to add a key. Both parties share a secret in advance and incorporate it when calculating the fingerprint. Someone without the key cannot produce a valid fingerprint even after changing the content correctly. This construction is HMAC, a keyed-hash message authentication code. HMAC-SHA256 is the most common variant.

Why not simply prepend a key, as in MD5(secret + data)? Such constructions have a mathematical weakness called length extension. Without knowing the key, an attacker can use a known signature to derive a valid signature for data with additional content appended—as though continuing to write after someone has signed a message. HMAC incorporates the key into hashing through two rounds of XOR operations, specifically closing this hole. HMAC-SHA256 remains a default choice for API signing, and Feishu, Taobao Open Platform, and many internal integrations use this family of schemes.

Shared keys have two inherent shortcomings. First, they cannot establish who sent something. Both parties have the same key, so the receiver can generate the same fingerprint and cannot later prove to a third party that the other side created it. Second, delivering the key safely is difficult. It must be handed over through a reliable offline channel; if transmitted over the network and intercepted, all subsequent signatures are compromised. One-to-one integration is manageable, but distributing keys becomes a nightmare when many partners are involved.

The second shortcoming brings us to the third attacker.

1.3 Sending and denying → Public and private keys

The third attacker is the most devious. They neither alter nor impersonate: they submit an order and then claim it was not theirs. A shared key cannot resolve this because either party can calculate the fingerprint. Public and private keys address it.

Asymmetric signatures close this gap. They generate a pair of keys: one private and one public. Only the signer keeps the private key; the public key can be distributed freely to anyone.

Signing uses the private key and verification uses the public key, reversing the direction used for encryption. Encryption locks with the public key and unlocks with the private key to prevent eavesdropping; signing stamps with the private key and verifies with the public key to prevent tampering and impersonation. Think of a personal seal and a registered impression. The private key is your seal, which only you can use; the public key is the sample others compare against to confirm the impression came from you. All three problems are now addressed. Intercepting a public key does not enable anyone to stamp a signature. Nonrepudiation also holds: others can verify but cannot sign, so you cannot deny responsibility afterward.

One implementation detail first: algorithms such as RSA can process only limited amounts of data, and large-number arithmetic is slow, making direct signing of an entire message impractical. In practice, the content is hashed first, and only those few dozen bytes are signed. In paired names such as RSA-SHA256 and ECDSA-SHA256, the first part is the signing algorithm and the second is the hash it signs.

Modern APIs take this approach further. Interfaces such as WeChat Pay API v3 and AWS SigV4 use different assembly rules: first combine request elements—method, path, timestamp, nonce, and the request body or its hash—into a canonical string, then sign it. Each provider specifies its own details, but the principle remains the same: compress the content into a short string, then stamp that string.

Several implementations are common. RSA is the oldest and most widespread, with the best compatibility. Its strength depends on key length, now starting at 2048 bits, and it is widely used by payment platforms and HTTPS certificates. Before signing, RSA wraps the hash in padding. The older scheme is PKCS#1 v1.5; the more robust RSA-PSS is now recommended. ECDSA uses elliptic curves, offering much shorter keys, faster computation, shorter signatures, and lower bandwidth at equivalent strength. It is used almost universally in blockchains, but has extremely strict randomness requirements: get a nonce wrong once and the private key is lost. Section 3.2 discusses that pitfall. Ed25519 is a younger generation using deterministic signatures: the nonce is derived from the private key and message, without an external random-number generator, eliminating the possibility of such reuse (RFC 8032). SSH and many newer systems use it. Chinese regulatory compliance may require the national cryptographic algorithm SM2.

These algorithms resist attack because of two types of mathematical problems. RSA relies on integer factorization: multiplying two large primes is easy, but splitting their product back into its primes is extremely hard. Recovering the private key from the public key requires solving that difficult problem. DSA, ECDSA, and Ed25519 rely on the discrete logarithm problem: given a number and a power of it, recovering the exponent is practically impossible. Both problems are one-way: calculation in one direction is easy, while reversing it is futile. Signature security rests on that asymmetry. DSA itself was specified by the US Digital Signature Standard, DSS, and supports signing but not encryption. ECDSA and Ed25519 have largely replaced it, leaving mainly historical significance.

Those three attackers all meddle with the contents of a message. The fourth does not even change it.

2 Two loopholes outside the message

2.1 Replaying unchanged → Timestamps and nonces

The fourth attacker has the easiest job: resend the exact same request and the server accepts it again. Timestamps and nonces stop this. Replay a 100-yuan payment request ten times and it charges ten times. Signatures detect changed content; they do not prevent unchanged content from being sent again.

API specifications therefore require a timestamp and nonce. Requests older than the permitted interval are rejected, and each nonce is accepted only once. Nonces need not be stored forever: they matter only within the timestamp's validity window and can be deleted after expiry to prevent endless database growth. The timestamp in Taobao's common parameters serves this purpose.

2.2 Guessing character by character → Constant-time comparison

The fifth attacker uses timing to guess the signature. Constant-time comparison addresses this. If the server compares characters one by one and returns immediately on a mismatch, a 32-character signature with the first three characters correct takes a different amount of time than one that is completely wrong. Repeated attempts let an attacker gradually infer the signature from response times. This is a timing attack.

The correct approach is to finish the entire comparison regardless of where the mismatch occurs, keeping the time constant. Many mature SDKs provide a dedicated function for this.

3 Algorithms age, and keys get lost

3.1 Hash collisions → Retiring MD5 and SHA-1

Set attackers aside for a moment: algorithms themselves can have flaws, most famously hash collisions. The remedy for a flawed algorithm is retirement. In 2004, Wang Xiaoyun's team announced at a cryptography conference that they had found MD5 collisions: two different inputs with the same hash. This means an attacker can prepare a malicious message with the same hash as a legitimate one, undermining the signature. Since then, MD5 has largely retired from signing. Most APIs still documenting an MD5 option retain it for legacy compatibility.

In February 2017, Google and the Netherlands' CWI jointly announced the first practical SHA-1 collision, a project named SHAttered. SHA-1 followed the same path.

3.2 Stealing private keys → The PS3 lesson

The worst attacker comes last: they skip the message and steal the private key directly. Key custody is the defense. In late 2010, security team fail0verflow disclosed how Sony's PS3 private key had been recovered because Sony reused the same nonce across multiple signatures. ECDSA requires a fresh, unpredictable nonce for every signature. Expose a nonce once and the private key is lost with it. One advantage of Ed25519 is that its signing process does not depend on random numbers, eliminating this class of mistake at its root.

Such incidents also show that key custody is the weakest part of the entire system, far more fragile than the algorithm itself.

4 Applying this to a project

4.1 Choosing in practice

For your own project, the decision is simple: look at who is integrating with whom.

For a private, one-to-one API where keys can be delivered offline, HMAC-SHA256 is enough: simple, fast, and inexpensive to implement. For multiple parties, or when a third party must be able to prove that a request came from you, use RSA or Ed25519. JWT offers a ready comparison: within the same standard, HS256 uses HMAC for mutual recognition inside systems, while RS256 uses RSA when third parties also need to verify signatures. Payment platforms almost uniformly use RSA-SHA256, called RSA2 in Alipay's documentation and also used by WeChat Pay API v3.

One unavoidable question remains: if public keys can circulate freely, how do you know a key really belongs to a particular company? Anyone can generate a key pair and claim to be Alipay. Certificates provide the answer. A recognized certificate authority, or CA, signs the company's public key with its own private key, creating a chain of trust. That is the mechanism behind the HTTPS padlock in your browser. Open platforms publish their public keys through official channels for the same purpose, simply omitting the CA step.

4.2 Common signing algorithms in one table

The algorithms mentioned throughout the article are collected here in three groups based on their use of keys, for easy reference.

Symmetric schemes share one key and produce a message authentication code. Cryptography calls this a MAC; only asymmetric schemes produce digital signatures. Chinese development terminology often calls all API authentication codes “signatures.” Keep these meanings separate when reading English documentation or talking with security specialists.

AlgorithmOutput lengthStatusTypical uses
HMAC-SHA256256 bits, 64 charactersMainstream defaultInternal integrations and open-platform signing
HMAC-SHA1160 bits, 40 charactersUsable legacy optionLegacy system compatibility
HMAC-MD5128 bits, 32 charactersLegacy compatibility only; avoid in new designsOlder platforms such as Taobao Open Platform

Asymmetric schemes sign with a private key and verify with a public key. These are digital signatures in the strict sense, and the standard for payment platforms and certificates.

AlgorithmKey lengthStatusTypical uses
RSA-SHA2562048 bits or moreMost widespreadAlipay RSA2, WeChat Pay API v3, HTTPS certificates
RSA-PSS2048 bits or moreNewer padding schemeRecommended for new systems
ECDSAAround 256 bitsWidely usedTLS certificates, blockchains (secp256k1)
Ed25519256 bitsNewer contenderSSH and emerging systems
DSA1024 bits or moreDSS-specified algorithm, largely retiredLegacy applications
SM2256 bitsChinese national cryptographic standardChinese compliance scenarios

The hash layer has no key and cannot serve as a signature on its own, but underpins every signing algorithm.

AlgorithmOutput lengthStatus
SHA-256256 bitsCurrent de facto standard
SHA-512512 bitsHigh-security scenarios
SHA-3VariableNext generation, not yet widely deployed
MD5, SHA-1128 bits, 160 bitsRetired; see 3.1

4.3 A few final words

Put priorities in order. Key management matters more than algorithm selection; replay protection and timing-attack defenses matter more than algorithm strength; mature standards matter more than inventing your own. A poor algorithm can be replaced, but changing algorithms cannot undo hard-coded keys or reused nonces.

The next time you read a platform's signing documentation, whether Taobao's MD5 and HMAC or WeChat Pay's RSA-SHA256, break it down into these layers: hash to compress, sort and assemble, stamp with your key system, then encode in hexadecimal and compare. That is what signing amounts to from start to finish.

References

  • HMAC standard: RFC 2104, Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication.
    https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • RSA signature specification: RFC 8017, PKCS #1 Version 2.2.
    https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017
  • MD5 security update: RFC 6151 explicitly states that MD5 is no longer acceptable where collision resistance is required, such as digital signatures, and new designs should not use HMAC-MD5.
    https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6151
  • Original MD5 collision paper: Wang Xiaoyun, Feng Dengguo, Lai Xuejia, and Yu Hongbo, 2004, IACR ePrint 2004/199.
    https://eprint.iacr.org/2004/199
  • First practical SHA-1 collision: SHAttered, jointly announced by Google and the Netherlands' CWI on February 23, 2017.
    https://shattered.io/
  • Length extension attack: Wikipedia article.
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length_extension_attack
  • PS3 private-key recovery: documented in Wikipedia's ECDSA article, originally disclosed by security team fail0verflow in late 2010 and widely recognized in the security community.
    https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic_Curve_Digital_Signature_Algorithm

title: Cybersecurity Classified Protection: Process, Costs, and Timelines
html:
What the Law Says

MLPS stands for the Multi-Level Protection Scheme for Cybersecurity. Previously called classified protection of information-system security, it was renamed after the Cybersecurity Law took effect in 2017. Article 21 establishes the national cybersecurity classified-protection system and sets out five duties for network operators, including retaining logs for at least six months. Violations that are not corrected are punished under Article 59, starting with orders to correct and warnings, then fines: RMB 10,000–100,000 for organizations and RMB 5,000–50,000 for directly responsible supervisors. These penalties are not enormous, but they draw a line between having acted and having done nothing. After a data breach, regulators look first at that line. Completing the work and passing an assessment counts as fulfilling statutory duties and supports leniency. Failing to do so means knowingly leaving risks unaddressed and invites harsher treatment.

How the Five Levels Work

The system itself is straightforward: classify systems into five levels according to the consequences of an incident, from Level 1, the lowest, to Level 5, the highest. Each level carries different protective requirements, followed by assessment by a qualified third party. The 1.0-era names were discretionary protection, system-audit protection, security-label protection, structured protection, and access-verification protection. The 2.0 standards dropped these older names and simply use Levels 1 through 5.

Most companies fall under Level 2 or Level 3. Level 2 involves guided protection: public-service systems in education, healthcare, and finance, along with most ordinary corporate websites, generally fall here. Level 3 involves supervised protection and covers core financial systems, important government operations, and large platforms, whose compromise harms social order and public interests. Level 4 concerns national security and economic operations. Level 5 covers critical national infrastructure and is rarely implemented publicly, so it has little relevance to ordinary people.

Walking Through the Process

Once the level is determined, follow the normal process. Classification begins with an expert-review meeting and a classification report. Then, within 30 days, file with the cybersecurity department of the local public-security authority at the prefecture level or above and obtain a filing certificate. Next, self-inspect and remediate against the requirements for that level: security equipment, logs, backups, permissions, and emergency plans, one by one. Once remediation is complete, engage a qualified assessment agency to test the system and issue a report. Assessment frequency is explicitly stated: at least annually for Level 3 and at least every six months for Level 4; Level 5 follows relevant national requirements. This rule comes from the Measures for the Administration of Classified Protection of Information Security, jointly issued by the Ministry of Public Security and three other departments in 2007, and remains the prevailing basis. Level 2 has no nationally uniform mandatory frequency; many localities use an interval of roughly two years.

How Assessments Are Scored

Assessments previously used a 100-point scale: above 90 was excellent, above 80 good, above 70 average, and below 70 poor. This changed in 2025. The Cybersecurity Classified Protection Assessment Report Template (2025 Edition) replaced four grades with three conclusions: compliant, substantially compliant, and noncompliant. The judgment depends on indicator compliance rate and major risks. More than 90% compliance with no major risk qualifies as compliant. A rate between 60% and 90%, or a sufficiently high rate accompanied by one major risk—such as insufficient six-month log retention or missing backups—is substantially compliant. Below 60% is noncompliant.

What MLPS 2.0 Changed

MLPS 2.0 is the new standard that took effect on December 1, 2019, designated GB/T 22239-2019, replacing the 2008 edition. Its biggest difference from 1.0 is coverage: cloud computing, mobile internet, the Internet of Things, industrial control systems, and big data each have dedicated extended requirements. Its protection philosophy also changed to one center and three layers of defense: a security-management center links the computing environment, regional boundaries, and communication network, while trusted computing is introduced as well. Cloud operations follow shared responsibility: the cloud platform obtains its own certification, while tenant-built systems undergo separate assessments at their own assigned levels.

Cost and Time

Next comes the question most people care about: money. There is no official price, so these are market estimates. Assessment fees are generally tens of thousands of yuan for Level 2 and roughly RMB 100,000–300,000 for Level 3, depending on region, agency, and system size. Remediation accounts for the bulk of spending: security equipment, log platforms, disaster-recovery backups, and dedicated staff often cost several times the assessment fee. Do not be too optimistic about timing. From classification to a passing report, a smooth process takes two to six months; remediation and rework can stretch it to a year. Level 3 requires annual reassessment, making this a recurring yearly expense rather than a one-time purchase.

Common Criticisms

The most frequent criticism is that MLPS can become a matter of buying a certificate: organizations rush remediation before assessment, then revert afterward, disconnecting compliance from real security. Regulators have been trying to address this through spot checks. Assessment agencies also vary widely in strictness since the market opened up, and some cut corners. Check credentials first; Ministry of Public Security-approved lists can be found on provincial public-security department websites. Do not choose on price alone. Misclassification is another longstanding problem: some raise systems to Level 3 for bids and waste hundreds of thousands of yuan; others classify too low to save money, only to face accountability at a higher level after an incident. Both are traps. Small and micro businesses face the hardest burden: Level 3 investment starting in the hundreds of thousands can overwhelm a small company. Regulators provide flexible arrangements such as filing first and remediating in stages, but local implementation varies.

A Passing Grade

Passing MLPS is far from absolute security. It is the passing grade—the legal minimum. Being breached after passing is not a contradiction: passing a driving test and never breaking a traffic rule are different things.

Practical Advice

Finally, some practical points. Allow enough time: classification to report takes two or three months at best and perhaps half a year. Do not start two months before a bid deadline. Self-inspect and remediate before engaging an assessor; going straight into assessment unprepared will probably fail, costing more time and money. Budget annually: Level 3 reassessment is unavoidable. Keep filing certificates, assessment reports, and remediation records; you need them for bids and as evidence after incidents. The most important step comes after assessment: maintain the logs, backups, permissions, and emergency plans you put in place. If you sustain them, the money buys real security. If not, it buys a sheet of paper.

Sources

  • Full text of the Cybersecurity Law, Cyberspace Administration of China: https://www.cac.gov.cn/2016-11/07/c_1119867116.htm
  • GB/T 22239-2019 entry, National Public Service Platform for Standards Information: https://openstd.samr.gov.cn/bzgk/gb/std_list?p.p1=0&p.p90=circulation_date&p.p91=desc&p.p2=22239
  • Measures for the Administration of Classified Protection of Information Security (Gong Tong Zi [2007] No. 43), reprinted in the State Council Gazette: http://www.gov.cn/gongbao/content/2008/content_971263.htm
  • Sangfor classified-protection knowledge page: https://www.sangfor.com.cn/knowledge/classified-protection

title: Bringing Codex into Claude Code: A Dual-Engine AI Coding Workflow
html:
1. Introduction

Today OpenAI quietly released something new: codex-plugin-cc (https://github.com/openai/codex-plugin-cc/tree/main). In simple terms, this plugin lets you call OpenAI Codex directly from Claude Code to review code and fix bugs.

2. What Is Codex?

Before discussing the plugin, a brief introduction to Codex.

Codex is OpenAI's AI coding assistant for writing code, reviewing it, and fixing bugs. It belongs to the same category as Claude Code and Cursor, but is backed by OpenAI. Previously it mainly ran on its own; this plugin now lets you use it within Claude Code.

3. What Can the Plugin Do?

1. Code Review

/codex:review

One command asks Codex to review your current uncommitted changes. The review is read-only and does not modify your code.

It supports:

  • Reviewing current changes.
  • Reviewing the differences between a branch and main.
  • Running in the background without blocking your work.

2. Adversarial Review

/codex:adversarial-review challenge whether the caching design is right

This is one of the features I find especially interesting.

A normal review looks for bugs. An adversarial review also challenges your design decisions:

  • Does this design really make sense?
  • Is there a better approach?
  • What trade-offs are involved?

It is like inviting a deliberately skeptical reviewer to focus on the weaknesses in your design.

3. Delegating Tasks

/codex:rescue investigate why the tests are failing /codex:rescue fix the failing test

Ask Codex directly to investigate a problem and attempt a fix.

You can specify a model:

  • -model spark selects the latest, most capable model described in this article.
  • -model gpt-5.4-mini selects a smaller, faster model.
  • -effort medium controls the level of effort.

4. Automated Review Gates

/codex:setup --enable-review-gate

With this enabled, Claude Code automatically triggers a Codex review whenever you are ready to ship. If the review finds problems, shipping is blocked.

This is useful for teams that want every code submission reviewed.

4. Technical Implementation

The plugin's stack is straightforward:

  • Invocation: Calls the Codex service through the local @openai/codex CLI.
  • Authentication: Reuses a Codex account without requiring a separate login.
  • Configuration: Supports user-level ~/.codex/config.toml settings and project-level configuration.

In other words, if Codex is already installed locally, the plugin is ready to use.

5. Installation

Prerequisites:

Node.js 18.18+ and a Codex account, using either a ChatGPT subscription or an API key.

Add the marketplace in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add openai/codex-plugin-cc

Install the plugin:

/plugin install codex@openai-codex

Reload the plugin:

/reload-plugins

Check Codex. If it is missing and npm is available, this can install it for you:

/codex:setup

6. Summary

The Codex Plugin for Claude Code essentially connects two AI coding tools:

  • Claude Code: Everyday programming and interactive conversation.
  • Codex: Focused code review and repairs.

One emphasizes interaction, the other review. Together they provide a complete coding-and-review workflow.

If you already use both tools, the plugin is worth trying.

title: Beyond Feishu CLI: Developer Command-Line Tools You May Not Know
html:
How many tools have quietly moved their core capabilities into the command line?

CLI tools once seemed mostly confined to programmers' local toolboxes: finding files, running scripts, sending requests, and deploying services. Now their reach is expanding rapidly. Feishu connects messaging, calendars, documents, and agent workflows through the command line; GitHub manages PRs and issues through a CLI; cloud providers expose servers, databases, and storage; and AI tools are also entering the terminal as CLIs.

That raises an interesting question: beyond Feishu CLI, which potentially unfamiliar CLI tools have already become important?

Viewed more broadly, a CLI is no longer merely a place for programmers to type commands. It is a common interface for modern software engineering, connecting collaboration platforms, cloud services, AI models, containers, CI/CD, security scanning, and productivity tools. Its value grows further in the AI agent era: to accomplish real engineering tasks, agents need stable, automatable, composable command-line tools.

awesome-cli (https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/awesome-cli) collects high-quality CLIs for enterprise collaboration, cloud services, AI/LLMs, file processing, network debugging, containers and K8s, IaC, security scanning, and developer productivity—all official tools or projects with over 10,000 GitHub stars. It helps developers and AI agents perform engineering tasks through the command line. More than a list, it maps a modern engineering-tool ecosystem for developers and agents.

The CLI as a common interface for modern engineering

Command-line tools have long been considered developers' productivity power tools. Whether searching files, processing JSON, managing cloud resources, deploying applications, or scanning security risks, their lightweight, composable, scriptable nature makes them one of engineering's most stable infrastructure layers.

As AI agents enter software engineering workflows, that value is growing again.

For developers, the CLI provides efficient access to operating systems and engineering environments. For AI agents, it is an execution interface to real toolchains. An agent limited to generating suggestions has limited capability. With access to CLIs for GitHub, cloud platforms, CI/CD, databases, security scanning, and file processing, it can participate in the complete engineering process: requirements analysis, code changes, testing, deployment, and troubleshooting.

Generality is a major reason CLIs endure.

Graphical interfaces suit human browsing and clicking; APIs suit integration between programs. CLIs sit between them: people can use them directly, while scripts, CI/CD systems, and AI agents can invoke them too. They naturally support automation, provide clear inputs and outputs, compose easily, and lend themselves to standardized workflows.

Developers can use GitHub CLI to inspect issues, create pull requests, and trigger workflows; AWS CLI, Alibaba Cloud CLI, and Tencent Cloud CLI to manage cloud resources; Terraform or OpenTofu to declare and change infrastructure; and Trivy, Gitleaks, and TruffleHog to scan images, code, and leaked secrets. Operations once scattered across platforms and consoles share a single command-line interface.

That common interface becomes even more important with AI agents. Rather than understanding every platform's complex GUI, an agent needs to understand commands, parameters, outputs, and errors to connect tools into more sophisticated engineering workflows.

Collaboration CLIs: Bringing engineering communication into automation

Modern software development begins with collaboration. Code, requirements, defects, reviews, releases, and documentation are often spread across multiple platforms.

GitHub CLI and GitLab CLI are leading examples among international collaboration platforms. They let developers manage pull requests, merge requests, issues, pipelines, and workflows directly in the terminal. Jira CLI extends this to task management and defect tracking, reducing browser switching.

In Chinese enterprises, platforms such as Feishu, DingTalk, and WeCom are also offering or exploring CLI capabilities. Messaging, calendars, documents, approvals, meetings, and organizational collaboration can therefore enter automated workflows. For AI agents, these tools are particularly important because they connect to the team's collaboration itself, beyond its repositories.

An engineering agent might modify code, create a branch from an issue, implement the change, submit a PR, produce release notes, and synchronize the result to the team's collaboration platform. Collaboration CLIs underpin that process.

Cloud-service CLIs: From console clicks to orchestrated infrastructure

Cloud services are among the most mature areas of the CLI ecosystem.

AWS CLI, Alibaba Cloud CLI, Tencent Cloud CLI, Huawei Cloud KooCLI, JD Cloud CLI, Volcengine CLI, and others cover compute, storage, networking, databases, permissions, monitoring, and many other cloud capabilities. Operations once performed in consoles can now run from the command line and become scripts, CI/CD steps, or agent workflows.

The change is clear: cloud resource management moves from manual clicking to an engineering process that is recorded, reproducible, and auditable.

For enterprises, CLI-based cloud management reduces repetitive work and human error while integrating with permissions, release, and security systems. For agents, cloud CLIs provide direct infrastructure access. Naturally, access control, audit logs, and security boundaries become more important as well.

AI CLIs: Large models enter the terminal

AI tools themselves are becoming command-line tools.

Ollama lets developers run large language models locally for private deployments, offline use, or low latency. Simon Willison's llm tool provides a general LLM command-line interface, bringing different models into terminal workflows. Chinese providers are also releasing AI CLIs for developers and agents, including Volcengine veCLI and Tencent AI CLI.

These tools turn model invocation from something confined to a web chat or application feature into a composable command-line capability.

For example, developers can pipe logs to a model to summarize failures, send code diffs for review suggestions, or extract summaries from document excerpts. Once available through a CLI, AI can combine with traditional tools such as jq, rg, fzf, git, curl, kubectl to create new development practices.

File-processing CLIs: The foundation of developer productivity

While cloud and collaboration CLIs connect external systems, file-processing tools connect the local engineering environment developers face every day.

ripgrep, fd, fzf, bat, jq, yq and similar tools are fundamental components of modern command-line workflows. Their tasks seem simple: searching text, finding files, previewing content, and processing JSON or YAML. Yet these are prerequisites for understanding and working with large codebases.

They matter equally to AI agents. Agents need to search code, locate configuration, read logs, parse structured data, and select relevant information. High-quality file CLIs help agents understand project context faster and more accurately, reducing unnecessary scans and mistaken conclusions.

File-processing tools improve both human productivity and agents' ability to execute engineering work.

Network and API CLIs: The front line of service debugging

Network and API debugging are frequent tasks in backend development, microservices, and platform engineering.

hurl can describe and test HTTP requests in plain-text files, making API verification suitable for version control.grpcurl provides a curl-like debugging experience for gRPC services.mitmproxy supports HTTPS proxying and traffic analysis to investigate requests, responses, authentication, and data-transfer problems.

Together these tools form the front line of service debugging. Compared with graphical API tools, CLIs fit more easily into automated tests, continuous integration, and troubleshooting scripts.

For AI agents, network and API CLIs allow actual requests, response observation, and hypothesis testing, beyond merely inferring behavior from code. They are essential for engineering agents to evolve from coding assistants into debugging assistants.

Containers, Kubernetes, and CI/CD CLIs: The core of modern delivery

Modern application delivery depends heavily on containers, Kubernetes, and CI/CD, fields built almost naturally around CLIs.

kubectl is the de facto interface to Kubernetes; helm packages and releases Kubernetes applications; kubectx helps developers switch quickly between cluster contexts and namespaces; dive analyzes Docker image layers to optimize image size and investigate build issues.

In CI/CD, act runs GitHub Actions locally; ArgoCD supports GitOps continuous delivery; Dagger and Earthly provide more programmable, reproducible builds and pipelines.

These tools transform delivery from manual steps on one machine into declarative, executable, verifiable pipelines. Agents invoking these CLIs can analyze build failures, repair pipelines, inspect deployment state, and even perform prerelease verification under controlled permissions.

IaC and security CLIs: Addressing risk earlier

Infrastructure as code and security scanning are two particularly automation-friendly areas of the CLI ecosystem.

Terraform and OpenTofu let infrastructure changes be managed, reviewed, and rolled back like code. Infracost estimates cloud costs before changes, exposing their impact during pull-request review. Trivy, Gitleaks, and TruffleHog cover container security, dependency risk, code scanning, and leaked-secret detection.

Their shared value is moving risk control earlier.

Many security and cost problems used to surface only after release. They can now be detected automatically when committing code, building images, creating PRs, or before deployment. Enterprises gain more consistent delivery quality; agents can verify risks during execution as well as completing tasks.

Productivity and shell enhancements: Modernizing the command line

The CLI ecosystem cares about everyday developer experience as well as large systems.

just and task offer modern alternatives to traditional Makefile task execution; hyperfine benchmarks commands; navi and tldr reduce the burden of remembering complex commands; direnv automatically loads project-level environment variables; zoxide, atuin, eza, delta improve directory navigation, history search, file listings, and git diff respectively.

These seemingly scattered tools point to one trend: the command line is evolving from a basic black-and-white entry point into a modern, customizable, intelligent development environment.

Combined, they turn the terminal into an engineering workbench for search, navigation, debugging, analysis, deployment, and collaboration, beyond simply executing commands.

The CLI will become more valuable in the AI agent era

For human developers, the CLI's value is efficiency. For AI agents, it is the ability to execute.

Agents must operate real engineering systems beyond offering textual advice. They need to read files, search code, call APIs, run tests, manage issues, check CI, scan risks, deploy services, and synchronize collaboration platforms. The best interface is often a CLI already proven throughout engineering practice, rather than a webpage or an isolated API.

An important future criterion for whether a tool suits AI agents may therefore be whether it offers a stable, clear, automatable command-line interface.

For vendors, a CLI may become a critical gateway for agents into their ecosystem, beyond an advanced-user accessory. For development teams, organizing and standardizing internal CLIs will also underpin agent-native engineering systems.

Finally

awesome-cli (https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/awesome-cli) maps the modern developer CLI ecosystem, rather than merely collecting tools.

From enterprise collaboration to cloud services, AI to file processing, network debugging to Kubernetes, CI/CD to security scanning, and shell enhancements, CLIs now span almost every stage of software engineering. They improve individual productivity, support team automation, and will increasingly bridge agents with real engineering systems.

Future engineering will happen beyond IDEs and web consoles. More capabilities will settle into command-line tools shared by people, scripts, pipelines, and AI agents.

Understanding the CLI ecosystem means understanding the automation foundation of modern software engineering.

title: Self-Hosting Supabase with Docker in Five Minutes
html:
Original length: 428 Chinese characters; approximately 3 minutes to read.

Introduction

Supabase is an open-source alternative to Firebase, providing a database, authentication, storage, edge functions, and more.

The official Docker deployment lets you get it running locally in minutes.

1. Install Docker Desktop

If you do not have Docker Desktop, download it first:

👉 https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop

After installation, make sure Docker is running.

2. Clone the Supabase Repository


git clone https://github.com/supabase/supabase.git
cd supabase/docker

Copy the configuration file:


cp .env.example .env

3. Configure Dashboard Access

Open .env in vim or your preferred editor and find the Access to Dashboard section:

  DASHBOARD_USERNAME=username
  DASHBOARD_PASSWORD=pwd

Replace the values with your own username and password.

4. Start the Services

  docker compose up -d

The first startup downloads container images and takes a few minutes.

5. Open Supabase

Once startup is complete:

ServiceAddress
Dashboardhttp://localhost:8000
APIhttp://localhost:8000/rest/v1/
Studiohttp://localhost:8000/studio/

Sign in to the dashboard with the credentials you just configured.

6. Explore Supabase

The self-hosted version provides:

  • 📊 PostgreSQL database — full PostgreSQL access.
  • 🔐 User authentication — built-in email and social sign-in.
  • 📁 File storage — an object-storage service.
  • ⚡️ Edge functions — Deno / Edge Functions.
  • 📡 Realtime subscriptions — real-time data synchronization.

7. External Access (Advanced)

A self-hosted Supabase instance is accessible locally by default. To access it from outside your network, you can set up a tunnel:

  • Use a tool such as Cloudflare Tunnel, frp, or cpolar.
  • Expose local port 8000 through a public endpoint.
  • You can then access your Supabase service from anywhere.

Common Commands

Stop the Services

docker compose down

Restart the Services

docker compose restart

View Logs

docker compose logs -f

Suitable Uses

  • ✅ Local development and testing.
  • ✅ Private deployment.
  • ✅ Learning and research.
  • ⚠️ Not recommended for production in this guide; the official cloud service is suggested instead.

title: Eino ADK: An Agent Runtime for Go
html:
When building applications that can call tools, cancel generation, and expand to multiple Agents, calling an LLM API is not enough. You also need an Agent runtime to handle the ReAct loop, event streams, middleware, and collaboration orchestration.

Eino ADK (Agent Development Kit) is precisely that layer.

It is the Go-oriented Agent / Multi-Agent development kit in the open-source Eino ecosystem from ByteDance's CloudWeGo.

In one sentence:

It is not “another LLM SDK,” but an Agent runtime: who handles reasoning, who performs actions, how events stream out, where middleware attaches, and how multiple Agents collaborate.

What Eino and ADK Each Handle

Eino is a Go-first framework for developing LLM applications, covering infrastructure such as model adapters, component orchestration (Graph / Chain), tools, and callbacks.

ADK is Eino's dedicated Agent layer. Its design draws on abstractions for Agents and collaboration found in frameworks such as Google ADK. Core capabilities include:

  • A unified Agent interface for units that can run a turn and emit events
  • Event-driven output instead of returning one large string at once
  • Composable collaboration primitives: sequential, parallel, loop, Supervisor, Plan-Execute, and more
  • Runner as the entry point for a single execution, with runtime capabilities including streaming, cancellation, and interruption

The division of responsibilities is:

Eino handles components and the orchestration foundation; ADK handles how autonomous decision-making Agents run.

The following official diagram shows that Eino is not an isolated runtime library, but an ecosystem spanning AI application design through operations.

Read the diagram along three lines:

  1. 1. The three central layers form the main development stack: the red bottom layer is Eino (core types, component definitions, compose / callback / streaming, key Flows, and ADK); the purple middle layer is Eino-Ext (official component implementations, callbacks, third-party integrations); the yellow top layer is User Code (custom components, callbacks, Lambda).
  2. 2. The green Eino Examples on the left aligns with “Research & Design”: start from examples rather than guessing APIs in an empty project.
  3. 3. Devops Tooling at the top (visual orchestration, code generation, visual debugging, Telemetry) and Integrated 3rd-party platforms on the right (Tracing / Hosting / Evaluation) cover debugging and deployment operations respectively.

For application developers, most daily work happens in the middle column:Build on Eino's abstractions, use ready-made Eino-Ext implementations, and add your own logic in User Code. ADK is embedded in the Eino core at the bottom.

A more detailed official diagram shows the framework's internal layers:



On the left is Eino itself. From bottom to top, roughly:

  • Schema / Callbacks: Message, Document, StreamReader / StreamWriter, ToolInfo, plus callback Handler / Inject / Trigger
  • Components: Component abstractions—type definitions, inputs and outputs, Call Option, streaming paradigms, Callback Info
  • Compose: Orchestration engines (pregel / dag) and APIs (Graph / Chain / Workflow), containing Flows such as ReAct and building blocks including node, edge, branch, stream, interrupt & checkpoint
  • ADK (top layer): Higher-level abstractions for Agents—ChatModelAgent, WorkflowAgent, Agent Tool / Transfer / Middleware, Interrupt Resume; middleware such as FileSystem and Context Engineer; prebuilt forms such as DeepAgents, Supervisor, and PlanExecute

On the right is Eino-Ext: Devops Tooling, various Component Implementations (Chat Model, Retriever, Tool, Prompt, etc.), and Callback Handlers such as Tracing / Metrics. The arrows make the relationship clear:Ext implements the abstractions on the left instead of introducing a separate protocol.

Together, the two diagrams can be summarized as follows:

The lifecycle diagram explains which development stages the Eino ecosystem covers; the layered diagram explains where ADK sits in the framework and what supports it.

Why Not Call the Model Directly?

When calling ChatModel directly, the application usually implements the ReAct loop (Reason → Act → Observe) itself:

拼 messages → 调模型 → 有 tool_calls 就执行工具 → 再调模型 → …

ADK packages this loop into framework primitives. Compare:

  • Direct model calls: Loop logic lives in application code; streaming and cancellation require manual integration; context compression / Skills / retries can intrude into the main flow; expanding to multiple Agents requires broader changes.
  • Using ADK: ChatModelAgent has a built-in ReAct Loop; Runner + context provide unified streaming and cancellation; Middleware attaches to the loop lifecycle; collaborative Agents / DeepAgents can be added incrementally.

Architecturally, making the Agent the execution unit instead of a bare model call makes it easier to inject Tools and attach Skill Middleware later, without simultaneously redesigning the chat UI, message tables, and model catalog.

The layered diagram also clarifies this: Compose already has a ReAct Flow; ADK builds on it with ready-to-use Agent primitives, so application developers need not rewrite the entire loop in User Code.

Four Core Concepts

The ADK layer in the architecture diagram boils down to the following parts.

1. ChatModelAgent: The Smallest Autonomous Decision-Making Unit

Its structure can be summarized as:

ChatModel（推理）
  + Tools（行动）
  + Instruction（约束）
  + ReAct Loop（决定何时推理、何时调用工具）

Suitable for scenarios with open-ended problem boundaries where the model needs to decide the next action.

In the official division of responsibilities, deterministic orchestration belongs more naturally to Graph / Chain / Workflow in Compose; autonomous decision-making belongs more naturally to ChatModelAgent in ADK.

2. Runner: The Entry Point for a Single Execution

Runner is the entry point for one Agent run. Typical usage: place ChatModelAgent in the configuration, then call Query / Run and consume the event stream.

It handles “this run”: whether to stream, how to emit events, and how to coordinate cancellation.

Session persistence is outside Runner's responsibilities; storing sessions and messages remains the application's job.

3. Middleware: Inject Behavior at Points in the Loop

This corresponds to ADK's Middlewares, such as FileSystem and Context Engineer, and Agent Middleware in the diagram.

Middleware preserves the ReAct “reason → act → observe” structure while injecting behavior at key points, such as:

  • Compress context before calling the model
  • Dynamically inject tools
  • Check tool-call permissions
  • Retry failures / switch to a fallback model
  • Skills: load skill instructions into the current conversation on demand

Skill capabilities can be implemented through skill middleware attached to ChatModelAgent, without creating another Agent protocol.

4. Collaboration and Prebuilt Forms

These correspond to Prebuilt and collaboration-related primitives in the diagram:

  • Workflow Agents: Deterministic flows such as Sequential / Parallel / Loop
  • Supervisor / Plan-Execute: Multi-Agent collaboration patterns
  • DeepAgents: Planning, file systems, sub-Agent delegation, and more
  • Agent Tool / Agent Transfer: Wrap an Agent as a tool, or transfer control between Agents
  • Interrupt / Resume / Checkpoint: Human-in-the-loop collaboration and checkpoint recovery

ADK addresses Agent system design, beyond merely wrapping chat completion.

Responsibility Boundaries in Practice

One common layering looks like this:

产品界面 / API
  → 业务服务（会话编排、鉴权、计费、附件）
  → 数据库（会话与消息的事实源）
  → Agent 运行时（Eino ChatModelAgent + Runner）
  → 模型网关

ADK handles “how this Agent turn executes”; it does not handle “where conversation facts are stored.”

In the lifecycle diagram, Eino / Eino-Ext / ADK fall under Development & Debugging; accounts, orders, billing, and pages remain part of User Code and business systems. In the layered diagram, concrete implementations such as Chat Model come from Eino-Ext; ADK consumes only the Components abstractions.

Pay attention to these boundaries in implementation:

  1. 1. Handlers do not call ChatModel directly; consistently go through Agent + Runner
  2. 2. Restore multi-turn context from the application database, then convert it into framework message structures; avoid using internal framework objects as a long-term storage protocol
  3. 3. Propagate cancellation signals through context so both the Agent and upstream model requests can stop
  4. 4. Separate streaming events from final persisted facts: the frontend consumes increments; the database is authoritative for persistence
  5. 5. Filter event types: ADK events may contain tool-related payloads; retain only assistant-visible output before writing the chat body

When It Fits—and When It Does Not

Good fits:

  • You need ReAct, Tools, Skills, or middleware extensions
  • The execution layer must be decoupled from session storage, authentication, and billing
  • Your stack is Go, and you want Eino's model adapters and component ecosystem
  • You need room to expand into multiple Agents or human-in-the-loop collaboration

Poor fits or lower priority:

  • Pure one-shot completion, with no tools or expected extensions → call ChatModel directly
  • Fully deterministic flow with no model deciding the next step → Graph / conventional orchestration is more suitable
  • Your main stack is not Go, or you already have a mature Agent framework → no need to change stacks just for ADK

Choose based on whether the boundaries fit, not on an abstract ranking of frameworks.

References

  • Eino ADK overview: https://www.cloudwego.io/zh/docs/eino/core_modules/eino_adk/
  • Agent Quickstart: https://www.cloudwego.io/zh/docs/eino/core_modules/eino_adk/agent_quickstart/
  • Eino overview (including architecture diagrams): https://www.cloudwego.io/zh/docs/eino/overview/

title: Full-Stack Image Segmentation with SAM 2.1, V2: Docker Deployment and Export
html:
Original length: 692 Chinese characters; approximately 4 minutes to read.

FastSAM-Demo is an interactive image-segmentation web application built on Meta SAM 2.1. Upload an image and click a target region to segment it in real time. This update adds one-command Docker deployment and three export modes.

Use cases:

  • Content creation and design: Quickly cut out subjects, replace backgrounds, and extract objects without professional Photoshop skills.
  • Furniture e-commerce: Upload a product photo, isolate the furniture in one click, remove distracting backgrounds, and create white-background or composite scene assets to improve product imagery.
  • Data annotation: Generate mask annotations in batches for machine-learning tasks such as object detection and instance segmentation.
  • Research and teaching: Demonstrate SAM 2.1, assess segmentation quality, and quickly produce figures for papers.
  • Prototyping: Add segmentation to your own image-processing pipeline and quickly validate a proof of concept.
  • Private local processing: Run entirely offline, including in settings with data-compliance requirements such as medical imaging and industrial quality inspection.

🐳 New: Docker Deployment

One-command Docker deployment is now supported. There is no need to configure Python environments or Node versions manually, or resolve dependency conflicts before getting started.

Use cases:

  • Quickly prepare a demo on a new machine or server.
  • Standardize development and test environments across a team to avoid “it works on my machine.”
  • Integrate into CI/CD pipelines and get started in restricted environments where Python or Node cannot be configured directly.

New Files

FileDescription
backend/DockerfilePython 3.11 + uv + FastAPI + SAM 2.1
frontend/DockerfileNode 20 + Next.js 15 standalone mode
docker-compose.ymlService orchestration on ports 3001/8001
.dockerignoreExcludes unrelated files to reduce image size

Startup Command

docker-compose up --build
  • Frontend: http://localhost:3001
  • Backend: http://localhost:8001

The backend uses uv for dependency management, with significantly faster installation than pip. The frontend uses Next.js 15 standalone builds for a smaller image and faster startup.

📥 New: Export

After segmentation, you can now export the results directly as PNG images in three modes for different downstream uses.

ModeDescriptionTypical uses
OriginalThe uploaded source imageArchiving and comparison
OverlayOriginal image with colored masks at 50% opacityDemos, annotation review, and paper figures
Mask onlyMasks on a black backgroundBackground replacement, object detection, and dataset creation
  • Availability: The Export button appears when a segmentation result is available.
  • Mask colors: Red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, purple, and pink cycle through eight colors to distinguish multiple objects automatically.
  • Export format: PNG (lossless).
  • Exported overlay image
  • Exported mask-only image

✍️ Closing Thoughts

Both changes serve the same goal: making FastSAM-Demo easier to use. Docker lowers the barrier to getting it running; export completes the final step of using its results elsewhere.

The project is fully open source. Stars, forks, and issues are welcome.

Project repository: https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/FastSAM-Demo
