title: FastSAM-Demo/V3: Interactive Image Segmentation with SAM 2.1 and a Go Gateway
html:
An open-source click-to-segment web application: upload an image and click an object to cut it out.
The frontend uses Next.js, the backend uses FastAPI + SAM 2.1, and a custom Go inference gateway between them provides sticky routing and horizontal scaling.

GitHub: https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/FastSAM-Demo
License: MIT

What the project looks like

Open the page → drag in an image → click an object → see the segmentation highlighted in real time. Multiple clicks select multiple objects with different colored overlays. Export the original image, the overlay, or masks only.

The model is Meta's SAM 2.1 (Segment Anything Model 2), open-sourced under Apache 2.0. Weights download directly without an application. The tiny version is as small as 39 MB and runs on a CPU; the 224 MB large version flies on a GPU.

This update: From one process to multiple workers and a Go gateway

The project originally connected Next.js directly to a single FastAPI process. This refactoring inserts a Go inference gateway between frontend and backend, upgrading it to horizontally scaled workers with business-aware routing.

Before and after

旧:  浏览器  ──▶  FastAPI 单进程  ──▶  SAM 2.1

新:  浏览器  ──▶  Go Gateway (:8080)  ──┬──▶  FastAPI worker-0  ──▶  SAM 2.1
                                       └──▶  FastAPI worker-1  ──▶  SAM 2.1
                                       (可水平扩展到 N 个)

Why this layer is needed

The central motivation is straightforward: sticky routing, rather than high concurrency.

SAM 2.1 inference has two steps:

  • set_image() computes image embeddings: 0.5–3 seconds (slow, compute-intensive)
  • predict() produces masks: 20–100 milliseconds (fast, decoder only)

Uploading computes the embedding and caches it in one worker's memory. Every later click on that image must return to the same worker to hit the cache; otherwise it requires recomputation, roughly 30 times slower, or produces an error.

Routing by image_id operates at the business level:

  • nginx's ip_hash / hash $cookie_xxx cannot do this—the sticky key lives in the multipart upload response's JSON body
  • Python cannot handle it alone either: separate processes cannot see each other's state

So I added a Go gateway. Its httputil.ReverseProxy.ModifyResponse hook intercepts response JSON, extracts image_id into a session table, and uses image_id to look up the worker for subsequent segmentation requests. A dozen or so lines solve the problem.

What the gateway does

Seven subpackages and just over a thousand lines of Go handle:

CapabilityImplementation
Sticky routingimage_id → worker_id session table with TTL and a background sweeper
Concurrency controlOne bounded channel and N consumer goroutines per worker; immediate 429 when full
Load balancingNew sessions go to the healthy worker with the shortest queue
Unhealthy worker removalPeriodically ping /health; consecutive failures remove the worker and clear its sessions, while consecutive successes restore it
Cold-start protectionWorkers start unhealthy and receive traffic only after passing probes
Cross-service tracingX-Request-Id generated at entry → forwarded by ReverseProxy → logged by the backend
Graceful shutdownAfter SIGTERM, stop accepting connections and wait for in-flight requests
ObservabilitySeven Prometheus metrics plus zerolog structured logging

Two layers of concurrency protection

Go does not handle everything. Python retains a fallback asyncio.Semaphore layer so even a misconfigured gateway concurrency limit cannot exhaust GPU memory. It is a small detail that keeps the system safe under configuration errors.

Frontend-friendly error semantics

Status codeMeaningFrontend action
200SuccessNormal processing
410image_id expired: worker restart, TTL expiry, or removalAutomatically upload the image again
429Worker queue fullBack off and retry according to Retry-After
503No available workersWait for health checks to restore availability

The frontend's lib/api.ts implements these semantics so network fluctuations and backend restarts are invisible to users.

Seven Prometheus metrics

/metrics connects directly to Prometheus. Key metrics:

MetricPurpose
gateway_queue_depthCurrent queue depth per worker—the basis for HPA scaling
gateway_inflightRunning inferences per worker
gateway_worker_healthyHealth state per worker
gateway_session_table_sizeCurrent active session count
gateway_request_duration_secondsP50/P95/P99 latency distribution
gateway_requests_totalQPS and error rate by route + status
gateway_rejections_totalRejection reasons: queue_full / unhealthy / session_missing / upstream_error

With Grafana connected, the health of the whole system is visible at a glance.

Current capabilities

Features

  • Drag-and-drop upload + real-time Canvas rendering
  • Click-to-segment, with millisecond responses when the embedding cache is hit
  • Multiple-object management, different colored overlays, and list-based addition and removal
  • Three export modes: Original image / overlay / masks only
  • Horizontal scaling + automatic recovery, with worker failures invisible to users
  • RLE-compressed mask transmission, achieving over 98% compression

Technology stack

LayerTechnology
FrontendNext.js 15 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS v4 + Framer Motion
GatewayGo 1.22 + chi + zerolog + Prometheus client
BackendFastAPI + Pydantic + uv + asyncio
ModelSAM 2.1 Hiera (tiny 39M / small 46M / base+ 81M / large 224M)
Package managementgo mod + uv + npm
DeploymentOne-command docker-compose startup / local multiworker setup with start.sh

Core data flow

upload:
  前端 ──multipart──▶ Gateway
                       ├─ 选最低负载 worker
                       ├─ ReverseProxy 流式转发(不读进 Gateway 内存)
                       ├─ 拦响应 JSON 截 image_id
                       └─ sessions.Put(image_id, worker_id)
                          │
                          └──▶ FastAPI ──▶ SAM 2.1 set_image() 缓存 embedding

segment:
  前端 ──{image_id, points}──▶ Gateway
                                ├─ 按 image_id 查会话表 → 命中粘性 worker
                                └─ 不命中返 410 → 前端自动重新上传
                                   │
                                   └──▶ 同一 worker ──▶ predict() 复用 embedding

Running in five minutes

Docker (recommended)

git clone https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/FastSAM-Demo.git
cd FastSAM-Demo

# 下载模型权重(只需一次)
mkdir -p models
wget -O models/sam2.1_hiera_tiny.pt \
  https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/segment_anything_2/092824/sam2.1_hiera_tiny.pt

docker-compose up --build

Open http://localhost:3001 to use it.

Local development

Requires Go 1.22+, Python 3.10+ with uv, and Node 18+.

./start.sh

Automatically starts two backends (:8000 / :8002), the gateway (:8080), and frontend (:3000).

Verifying the multiworker path

./scripts/verify-multiworker.sh

Automatically performs eight uploads to verify load balancing and sticky routing. Uploads should be evenly distributed between the two workers, and all segmentation requests for the same image_id should always reach the same worker.

What comes next

The project currently segments individual images, but the architecture and model offer several directions for expansion. The following roadmap is open to contributions.

Video segmentation

SAM 2.1's main advantage over SAM 1 / MobileSAM is video support through temporal propagation with memory attention. The current version does not use it. Adding this capability would give a compelling answer to why the project chose SAM 2.1.

Required technical work:

  • Introduce SAM2VideoPredictor in the backend for frame-by-frame inference and temporal propagation
  • Add long-running tasks to the gateway: POST to obtain task_id → progress over WebSocket → fetch results on completion
  • Build a frontend timeline, keyframe prompts, and per-frame mask overlays

Text-prompt segmentation: Grounding DINO + SAM

Upgrade interaction from clicking to typing: enter “cat,” let Grounding DINO detect bounding boxes, and have SAM generate masks. This popular open-vocabulary segmentation combination would move the project from single-modal to multimodal.

A data-annotation tool

Add batch uploads, annotation export (COCO / YOLO / Pascal VOC), manual mask editing, undo/redo, and user accounts to turn the demo into a small annotation tool people can actually use.

Making full use of the Go gateway

  • Move SessionTable to Redis: Make the gateway stateless, supporting multiple instances and rolling upgrades without lost sessions
  • Automatic scaling with Kubernetes HPA: Use gateway_queue_depth as a custom metric to scale GPU workers by queue depth
  • Replace configuration-based discovery with service discovery: List-watch Kubernetes endpoints so worker changes need no configuration edits

Other directions to explore

  • Real-time WebSocket segmentation, with local prediction and background correction while dragging continuously
  • Hot-switch models at runtime among tiny / small / base+ / large
  • iOS / Android clients using Expo + React Native
  • Grafana dashboards + alert rules

Project structure

FastSAM-Demo/
├── gateway/              # Go 推理网关
│   ├── cmd/gateway/      # main 入口
│   ├── internal/         # config / pool / session / health / handler / middleware / metrics
│   ├── configs/          # gateway.yaml(容器形态)/ gateway.dev.yaml(本地形态)
│   └── Dockerfile
├── backend/              # FastAPI 后端(可水平扩展)
│   ├── app/              # routers / services / schemas / utils
│   └── pyproject.toml    # uv 依赖
├── frontend/             # Next.js 前端
│   ├── src/
│   │   ├── app/          # App Router 页面
│   │   ├── components/   # UI 组件
│   │   ├── hooks/        # useSegmentation(含 410/429 自动恢复)
│   │   ├── lib/          # API 封装 + mask 渲染
│   │   └── types/        # TS 类型
├── docs/                 # 完整技术文档
├── scripts/              # 验证脚本(verify-multiworker.sh 等)
├── docker-compose.yml    # 2 backend + gateway + frontend
└── start.sh              # 一键本地启动

Documentation

Complete documentation is in the docs/ directory:

DocumentDescription
docs/architecture.mdSystem architecture, technology choices, and data-flow diagrams
gateway/README.mdGateway configuration, routing, and error semantics
docs/go/phase1.md & phase2.mdNotes on phased implementation of the Go gateway
docs/api.mdDetailed RESTful API reference, including gateway error codes
docs/model.mdSAM 2.1 architecture, model comparisons, and performance benchmarks
docs/quickstart.mdFive-minute quick start
docs/deployment.mdThree deployment options: local / Colab / Docker
docs/troubleshooting.mdFrequently asked questions and solutions

Final thoughts

This project started as a way to test SAM 2.1's interactive web experience. Along the way, I ended up refactoring the entire backend architecture.

I am sharing it to:

  • Give people building image segmentation a ready-to-use starting template
  • Provide a concrete example for anyone considering horizontal scaling for Python inference services—nginx really cannot handle this sticky-routing requirement
  • Gather feedback and issues to keep improving the architecture

Stars, forks, PRs, and issues are welcome, as is criticism—especially of the Go gateway. I would love to hear more elegant implementation ideas.

Repository:https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/FastSAM-Demo

title: Still Watching Monitors Manually? A Complete Guide to Feishu Webhook Alerts
html:
1. Why use a Feishu bot for alerts?

Team information is often scattered across systems: PR updates in repositories, service failures in monitoring platforms, builds in CI/CD pipelines, and operations in security audit logs. If someone must log into each system to check, information arrives much less promptly.

Through webhooks, a Feishu bot brings these separate event streams into one channel. It is easy to configure, requires no additional intermediary service, supports rich message cards, and fits naturally into team messaging. Once one person sets up the webhook, everyone in the group can receive updates in real time.

2. How webhooks work: One URL connects your systems

A custom Feishu bot is essentially an HTTP POST endpoint. Add a custom bot to a Feishu group, obtain its webhook address, and have any system capable of HTTP requests send messages there. JSON message bodies support plain text, rich text, cards, and other formats.

Any system that can call an external URL when an event happens can therefore connect to a Feishu bot. GitLab, Prometheus, Jenkins, Nacos, WAFs, and even your own scripts can produce messages.

3. Six practical scenarios

Scenario 1: GitLab collaboration updates

This is one of the most common integrations. Engineering teams produce many code changes daily, including merge request creation, approval, and merging, as well as code comments and triggered branch-protection rules.

Problems it solves: Prevent PRs from sitting unreviewed for hours and make reviews more transparent. When a PR merges into the main branch, testing and release staff can know immediately.

Configuration approach: In a GitLab project's Settings > Webhooks, enter the Feishu bot's webhook address and enable Merge Request events and Comment events. GitLab automatically sends event payloads. A simple relay, such as Nginx Lua, a Cloudflare Worker, or a lightweight custom service, can transform GitLab payloads into Feishu cards showing the PR title, author, changed-file count, and other key details.

Scenario 2: CI/CD pipeline results

Modern development depends heavily on automated pipelines, but build failures and deployment problems cannot wait until tomorrow's stand-up.

Problems it solves: Notify the responsible person immediately of build failures, announce version information after production deployment, and alert when nightly builds hang for too long.

Configuration approach: Jenkins can call the Feishu webhook directly through a Pipeline script's httpRequest step. GitLab CI can use after_script in .gitlab-ci.yml to send success or failure messages according to CI_JOB_STATUS. GitHub Actions can use community actions. Use green cards for success and red for failure, with build-log links for quick investigation.

Scenario 3: Production service alerts

When API latency spikes, error rates surge, disks fill up, or pods repeatedly restart, faster awareness means faster damage control.

Problems it solves: Deliver alerts from Prometheus, Zabbix, Nightingale, cloud monitoring, and similar platforms to the on-call group promptly, reducing mean time to repair (MTTR).

Configuration approach: With Prometheus Alertmanager, configure a webhook receiver pointing to your relay and map alert labels and annotations into Feishu messages. Classify severity: P0 alerts mention all on-call staff, P1 sends messages without mentions, and P2 aggregates low-priority alerts for scheduled delivery. Deduplicate and silence flapping alerts in the relay to avoid flooding the group with an alert storm.

Scenario 4: Security and audit events

Security events are often subtle and highly sensitive, requiring immediate awareness by security leads or managers.

Problems it solves: Detect unusual logins, such as from unexpected locations or outside working hours; sensitive permission changes, such as granting administrator roles or making repositories public; deletion of critical resources, such as production configurations; and high-frequency attacks blocked by a WAF.

Configuration approach: Most cloud ActionTrail and audit services support delivery to HTTP endpoints. Use a serverless function such as Alibaba Cloud Function Compute or AWS Lambda as a relay, filter event types, and forward to Feishu. For particularly sensitive events, send direct messages to designated people through the bot API as well as the group to ensure the responsible person sees them.

Scenario 5: Business-metric changes

Changes in business data deserve attention alongside technical metrics.

Problems it solves: Warn promptly when critical metrics fall unexpectedly, such as order volume or payment success rate; announce milestones, such as daily active users exceeding a threshold; and deliver completed reports proactively to the group.

Configuration approach: If your data platform supports scheduled queries and webhooks, such as Apache DolphinScheduler, Airflow, or a custom scheduler, decide whether to send a Feishu message from query results at task completion. For example, an Airflow PythonOperator can use requests to post a card summarizing yesterday's GMV. You can also point a BI system's data-alert feature to the bot to send automatic report-anomaly notifications.

Scenario 6: Closing the operations-feedback loop

Beyond receiving alerts, a bot can report the results of operational actions.

Problems it solves: After you ask the bot in a Feishu group to restart a service or scale a cluster, it posts the result back so everyone can see that the action took effect.

Configuration approach: This requires both receiving commands and sending messages, so a webhook alone is insufficient. Build a lightweight bot service and register Feishu event subscriptions. When someone mentions the bot with a command, it parses and executes the action, then returns the result through a webhook or OpenAPI. This is particularly useful in on-call groups: actions leave a record and results remain visible.

4. Making alerts more effective

First, control noise. Not every event belongs in a group chat; excessive notifications teach people to ignore them. Define clear severity levels, send immediate messages only for events requiring prompt action, and put summaries in daily reports or scheduled updates.

Second, include context. A good alert says what happened, what is affected, whom to contact, and where to investigate. Add direct links to cards whenever possible to reduce navigation effort.

Third, account for timezones and on-call schedules. For distributed or rotating teams, combine the Feishu bot API with the roster so alerts mention only current on-call staff rather than disturbing everyone at night.

Fourth, plan fallback channels. Feishu is an external service and may experience latency or temporary outages. Keep SMS or phone calls as backups for the highest-priority alerts.

5. Conclusion

Feishu webhook bots are not universal solutions, but they provide a lightweight, efficient hub for team information. From repositories and monitoring to security audits and business data, they offer low-cost integration whenever a group needs to learn about something promptly.

The real value lies beyond technical configuration: event severity, message design, and team response mechanisms matter most. Establish clear collaboration rules, then automate them to turn alerts from interruptions into assistance.

Configuration tutorial: https://open.feishu.cn/community/articles/7271149634339422210

title: From Terminals to Monitoring: Four GitHub Productivity Tools Worth Keeping
html:
Introduction

Here are four productivity tools I recently found on GitHub. They are all free, open source, and lightweight. Rather than trying to do everything, they address small but frequent needs that developers cannot avoid: better terminals, clipboard management, keyboard and mouse statistics, and system monitoring. None is especially complicated on its own, but together they can noticeably improve everyday computer use.

1. WaveTerminal — A Terminal with Integrated AI

GitHub: https://github.com/wavetermdev/waveterm

In one sentence: a cross-platform terminal with built-in AI.

Core Features

  • 🤖 Wave AI: Reads terminal output and automatically analyzes problems.
  • 🔐 Persistent SSH: Reconnects after network interruptions, including server restarts.
  • 📁 Remote file editing: A built-in editor lets you edit server files directly.
  • 📄 File previews: Preview Markdown, images, videos, and PDFs in place.
  • 🔌 Multiple model options: OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, Ollama, and LM Studio.

Who It Is For

  • People who use a terminal and AI assistance every day.
  • People who frequently work on remote servers.

Installation

# macOS
brew install wave-terminal

# 或直接下载：https://www.waveterm.dev/download

2. Maccy — Clipboard Management

GitHub: https://github.com/p0deje/Maccy

In one sentence: a lightweight clipboard manager exclusively for macOS.

Core Features

  • ⌨️ Shortcut: Open it quickly with Shift + Command + C.
  • 🔍 Search: Find clipboard history by keyword.
  • 📌 Pinning: Keep frequently used clips pinned.
  • 🔒 Security: Ignores certain clipboard types marked confidential or temporary, and supports custom ignore rules.

Who It Is For

  • People who copy and paste frequently.
  • People who often switch between different pieces of content.

Installation

brew install maccy

3. keyStats — Keyboard and Mouse Statistics

GitHub: https://github.com/debugtheworldbot/keyStats

In one sentence: see how much you type every day.

Core Features

  • ⌨️ Keyboard statistics: Count daily keystrokes.
  • 🖱️ Mouse statistics: Track clicks, movement distance, and scroll distance.
  • 📊 Menu-bar display: See key metrics directly in the menu bar.
  • 🔄 Daily reset: Automatically clears the daily counters at midnight.

Who It Is For

  • People curious about their productivity.
  • People who want to quantify their work habits.

Installation

# macOS
brew tap debugtheworldbot/keystats
brew install keystats

# Windows
scoop bucket add keystats https://github.com/debugtheworldbot/scoop-keystats
scoop install keystats

4. Stats — System Monitoring

GitHub: https://github.com/exelban/stats

In one sentence: a system monitor in the macOS menu bar.

Core Features

  • 📈 CPU/GPU utilization.
  • 💾 Memory usage.
  • 💿 Disk usage.
  • 🌐 Network traffic.
  • 🔋 Battery level.
  • 🌡️ Sensor temperatures.

Who It Is For

  • People who would rather not open Activity Monitor.
  • People who need a live view of system status.

Installation

brew install stats

Summary

ToolPurposePlatform
WaveTerminalAI terminalmacOS / Linux / Windows
MaccyClipboard managementmacOS
keyStatsKeyboard and mouse statisticsmacOS / Windows
StatsSystem monitoringmacOS

All four tools are free and open source, easy to install, and light on memory.

Give them a try if you want to improve your workflow. 🚀

title: GitHub Weekly: Financial Agents, AI Swarms, and an Open-Source Terminal
html:
This week's GitHub Trending chart sends a clear signal:AI Agents are no longer just upgraded chatbots; they are moving into specific industries and developers' everyday tools.

Three projects represent three directions: Anthropic brings Agents into investment-banking workflows; Ruflo lets 100 Agents collaborate on code like a swarm; and Warp has open-sourced a terminal built for Agents.

What do they share? They no longer ask “Can AI be used?” They answer “How does AI fit into real work?”

1. anthropics/financial-services — Anthropic Builds Financial Agents Itself

⭐ 17.9k | Fork 2.3k

What Is It?

Anthropic's official open-source reference implementation of AI Agents for financial services. It is not a demo, but a collection of Agents, Skills, and data connectors you can install directly in Claude.

Its use cases are specific: investment banking (pitch decks, CIMs, M&A models), equity research (earnings analysis, morning meeting notes), private equity (due diligence, IC memos, portfolio management), wealth management (client reviews, rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting), and fund operations (GL reconciliation, month-end close).

What Problem Does It Solve?

Finance's pain point is not “We have no AI,” but “AI does not understand my workflow.”

An investment-banking analyst's routine includes pulling comps, building DCFs, modeling LBOs, and preparing pitch decks. These tasks are highly structured, but each step connects to different data sources, follows specific formats, and passes through specific approval processes.

This project breaks those workflows into:

LayerPurposeExample
AgentRun a workflow end to endPitch Agent, GL Reconciler
SkillsAn individual capability modulecomps-analysis, dcf-model
CommandsAn action explicitly triggered by the user/comps, /earnings, /ic-memo
ConnectorsMCP data sourcesFactSet, Morningstar, S&P Global

Why Is It Worth Watching?

First, this is Anthropic's first complete Agent solution for a specific industry. It is not a paper or a blog post; it is something you can use directly with claude plugin install.

Second, it demonstrates two new capabilities in the Claude ecosystem: Cowork (a collaborative plugin platform) and Managed Agents API (headless deployment). The same Agent definition can run in the Claude desktop app or be embedded into enterprise systems through an API.

Third, its 11 MCP data-source integrations—Daloopa, Morningstar, S&P Global, FactSet, Moody's, PitchBook, and others—cover most major Wall Street data vendors.

Who Is It For?

  • Fintech companies looking for best practices for AI Agents in finance
  • Enterprise AI teams seeking an architectural reference for decomposing Agents into Skills + Connectors
  • Developers interested in the Claude ecosystem (Cowork, Managed Agents)

One-Sentence Verdict

Anthropic is using this project to tell the market that Claude is more than a chat model: it is an Agent platform that can be embedded in enterprise workflows. Finance is only the first vertical.

2. ruvnet/ruflo — Give Claude Code a “Swarm Nervous System”

⭐ 48.1k | Fork 5.3k

What Is It?

A multi-Agent AI orchestration platform. Its main pitch: take Claude Code from “working solo” to “100+ Agents working together.”

With a single command, npx ruflo init, Claude Code gains swarm coordination, cross-session memory, self-learning, and federated communication for Agents collaborating across machines.

What Problem Does It Solve?

When used alone, each Claude Code session is isolated. There is no shared memory, task coordination, or background workers.

If you want several Agents to divide the work—one writing code, another tests, another reviewing, and another scanning for security issues—you have to orchestrate them yourself.

Ruflo turns that orchestration layer into infrastructure:

CapabilityClaude Code alone+ Ruflo
Agent collaborationIsolated, with no shared contextSwarm + shared memory + consensus mechanisms
MemoryCurrent session onlyHNSW vector memory with submillisecond retrieval
LearningStatic behaviorSONA self-learning and pattern matching
Task routingManual decisionsIntelligent routing (89% accuracy)
Background workersNone12 automatically triggered workers
LLM providersAnthropic onlyFive providers + failover

Technical Highlights

Federated communication is the most interesting part. It enables Agents on different machines and in different organizations to collaborate securely:

  • mTLS + ed25519 authentication
  • Automatic PII redaction for outbound messages (14 detected types)
  • Behavioral trust score (success rate × 0.4 + uptime × 0.2 + threat × 0.2 + integrity × 0.2)
  • Trust upgrades require accumulated history; downgrades take effect immediately

This essentially brings the idea of “zero-trust networking” to the Agent communication layer.

Why Is It Popular?

Forty-eight thousand stars is no accident. It addresses a real need: Claude Code's user base is growing, but the ceiling of a single Agent is obvious. Ruflo offers an upgrade path from “coding with AI” to “coding with an AI team.”

Its 32 Claude Code plugins also cover a broad range: code quality, security audits, documentation generation, architecture decision records, domain-driven design scaffolding, and more. It effectively turns every stage of software engineering into Agent work.

Who Is It For?

  • Heavy Claude Code users seeking multi-Agent collaboration
  • Developers interested in Agent orchestration architecture
  • Technical leads who want AI development workflows inside their teams

One-Sentence Verdict

If Claude Code is “a very capable AI programmer,” Ruflo wants to be “the management system for an AI development team.” The direction makes sense, though the actual production validation behind those 48,000 stars remains to be seen.

3. warpdotdev/warp — The Terminal Is Open Source, and Built for Agents

⭐ 57.1k | Forks 4.3k | First public source release two weeks ago | Built in Rust

What Is It?

Warp is a modern terminal written in Rust that open-sourced its client code two weeks ago.

Its positioning now goes beyond “a better terminal.” The official description is: Agentic Development Environment—a development environment built for Agents.

Core product lineup:

ProductPositioning
Warp TerminalModern terminal with a code-editor-level UI
Oz AgentBuilt-in SOTA Agent, with parallel cloud execution
Warp CodeCode editing capabilities
Warp DriveTeam-shared commands and workflows

What Problem Does It Solve?

Two problems.

First, terminals are old. Most developers still use interfaces designed 20 years ago, without intelligent completion, block-level editing, or collaboration features.

Second, agentic development tools cannot run only locally. A laptop cannot handle 10 parallel Agent tasks. Warp's Oz can launch unlimited parallel Agents in the cloud, with programmability, auditing, and control.

Why Open Source Now?

Warp was previously closed source, which drew considerable community criticism. The “Initial public release” two weeks ago marks an important turning point.

The repository structure shows that the open-source portion is the Rust client code (the .cargo directory and the app directory); the server remains closed source. Still, this lets the community:

  • Audit code security
  • Contribute themes and workflows
  • Understand Warp's rendering and input-handling architecture

Competitor Comparison

TerminalLanguageAI capabilitiesOpen sourceCloud Agents
WarpRustBuilt-in Oz + support for Claude Code/Codex/Gemini CLIOpen-source client✅
iTerm2Objective-CNo native AIFully open source❌
AlacrittyRustNoneFully open source❌
KittyC/PythonNoneFully open source❌
GhosttyZigNoneFully open source❌

Warp's differentiation is clear: it is more than a faster terminal; it is a “terminal + AI Agent runtime.”

Who Is It For?

  • Developers seeking a modern terminal experience (macOS/Linux/Windows)
  • People who need AI Agents directly in the terminal
  • Developers interested in Rust GUI frameworks (Warp plans to open-source its UI framework)

One-Sentence Verdict

Fifty-seven thousand stars show strong demand for “a better terminal.” Open-sourcing is the right move. But Warp's real bet is on becoming the default runtime for Agents, beyond the terminal itself.

This Week's Observation

Taken together, these three projects reveal a clear trend:

Competition among AI Agents is moving from “whose model is stronger” to “whose toolchain is more complete.”

  • Anthropic is going beyond selling APIs to build industry-specific Agent solutions
  • Ruflo is going beyond individual Agents to build multi-Agent orchestration infrastructure
  • Warp is going beyond the terminal to build an Agent runtime platform

Their underlying logic is shared: as model capabilities converge, differentiation comes from making Agents easier to embed into real workflows.

This is not a short-lived trend. It is AI's transition from a “conversation tool” into “work infrastructure.”

See you next week.

title: GitHub Weekly: AI Projects Worth Watching
html:
1,727 Chinese characters; approximately 9 minutes to read

The open-source community has been moving at an outrageous pace lately, especially in AI coding tools: a new “champion” seems to emerge almost daily. To save everyone time filtering through them, I am starting a new series: a weekly deep dive into the top three—or most noteworthy—projects on GitHub Trending.

This week's preview:

1.claw-code - A Rust version of the Claude Code CLI, the fastest project ever to reach 100,000 stars
2. oh-my-codex - An enhancement toolkit for Codex, complete with workflows, agent teams, and a HUD
3. claude-howto - A practical introductory guide to Claude Code: from beginner to proficiency in 11–13 hours
4. VibeVoice - Microsoft's open-source speech AI, supporting 50+ languages, with long-audio processing as a highlight

1. claw-code: The Fastest Project Ever to Reach 100,000 Stars

  • GitHub: ultraworkers/claw-code
  • Stars: 172k
  • Language: Rust

What It Is

claw-code is an open-source Rust implementation of the Claude Code CLI. Anthropic's official version is TypeScript-only; this is the community's Rust rewrite. Interestingly, the project itself was built with oh-my-codex—something of a “build itself” story.

Core Contents

  • Rust implementation: A Rust rewrite of the Claude Code CLI
  • Workspace: A complete Rust workspace
  • CLI: A command-line interface similar to Claude Code
  • Tests: A companion Python reference workspace and auditing tools

Quick Start

cd rust
cargo build --workspace
./target/debug/claw --help
./target/debug/claw prompt "summarize this repository"

Authentication methods:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."
# 或者
cd rust
./target/debug/claw login

My Take

What does 100,000 stars mean? It reached that milestone in just a few days, faster than any project before it. The reason it took off is simple: this week, 500,000 lines of Claude Code's TypeScript source leaked through source maps. This project is a Rust version of Claude Code, with better performance and easier deployment. If you like Claude Code but want Rust's performance, it is worth watching.

2. oh-my-codex: Turn Codex into a “Workstation”

GitHub: Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-codex
Stars: 16,941
Language: TypeScript

What It Is

oh-my-codex, or OMX, is an enhancement toolkit for OpenAI's Codex CLI. Its official description is a “workflow layer”: it wraps Codex in a better workflow. In simple terms, it makes a previously solo Codex more capable, adding hooks, agent teams, a HUD, and customizable workflows.

Core Features

  1. 1. Standard workflow: Use $deep-interview to clarify requirements → $ralplan to plan → $ralph to keep executing → $team for parallel collaboration
  2. 2. Agent teams: Multiple agents working together, with persistent execution through tmux
  3. 3. Persistent state: Stores plans, logs, memories, and runtime state in the .omx/ directory
  4. 4. HUD interface: Monitors agent activity in real time
  5. 5. Skills extensions: Includes a set of common skills

Who It Is For

  • People already familiar with Claude Code who want to improve efficiency
  • People handling complex tasks who want multiple agents to collaborate
  • People who want to turn Codex into a complete workbench

Quick Start

npm install -g @openai/codex oh-my-codex
omx setup
omx --madmax --high

Then use Codex as usual, with a few additional commands:

  • $deep-interview "..." - Clarify the boundaries of the requirements
  • $ralplan "..." - Create and approve a plan
  • $ralph "..." - Continue executing until completion
  • $team 3:executor "..." - Execute in parallel

My Take

There is a reason this project is popular. Codex itself is powerful, but it lacks a standardized framework for getting the most out of it. OMX fills that gap, and its thinking resembles OpenClaw's in some ways: both add workflows, state management, and multi-agent collaboration. If you use Codex, give it a try.

3. claude-howto: A Practical Introductory Guide to Claude Code

GitHub: luongnv89/claude-howto
Stars: 20,707
Language: Python

What It Is

This is a visual introductory guide to Claude Code, covering everything from basic concepts to advanced agents. Most importantly, it provides plenty of copy-and-paste templates you can use immediately.

The Problem It Solves

Many people install Claude Code and know how to use it, but do not know what else it can do:

  • Official documentation explains features without teaching how to combine them
  • There is no clear learning path
  • Examples are too basic; “hello world” demonstrations cannot be used in production

This project addresses those problems.

Content Structure

Ten tutorial modules cover all Claude Code features:

  • Slash Commands (basics)
  • Memory
  • Checkpoints
  • CLI Basics
  • Skills
  • Hooks
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol)
  • Subagents
  • Advanced Features

Each module includes visual Mermaid diagrams, ready-to-copy configuration templates, and an estimated learning time.

Learning Paths

LevelWhat you can doStart hereTime
BeginnerLaunch Claude Code and chatSlash Commands~2.5h
IntermediateUse CLAUDE.md and custom commandsSkills~3.5h
AdvancedConfigure MCP servers and hooksAdvanced Features~5h

Completing all 10 modules takes approximately 11–13 hours.

Notable Features

  • Self-assessment quiz: Run /lesson-quiz or /self-assessment to identify gaps in your knowledge
  • Personalized paths: Recommends what to learn next based on your current proficiency
  • Production-ready templates: Actual project configurations, not simple demos

My Take

This project is particularly suitable for newcomers to Claude Code. The official documentation is good, but scattered, without a clear route through it. This guide connects that scattered knowledge, and its templates really are ready to use. More than 20,000 stars suggest others find it useful too.

4. VibeVoice: Microsoft's Open-Source Speech AI

GitHub: microsoft/VibeVoice
Stars: 36,564
Language: Python

What It Is

VibeVoice is Microsoft's open-source speech AI family, covering speech recognition (ASR) and speech synthesis (TTS). Its key innovation is a continuous speech tokenizer with an extremely low frame rate of 7.5 Hz, substantially improving computational efficiency while preserving audio quality. It supports processing audio up to 60 minutes long in one pass.

Main Models

ModelPurposeTry it
VibeVoice-ASR-7BSpeech recognitionPlayground
VibeVoice-TTS-1.5BSpeech synthesisColab
VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5BReal-time speech synthesisColab

Supported Features

  • Multilingual: Supports 50+ languages
  • Long audio: ASR supports 60 minutes per pass; TTS supports 90 minutes of synthesis
  • Multiple speakers: TTS supports up to four distinct speakers
  • Fine-tuning: Includes fine-tuning code for training your own model
  • vLLM inference: Supports fast inference deployment
  • HuggingFace Transformers: Integrated into Transformers v5.3.0

Real-World Applications

The open-source community has already adopted the project. Vibing, a voice-driven input method built on VibeVoice-ASR, supports macOS and Windows.

My Take

Microsoft has put real effort into this release. Although the TTS code was previously taken down for various reasons, the newly open-sourced ASR and Realtime TTS are both strong. Thirty-six thousand stars is a high figure in speech technology. If you want to build speech applications, this is worth following.

Summary

Toolchain integration is the defining theme of this week's rankings.
We are moving from “tuning a single AI” to “managing an AI team.” Whether it is OMX's workflows or claw-code's high-performance foundation, the message is the same: coding in 2026 is no longer a contest of typing speed, but of your ability to build and manage Agent workflows.

That wraps up this edition of GitHub Trending Watch.

title: GitHub Weekly: Hermes, MarkItDown, and OpenScreen—Unlocking Productivity
html:
This week, I selected three widely discussed, practical open-source projects setting new benchmarks in AI automation, document processing, and content creation.
Beyond winning recognition from developers, these projects address real pain points for developers and content creators:

  • Hermes Agent redefines the intelligence of AI assistants through a closed-loop self-learning mechanism
  • MarkItDown converts complex, diverse file formats into LLM-friendly Markdown
  • OpenScreen provides professional screen recording comparable to paid tools

Whether you develop AI, engineer data pipelines, or create content, these projects can substantially improve your productivity. Let's explore their design philosophies, core features, and practical use cases.

I. Hermes Agent — A Personal AI Assistant That Evolves

Project: https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent

Statistics: ⭐ 61.2k | Forks 8.2k

Note: I plan to start a dedicated series explaining this project later.

Positioning

Hermes Agent is an open-source autonomous AI agent system from Nous Research. Its fundamental difference from ordinary AI chat tools is closed-loop self-learning: it creates skills from experience, accumulates memories, and continuously builds an understanding of the user across sessions, becoming smarter with use.

Core Architecture

The system is built on three core mechanisms:

1. Persistent Memory

  • Honcho-powered dialectical user modeling retains preferences, habits, and historical context across sessions
  • A built-in FTS5 full-text search engine combines with LLM summaries for cross-session semantic recall
  • Session trajectories can be compressed into model-training data, with support for the Tinker-Atropos RL submodule

2. Automatic Skill Generation

  • The agent can automatically create and refine skill modules following the agentskills.io open standard
  • Periodic nudges help persist knowledge, enabling a true self-improvement loop

3. Multiplatform Messaging Gateway

One AI assistant connects across major communication platforms—Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and Email—without configuring a separate assistant for each.

Feature List

ModuleDescription
Rich terminal UIMultiline editing, slash-command completion, streaming tool output, and history browsing
40+ built-in toolsFile operations, web requests, code execution, system administration, and more
MCP server integrationConnect third-party MCP services to extend capabilities
Natural-language scheduled tasksDescribe cron jobs in natural language, such as "send a summary every morning at 8"
Parallel subagentsSpawn independent subagents to execute workflows concurrently
Python RPC tool callsInvoke external Python scripts as tools
Speech transcriptionConvert voice input to text
Context filesShape project knowledge through files so the agent understands your project

Supported Models and Runtime Environments

LLM providers: Nous Portal, OpenRouter (200+ models), z.ai, Kimi, MiniMax, OpenAI, and custom endpoints

Execution backends (choose one of six):

  • Local
  • Docker
  • Remote SSH
  • Daytona
  • Singularity (HPC environments)
  • Modal (serverless)

Operating systems: Linux, macOS, WSL2, and Android (Termux). Native Windows is unsupported; use WSL2.

Typical Use Cases

  • Personal automation: Schedule the agent to generate daily reports, back up files, and perform periodic audits
  • A unified cross-platform entry point: Talk to the same AI that remembers you, whether on Telegram or Slack
  • RL training-data collection: Generate batch trajectories to supply high-quality model-training data
  • Development assistance: Combine MCP servers and context files into an intelligent coding assistant that understands the whole project

II. MarkItDown — An All-purpose Document Converter Built for LLMs

Project: https://github.com/microsoft/markitdown

Statistics: ⭐ 102.9k | Forks 6.4k

Positioning

MarkItDown is a Python library from Microsoft's AutoGen team that aims to convert almost every common file format into Markdown. Unlike other document converters, its output prioritizes machine consumption by LLMs over human reading experience: it preserves structural semantics as far as possible rather than reproducing visual appearance.

Reaching more than 100,000 stars in a short period suggests it precisely addresses pain points in RAG, knowledge-base construction, and document-ingestion pipelines.

Supported Formats

CategoryFormats
Office documentsPDF, Word (DOCX), Excel (XLSX/XLS), PowerPoint (PPTX)
Web contentHTML, YouTube URLs with automatic subtitle and description extraction
Data formatsCSV, JSON, XML
MultimediaImages, including EXIF metadata and OCR text extraction; audio, with speech transcription
OtherEPUB ebooks and ZIP archives, with recursive processing of files inside

Core Capabilities

Structure preservation: Retains semantic structure such as heading levels, lists, tables, and hyperlinks so LLMs can understand how a document is organized.

Multimedia metadata extraction: Image conversion goes beyond OCR, also extracting EXIF metadata such as capture time, GPS coordinates, and device information into text.

LLM vision enhancement: Integrates vision models such as OpenAI's to automatically generate semantic image descriptions and improve discoverability.

Azure Document Intelligence integration: Optionally uses Azure's advanced OCR for scanned documents and complex layouts to substantially improve recognition accuracy.

Plugin architecture: Supports custom converter extensions and includes MCP server support for direct use with Claude Desktop.

Version Notes (Breaking Changes in v0.1.0)

  • Optional dependencies move to grouped installation, deprecating the monolithic format (still supported in newer versions)
  • convert_stream() now accepts only binary file objects, opened in rb mode
  • DocumentConverter changes from file paths to stream processing

Typical Use Cases

  • RAG knowledge-base construction: Batch-convert internal PDFs and Word documents to Markdown before embedding and storing them
  • LLM data-preprocessing pipelines: Use it as a standardized component in document ingestion
  • Multisource document integration: Process content from websites, files, and videos into a consistent output format
  • Automated report processing: Regularly convert Excel reports and PowerPoint presentations into text for LLM analysis

III. OpenScreen — Free Professional Screen Recording

Project: https://github.com/siddharthvaddem/openscreen

Statistics: ⭐ 28.4k | Forks 1.9k

Positioning

OpenScreen is an open-source alternative to Screen Studio, a highly regarded macOS screen-recording tool requiring a paid subscription. OpenScreen aims to provide the same core experience, completely free, without watermarks, for personal and commercial use. It is currently in beta, but stable, usable releases are already available.

Features in Detail

Recording Controls

  • Record a specific window or the full screen
  • Record microphone and system audio on independent channels with separate volume controls
  • Pause and resume during recording

Camera Effects

  • Automatic zoom: Automatically enlarges the focus area based on mouse position, simulating a camera operator following the action
  • Manual zoom: Precisely control zoom position, amount, and duration on the timeline
  • Depth-of-field effect: Add a blurred background to highlight the active area
  • Motion blur: Pan and zoom effects include realistic motion-blur transitions

Editing

  • A visual timeline editor powered by dnd-timeline
  • Trim video clips to remove unnecessary segments
  • Segment-specific speed changes: accelerate dull portions and slow down detailed demonstrations
  • Crop video to hide or remove areas that should not be shown

Visual Customization

  • Background options: system wallpapers, solid colors, gradients, and custom images
  • Rounded corners, shadows, and other window enhancements produce professional floating-window demos in one click

Annotation Tools

  • Text annotations with customizable fonts, colors, and sizes
  • Directional arrows
  • Insert images such as logos and screenshots

Export Options

  • Multiple resolutions: 720p, 1080p, 2K, and 4K
  • Multiple aspect ratios: 16:9, 4:3, 1:1, portrait, and more
  • Common formats including MP4 and GIF

Technical Architecture

TechnologyPurpose
ElectronCross-platform desktop application framework
React + TypeScriptUI framework and type-safe frontend logic
ViteFast builds and hot reload
PixiJSHigh-performance WebGL rendering for real-time previews and effects
dnd-timelineDraggable timeline-editor component

Platform Support and Requirements

PlatformSystem Audio SupportSpecial Requirements
macOS (Intel/Apple Silicon)Supported on macOS 13+; unsupported on 12 and earlierManually remove Gatekeeper quarantine and grant screen-recording and accessibility permissions
WindowsWorks out of the boxNo special requirements
Linux (AppImage)Requires PipeWirePulseAudio-only systems may be unable to record system audio

Installation

Download the installer for your platform from GitHub Releases:

  • macOS:.dmg
  • Windows:.exe installer
  • Linux:.AppImage

On macOS, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

Typical Use Cases

  • Product demo videos: Record SaaS workflows with automatic zoom and polished backgrounds to produce professional demonstrations directly
  • Technical tutorials: Improve code walkthroughs and command-line demonstrations with speed adjustments and annotations
  • Design-review recordings: Record Figma prototype walkthroughs and add arrows and text to explain design intent
  • Customer-support videos: Record operating steps for users in place of written instructions

Comparison Summary

DimensionHermes AgentMarkItDownOpenScreen
TypeAI agent frameworkPython libraryDesktop application
Stars61,200103,00028,400
Primary languagePythonPythonTypeScript
Core valueCross-platform, self-learning AI assistantMultiple document formats → MarkdownFree professional screen recording
Target usersAI and Python developersData engineers and LLM application developersProduct managers, content creators, and developers
MaturityActively maintainedActively maintained, with rapid iterationBeta

These tools address pain points in three different areas: AI automation, document preprocessing, and content recording. All use the MIT license and are free for personal and commercial projects. Choose which to bookmark and try according to your needs.

title: GitHub Weekly: Better Coding Habits, Persistent Memory, and Agent Teams
html:
Writing code with AI is nothing new, but most people's experience stalls at the same stage: it works reasonably well, yet a few things remain maddening. Ask it to change one function and it casually refactors half a module. Spend twenty minutes explaining the project yesterday, and you must start over in today's new session. Try running several tasks at once, and the Agents have no idea what the others are doing. The problem is not insufficient model intelligence; the tooling has not caught up. Three GitHub projects this week are worth watching and may address these issues.

1. andrej-karpathy-skills

Repository: multica-ai/andrej-karpathy-skills
Stars: 58.6k ⭐ | Forks: 5.1k

Background

This project starts with a question:Why does AI keep making the same coding mistakes?

Andrej Karpathy—OpenAI co-founder and former Tesla AI director—has systematically observed and summarized common LLM shortcomings in coding tasks. This project turns his insights into a CLAUDE.md configuration file that attaches directly to Claude Code, using rules to constrain AI behavior.

The project itself is remarkably restrained: its core is just one file. Yet it has nearly 60,000 GitHub stars, suggesting these “bad AI habits” are a shared pain point for almost all heavy users.

Four Core Principles

1. Think Before Coding

AI's default behavior is to act as soon as it receives instructions. When uncertain, it tends to make assumptions instead of asking questions. This principle requires it to state uncertainties explicitly and ask questions before coding, rather than silently treating assumptions as confirmed. Silence often costs much more than one extra question.

2. Simplicity First

AI has a clear tendency to overengineer: turning a 50-line solution into 200 lines, or introducing design patterns where a simple function would suffice. This principle requires only the minimum code needed for the current problem and explicitly says that code must be rewritten if it can be simplified.

3. Surgical Changes

Give AI a small task and it often “optimizes” surrounding code, changes the style, or even refactors unrelated modules. This is dangerous in collaborative projects because you do not know what changed. The principle requires changes only to code directly related to the request, strict adherence to existing style, and no unrelated modifications.

4. Goal-Driven Execution

AI sometimes “completes the task” without solving the problem. This principle requires translating the task into verifiable success criteria before execution, then continuing until the goal is actually achieved rather than treating runnable code as the finish line.

How to Use It

The project supports three integration methods:

  • Plugin Marketplace (recommended): Install the karpathy-skills plugin in one step through Claude Code's plugin marketplace
  • Per-project mode: Download CLAUDE.md into the project root; it applies only to that project
  • Global mode: Place it in Claude Code IDE's rules directory (.Claude Code/rules/karpathy-guidelines.mdc), applying it to all projects

The repository also includes EXAMPLES.md (practical examples) and README.zh.md (a Chinese version).

Why It Matters

This project represents more than a configuration file. It expresses a view:The ceiling of AI coding tools depends not only on model capabilities, but also on how we constrain and guide their behavior. Sixty thousand stars are users voting for that view.

2. claude-mem

Repository: thedotmack/claude-mem
Stars: 62.6k ⭐ | Forks: 5.2 k

Background

Claude Code sessions are stateless. Each new session knows nothing about your project: architecture decisions, past pitfalls, and agreed coding conventions all reset to zero.

claude-mem was created by developer Alex Newman (@thedotmack) to add a persistent cross-session memory system to Claude Code. It does not modify the model or rely on external AI services; hooks locally capture, compress, and store session content, then intelligently inject relevant context into the next session.

How It Works

Five lifecycle hooks drive the system, covering the full session lifecycle:

SessionStart → UserPromptSubmit → PostToolUse → Stop → SessionEnd

After each hook fires, relevant content is sent to a local Worker HTTP API on port 37777, semantically processed, and written into two storage layers:

  • SQLite (with FTS5): Fast, precise full-text retrieval
  • Chroma vector database: Semantic retrieval that understands fuzzy queries

At the start of the next session, the system automatically retrieves relevant memories from both layers and injects them into the context.

Core Features

Progressive Disclosure (Three-Level Retrieval, About 10× Token Savings)

This is one of claude-mem's most important designs. Memory retrieval has three levels, accessed on demand to avoid overflowing the context by loading too much history at once:

  1. 1. search — Compact index summaries, about 50–100 tokens, quickly locate relevant memories
  2. 2. timeline — Timeline context for understanding event order
  3. 3. get_observations — Retrieve full details by ID, about 500–1,000 tokens

Natural-Language Skill Search

Through the mem-search command, you can query past coding experience in natural language, such as “How did we handle authentication last time?”

Real-Time Web UI

At http://localhost:37777, a visual memory-stream interface lets you see what the AI is remembering in real time and manage memory entries manually.

Privacy Controls

Content marked with <private> tags is automatically excluded from the memory store. This is useful for sensitive content such as API keys and personal information.

Citation System

Every memory has a unique observation ID for tracing its source, ensuring recalled content can be verified and tracked back.

Compatibility and Installation

Besides Claude Code, claude-mem supports mainstream Agent tools such as Gemini CLI and OpenCode through the MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool protocol.

Installation options include npm, a bash script, and one-click Plugin Marketplace installation. It requires Node.js 18+; the Bun runtime is configured automatically during installation, and SQLite 3 is bundled, requiring no separate installation.

The project provides a complete documentation site at docs.claude-mem.ai and a Discord community.

Limitations and Considerations

The project currently has 142 open Issues, indicating active iteration; some edge cases may still be unstable.ragtime uses the PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 license, so commercial use must respect its licensing restrictions.

3. multica

Repository: multica-ai/multica
Stars: 16.3k ⭐ | Forks: 2k

Background

multica's ambition goes further than the first two projects. It is building an AI Agent collaboration platform where multiple coding Agents cooperate like actual team members, rather than improving one AI's behavior.

The project's slogan is: “Your next 10 hires won't be human.”

This is more than a gimmick. multica's core idea is that AI Agents should appear on project boards, join conversations, create Issues, and report blockers like real remote colleagues, rather than merely wait for commands in a terminal.

Core Features

Agents as Team Members

Each Agent has an independent member profile in multica. Agents can:

  • View and claim tasks on project boards
  • Join task discussions, ask questions, and report progress
  • Automatically create Issues when blocked
  • Push execution progress in real time through WebSocket

This differs fundamentally from traditional AI tools' question-and-answer interaction: the Agent is an active participant rather than a passive responder.

Autonomous Execution Across the Full Lifecycle

From assignment to completion, the Agent independently understands requirements, breaks down steps, writes code, runs validation, and submits results. Users assign tasks on the board and can leave the entire process to the Agent.

Skill Reuse (Skill Compounding)

Solutions accumulated during task execution can become shareable “skills” reused by other Agents or projects. This builds knowledge assets, addressing the problem of AI capabilities disappearing after use rather than accumulating.

Unified Runtime Management

The multica CLI automatically detects and centrally manages local daemons and cloud compute resources, so users need not manually distinguish where tasks execute. Multiple isolated workspaces support team collaboration.

Technical Architecture

LayerTechnology
FrontendNext.js 16 (App Router), TypeScript (53.4%)
BackendGo + Chi router + sqlc (43%)
Real-time communicationgorilla/websocket
DatabasePostgreSQL 17 + pgvector

Go handles highly concurrent task scheduling and Agent communication, Next.js handles the web interface, and pgvector provides vector retrieval for Agent skills. The architecture emphasizes performance and scalability for running multiple Agents simultaneously.

Supported Agents

As a platform layer, multica supports mainstream coding Agents including Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Hermes, Gemini, and Pi. Users can mix different Agents on the same board, assigning tasks to the best-suited executor.

Deployment Options

  • macOS/Linux: Install the CLI through Homebrew (brew install multica-ai/tap/multica)
  • Windows: Install through a PowerShell script
  • Self-hosted: Complete Docker deployment; see SELF_HOSTING.md
  • Cloud service: Official hosted instance at multica.ai/app

Project Status

The latest version, v0.2.6, was released on April 18, 2026. At publication, the project remains under active development, with 43 releases and 109 open PRs. With 16,000+ stars and 54 contributors, it is still in an early stage of rapid growth, with stability and completeness continuing to improve.

Summary

The three projects pursue different directions and serve somewhat different audiences. andrej-karpathy-skills has almost no entry barrier: add one file and you can feel the difference that day; it suits anyone using Claude Code. claude-mem grows more valuable over time: the longer a project runs, the more useful its accumulated context becomes; it suits developers working on long-term projects. multica is the heaviest of the three and is still iterating rapidly. Its features are already usable, but setup takes some effort, making it best suited to teams serious about multi-Agent workflows.

Source: public GitHub pages, as of April 19, 2026. Live metrics such as star counts should be checked at the time of access.

title: Why Does Simple grep Outperform Complex Vector Retrieval on Multi-hop Reasoning Tasks?
html:
Where the Question Comes From

Have you ever wondered why AI retrieval systems always give you top-k results before they begin reasoning?

The design seems sensible: first filter with BM25 or a vector database, retrieve the most relevant documents, and then let a large model interpret them. It is fast, inexpensive, and easy to implement.

But here is the problem:What if useful evidence is filtered out in the very first step?

Traditional retrieval systems, whether sparse or dense, essentially perform "compression": they compress the entire corpus into a fixed top-k interface. That interface works for simple question answering but becomes a bottleneck for agent tasks requiring multistep reasoning:

  • Precise lexical constraints, such as "must contain both A and B," are difficult to express
  • Combining sparse clues, such as "a report from 2024," requires multiple queries
  • Inspecting local context, such as "what are the ten lines around this keyword?", is simply impossible
  • Multistep hypothesis refinement, such as "find the entity first, then the relationship," is broken into independent retrieval steps

Worse still, once evidence is filtered out at the first step, no amount of subsequent reasoning can recover it.

This is the central problem the paper addresses.

Their Approach: Interact Directly with the Corpus

The paper proposes a seemingly counterintuitive approach:Direct Corpus Interaction (DCI) — Let agents search the raw corpus directly using terminal tools—grep, file reads, shell commands, and lightweight scripts—with no embedding model, vector index, or retrieval API.

Sounds primitive? The results are remarkable.


This chart shows a Pareto frontier analysis: cost (API call count) on the horizontal axis, accuracy on the vertical axis. We can see:

  • The DCI-Agent family (red) clearly outperforms all traditional retrieval methods (blue)
  • Even the lightest DCI-Agent-Lite achieves higher accuracy at lower cost

The Core Idea

Traditional retrieval pushes "semantic understanding" down to the indexing layer—embedding model plus vector database—and gives the agent a compressed interface.

DCI reverses this:It brings semantic understanding back to the LLM layer and gives the agent a high-resolution raw interface.

Specifically, agents can:

  • Use grep 'foo' file | grep 'bar' to enforce multiple lexical constraints
  • Use find . | grep 'report' | grep '2024' to combine weak clues
  • Use grep -n 'keyword' file | head to verify local context
  • Use head, tail, and sed for fine-grained snippet inspection

These operations can be composed into pipelines, iteratively refined, and precisely targeted—what the paper calls "interface resolution."

On the left is traditional retrieval: a black box takes a query and returns a document list.
On the right is DCI: a toolbox lets you browse, search, locate, and extract information, interacting with the corpus like a person.

How Good Are the Results?

The paper tests three categories of tasks:

1. Deep Research Tasks (BrowseComp-Plus)

This is a complex question-answering benchmark requiring multistep reasoning.

Results:

  • Using the same Claude Sonnet 4.6 model
  • Replacing the Qwen3-Embedding-8B retriever with DCI
  • Accuracy rises from 69.0% to 80.0% (+11 percentage points)
  • Cost falls from 1,016 (−29.4%)

The lighter DCI-Agent-Lite, using GPT-5.4 nano, costs only 740), while achieving comparable performance.

2. Multi-hop Question Answering

Across six datasets, including NQ, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue:

  • DCI-Agent-CC (Claude Sonnet 4.6) achieves 83.0% average accuracy
  • The strongest retrieval-agent baseline, ASearcher-Local-14B, achieves only 52.3%
  • An improvement of 30.7 percentage points

Gains are particularly pronounced on multi-hop tasks:

  • HotpotQA: +30 points
  • 2WikiMultiHopQA: +26 points
  • MuSiQue: +50 points


    The upper half is Table 2 (multi-hop QA); the lower half is Table 3 (IR ranking).
    DCI-Agent ranks first on almost every dataset.

3. Information Retrieval Ranking

On BRIGHT and BEIR:

  • DCI-Agent-CC reaches an average NDCG@10 of 68.5
  • The strongest retrieval baseline, ReasonRank-32B, reaches only 47.0
  • An improvement of 21.5 points

Why DCI Works

A series of controlled experiments leads the paper to this conclusion:

DCI's advantage is not that it finds more relevant documents, but that it makes finer-grained use of the documents it has already found.

Key Numbers

On BrowseComp-Plus, using the same Sonnet 4.6 model:

  • DCI-Agent-CC correctly answers 176 questions that the retrieval agent gets wrong
  • The retrieval agent correctly answers only 76 questions that DCI gets wrong

But here is the key point:Of those 176 questions, only 34 involve the retrieval agent failing to find any relevant documents.

For the other 142, the retrieval agent actually finds at least one relevant document but still answers incorrectly. These failures fall into two categories:

  1. 1. Partial-chain failures (83 questions): Some evidence is found, but it is incomplete and cannot support the next reasoning step
  2. 2. Post-retrieval failures (59 questions): All relevant documents are found, but are not used effectively

Tool-use Analysis

DCI-Agent-CC's tool-call distribution:

  • Bash commands: 62.4%
    • Chained search: 22.3%
    • Local context peeking: 18.0%
    • Regex matching: 17.0%
    • File localization: 14.0%
    • Full-document reads: only 9.1%
  • Grep searches: 33.0%

What does this tell us?DCI's advantage comes from composing Bash commands to manipulate documents precisely: combining lexical constraints, verifying exact snippets, and selectively expanding promising passages.

This figure reveals why DCI succeeds.The left panel shows that its advantage extends beyond finding documents: fine-grained operations extract evidence that traditional interfaces obscure, even from documents already discovered by the retriever.The right panel shows what this "high resolution" looks like in practice: instead of reading blindly, agents frequently use precise tools such as chained search (22.3%) and snippet peeking (18.0%) to pinpoint answers.

Coverage vs. Localization

The paper defines two metrics:

  • Coverage: How many relevant documents are found
  • Localization: How precisely useful snippets can be located within those documents

The results are interesting:

MethodCoverage (mean)Coverage (any)LocalizationAccuracy
Qwen3-Embedding-8B56.774.021.745.0%
DCI-Agent-Lite28.070.048.473.0%

DCI's mean coverage (28.0) is far below the retrieval baseline (56.7), but its coverage of "at least one" relevant document (70.0) is close to the baseline's 74.0, while its localization score (48.4) is more than twice the retrieval baseline's 21.7.

In other words:DCI wins through precise use, rather than exhaustive discovery.

This table compares the coverage and localization of three strategies (L1/L2/L3).
Although L3 has the lowest coverage (27.0), it has the strongest localization and ultimately the highest accuracy (77).

Once DCI finds a useful document, it can switch from broad retrieval to detailed inspection and verification, extracting more value from what it already has.

DCI's Limitations

The paper also candidly identifies DCI's boundaries:

1. Sensitivity to Corpus Size

DCI performs well on search depth, but its cost rises quickly with search breadth.

Expanding the BrowseComp-Plus corpus from 100,000 to 200,000 documents:

  • Tool calls rise from 38.5 to 86.9
  • Latency doubles
  • Cost doubles
  • Accuracy drops by 13.6 points

At 400,000 documents:

  • Accuracy falls to 37.5%
  • Average tool calls reach 122.4
  • Twenty samples terminate after exceeding the tool budget

Conclusion: DCI suits small-to-medium corpora around 100,000 documents, rather than large corpora numbering in the millions.

2. Context Management Is Critical

The paper tests five context-management strategies, L0 through L4, and finds:

  • The most aggressive compression (L2) has the lowest cost but the worst accuracy (69%)
  • The most conservative strategy (L1) retains the most evidence but does not achieve the highest accuracy (75%)
  • The best strategy (L3) achieves the highest accuracy (77%) and also the highest cost

Conclusion: Context management is not about keeping more of everything; it requires selective forgetting—retaining intermediate structures useful to later searches while discarding redundant verbatim evidence.

3. Tool Expressiveness Matters

The paper compares two tool configurations:

  • read + grep (restricted toolset): 61% accuracy, $0.0355 cost
  • Open bash (full toolset): 73% accuracy, $0.1021 cost

Conclusion: Composable tools—Bash pipes, regex, and conditionals—are critical to DCI's effectiveness.

Why This Paper Matters

1. Redefining the Retrieval Bottleneck

Traditional view: the bottleneck is failing to find relevant documents.

This paper: the bottleneck is low interface resolution—even found documents cannot be manipulated precisely.

2. Introducing "Interface Resolution"

Interface Resolution: How fine-grained is the smallest unit the agent can manipulate?

  • Traditional retrieval: documents or paragraphs (coarse-grained)
  • DCI: lines, snippets, or regex matches (fine-grained)

Higher resolution allows finer operations: verifying hypotheses, combining clues, and iteratively refining searches.

3. Challenging the Assumption That an Index Is Necessary

Traditional RAG systems require an index—embeddings plus a vector database—before retrieval.

DCI needs no index and operates on raw files through terminal tools.

This is particularly useful for local, dynamic, and heterogeneous corpora: no offline indexing is required, and changes to files are handled naturally.

4. Pointing the Way for Agent Design

When a model is strong enough to search like a human researcher—forming hypotheses, testing patterns, reading context, and refining queries—a compressed similarity index becomes a bottleneck. At that point, a high-resolution interface matters more than a high-quality retriever.

In other words:Retrieval is not just a retriever-design problem; it is an interface-design problem.

Use Cases

Based on the paper's experimental results, DCI is suitable for:

✅ Suitable Scenarios

  1. 1. Small-to-medium corpora (up to 100,000 documents)
  2. 2. Complex tasks requiring multistep reasoning (multi-hop QA and deep research)
  3. 3. Tasks requiring precise lexical constraints ("must contain both A and B")
  4. 4. Local or dynamic corpora (files change frequently and you do not want to maintain an index)
  5. 5. Tasks requiring precise evidence localization (finding specific snippets as well as documents)

❌ Unsuitable Scenarios

  1. 1. Large corpora (millions of documents or more)
  2. 2. Simple single-hop QA (traditional retrieval is already sufficient)
  3. 3. Tasks requiring semantic generalization (such as finding similar concepts)
  4. 4. Latency-sensitive tasks (DCI requires multiple tool calls)

Technical Details

Two Implementations

The paper implements two versions:

  1. 1. DCI-Agent-Lite
    • Built on Pi, a minimal terminal harness
    • Exposes only bash and read as its two tools
    • Uses GPT-5.4 nano, a lightweight model
    • Low cost ($93 for 830 questions)
    • 62.9% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus
  2. 2. DCI-Agent-ClaudeCode (CC)
    • Built on Claude Code
    • Uses Claude Sonnet 4.6, a high-performance model
    • High cost ($1,016 for 830 questions)
    • 80.0% accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus

Evaluation Metrics

The paper introduces a new metric:Localization Score

  • Measures how precisely an agent locates useful snippets
  • Measures finding specific evidence within a document, rather than merely finding the document
  • Calculation: find the best snippet-level match score for each relevant document, then average

This metric matters because it distinguishes finding documents from using them well.

Future Directions

The paper also identifies several directions worth exploring:

1. Hybrid Interfaces

Instead of choosing exclusively between retrievers and DCI:

  • Use a retriever for coarse filtering to narrow the search quickly
  • Use DCI for detailed inspection of candidate documents

This can combine scale with precision.

2. Better Context Management

The paper finds that context-management strategies strongly affect DCI, but has not yet found the optimal strategy.

Future possibilities include:

  • Learning context-management policies through reinforcement learning
  • Adjusting compression strength dynamically by task type
  • Retaining useful intermediate structures instead of verbatim evidence

3. Tool Learning

Teach agents:

  • When to use grep versus find
  • How to combine tools through Bash pipelines
  • How to adjust search strategies based on intermediate results

4. Scaling

How can DCI handle larger corpora?

Possible directions:

  • Hierarchical indexing: coarse-grained indexes plus fine-grained DCI
  • Incremental indexing: index only metadata and use DCI for content
  • Distributed DCI: search multiple subcorpora in parallel

Summary

Retrieval's bottleneck lies in using evidence poorly, rather than failing to find it.

Traditional retrieval gives agents a low-resolution interface—top-k documents—that limits their action space.

DCI provides a high-resolution interface—raw files plus terminal tools—so agents can work precisely like human researchers: combining clues, testing hypotheses, and refining their approach.

The experiments demonstrate:When the model is strong enough, interface resolution matters more than retriever quality.

This does not mean retrievers are useless. It means:We need to rethink how agents interact with corpora.

Retrieval is not just a retriever-design problem; it is an interface-design problem.

Paper Information:

  • Title: Beyond Semantic Similarity: Rethinking Retrieval for Agentic Search via Direct Corpus Interaction
  • Authors: Zhuofeng Li et al. (Texas A&M, U Waterloo, Stanford, UIUC, and others)
  • Published: arXiv:2605.05242v1 [cs.IR], May 3, 2026
  • Code: https://github.com/DCI-Agent/DCI-Agent-Lite
