title: An Introduction to Knowledge Graphs: From Relationships to an AI Knowledge Foundation
html:
Introduction

The first time you hear “knowledge graph,” several questions may come to mind. How can knowledge be a graph? How does it differ from a database? What does it have to do with large models, RAG, and intelligent question answering?

Think of it this way: a knowledge graph organizes real-world things and their relationships in a form computers can understand, query, and reason over.

For example, these relationships:

乔布斯 → 创立 → 苹果公司
苹果公司 → 发布 → iPhone
iPhone → 属于 → 智能手机
苹果公司 → 总部位于 → 库比蒂诺

One relationship looks like a fact. Connect many of them and you have a network.

The network's value goes beyond visualization. Machines can use it to follow relationship paths to answers, determine whether objects are related, explain recommendations, uncover chains of potential risk, or supply large models with more solid context.

A knowledge graph is therefore not essentially about drawing an attractive diagram. It is about turning knowledge relationships scattered across tables, documents, webpages, systems, and people's minds into structures computers can understand and reuse.

1. Starting with a search question

Suppose you ask a search engine:

苹果创始人是谁？

Here, “Apple” can mean several things: a fruit, Apple Inc., a project, a brand, or someone's nickname.

The traditional keyword-search approach

The system sees words such as “Apple” and “founder,” matches webpages containing them, and ranks their relevance. The result depends on page popularity and inbound links.

The knowledge-graph approach

The system first determines that “Apple” probably means the entity Apple Inc. It then retrieves directly from the graph:

苹果公司 → 创始人 → 史蒂夫·乔布斯
苹果公司 → 创始人 → 史蒂夫·沃兹尼亚克
苹果公司 → 创始人 → 罗纳德·韦恩

What is the difference?

  • Keyword search guesses which webpage most resembles an answer
  • A knowledge graph uses explicitly structured facts

That is its central advantage over traditional text search:it goes beyond finding words to understanding what a word refers to and how that entity relates to others.

2. What exactly is a knowledge graph?

A one-sentence definition: A knowledge graph is a graph structure that organizes knowledge through entities and relationships.

There are three key elements:

Entities
Identifiable real-world objects: a person, company, book, city, disease, product, or system API can all be entities.

Relationships
Connections between entities, such as:

人 → 任职于 → 公司
公司 → 位于 → 城市
疾病 → 表现为 → 症状
药物 → 治疗 → 疾病
项目 → 依赖 → 系统

Graph structure
Entities become nodes and relationships become edges, forming a queryable network.

Components of a knowledge graph

ElementMeaningExample
EntityIdentifiable objectApple Inc., iPhone, Steve Jobs
RelationshipConnection between objectsFounded, released, belongs to, located in
AttributeAn object's own characteristicFounding year, headquarters address, price, date of birth
TypeThe category an entity belongs toCompany, person, product, city
OntologyRules defining concepts and relationshipsA company can have a founder; a product can belong to a company
SourceWhere a fact comes fromOfficial website, database, document, human review
ConfidenceHow trustworthy a fact is0.95, reviewed, awaiting confirmation

The basic form of knowledge: Triples

Knowledge graphs most commonly express information as triples: subject–predicate–object.

乔布斯 → 创立 → 苹果公司
苹果公司 → 发布 → iPhone
北京 → 是首都 → 中国
阿司匹林 → 可缓解 → 疼痛

Each triple records one fact. Many connected triples form a knowledge graph.

3. Why not just use a database?

People often ask: couldn't this data simply go into a database?

Of course it could. Relational databases excel at storing and managing structured data, including users, orders, products, and employees.

The distinction lies in the design philosophy:a database optimizes organizing data into tables; a knowledge graph optimizes expressing relationships clearly.

A financial risk-control example

A risk-control system might have tables for users, devices, bank cards, phone numbers, transactions, and merchants.

Viewed separately, every user in each table looks normal.

Connect their relationships, however, and hidden risks emerge:

用户A → 使用 → 设备X
用户B → 使用 → 设备X
用户C → 使用 → 设备X

用户A → 绑定 → 银行卡Y
用户B → 收款至 → 银行卡Y

用户A、B、C → 登录自 → 同一IP地址

The risk lies not in a single record, but in the pattern formed by these relationships.

Databases can query relationships with JOINs, but many relationship types, deep traversals, and mixed data sources make schemas complex and difficult to maintain. Knowledge graphs are better suited to questions such as:

  • Who is related to whom?
  • What paths connect them?
  • What does a path mean?
  • Does this set of relationships reveal a risk, opportunity, or dependency?

A knowledge graph does not replace the database; it adds a layer of relationship understanding between databases and applications.

4. Knowledge graphs versus search and vector databases

Search engines, vector databases, and knowledge graphs are all common in modern AI applications. Each has its strengths:

数据库 → 擅长存储精确的记录
搜索引擎 → 擅长找包含关键词的文本
向量数据库 → 擅长找语义相似的内容
知识图谱 → 擅长表达实体之间的关系

An enterprise knowledge-base example

A user asks:上次 Chat 接口为什么重构？

Keyword search finds documents containing “Chat,” “API,” and “refactoring.”

Vector retrieval finds semantically similar passages, such as “API modernization” or “request-path changes.”

A knowledge graph finds documents and also reveals:

  • Which system owns the Chat API
  • Which services it depends on
  • Which errors have occurred historically
  • Which logs, tests, and meeting notes mention it
  • Who has been responsible for that request path
  • Which upstream and downstream systems the refactoring affected

The advantage is organizing context along entity relationships, beyond merely finding similar content.

5. Core knowledge-graph concepts

You need not dive straight into RDF, OWL, or SPARQL. Start by understanding the following concepts.

1. Entities: Identity matters

Entities are a graph's basic nodes. The hard part is not recognizing a word, but identifying the exact object it refers to.

"苹果" → 水果？苹果公司？内部项目代号？
"张伟" → 销售同事？客户联系人？
"Chat" → 页面组件？后端接口？产品模块？

Get identity wrong and every subsequent relationship becomes wrong. The first crucial task is therefore entity recognition and disambiguation.

2. Relationships: Not every line is meaningful

Relationships are the heart of a graph, but two entities cannot be connected arbitrarily. A meaningful relationship must answer:

  • What does it mean?
  • Does it have a direction?
  • Does it have a time range?
  • What is its source?
  • Can the business explain it?

Consider this chain:

员工A → 负责 → 项目B
项目B → 依赖 → 系统C
系统C → 出现 → 错误D
错误D → 记录于 → 日志E

This path clearly explains why Project B is affected. An arbitrary “related to” edge would offer far less business value.

3. Ontology: Defining the rules

Think of an ontology as the knowledge graph's architectural blueprint. It specifies:

  • Which entity types exist?
  • Which relationship types exist?
  • Which relationships are valid? For example, a person may have a birthplace, but a company may not
  • Which attributes are required?
  • What hierarchies exist between entities?

Without ontology constraints, a graph easily becomes a tangle of lines.

4. Sources and confidence: Traceability matters

A production knowledge graph must record the source of every fact.

来自官网 → 高信任
来自数据库 → 中高信任
来自模型自动抽取 → 低信任
来自人工审核 → 最高信任

Especially in finance, healthcare, and law, saying “the graph contains this relationship” is insufficient. You must also explain:

  • Where did it come from?
  • When was it created?
  • Who reviewed it?
  • Is it still valid?
  • How can it be rolled back if wrong?

6. How knowledge graphs are built

Knowledge graphs are not drawn manually one line at a time. The practical process is:

确定业务问题
  ↓
设计 schema / 本体
  ↓
接入数据源
  ↓
抽取实体和关系
  ↓
实体链接与消歧
  ↓
融合多源数据
  ↓
质量校验
  ↓
存储和查询
  ↓
接入应用
  ↓
持续迭代更新

Step 1: Define the business objective

Rather than starting with “I want an enterprise knowledge graph,” ask:

  • What specific questions must it answer?
  • Will it help support agents answer product questions faster?
  • Will it help risk teams detect fraud rings?
  • Will it help engineers understand system dependencies?
  • Will it help doctors find relationships between diseases and medications?

The more concrete the objective, the easier implementation becomes.

Step 2: Design the schema

The schema is the graph's skeleton. For enterprise engineering knowledge, an initial version could simply define:

Entity types: Project, system, API, document, person, error, test record

Relationship types: 

人员 → 负责 → 项目
项目 → 包含 → 系统
系统 → 提供 → 接口
接口 → 出现 → 错误
错误 → 记录于 → 日志
文档 → 描述 → 系统
测试记录 → 验证 → 接口

Key principle: Do not aim for comprehensive coverage initially. Correct connections among core entities matter more than accumulating many types.

Step 3: Extract knowledge from data

Data sources generally fall into three categories:

Structured: Databases, tables, APIs

  • Rules can map them directly into the graph

Semistructured: Webpages, JSON, configuration files

  • Require parsing and transformation

Unstructured: Documents, emails, support tickets, meeting notes

  • Require NLP or large models to extract entities and relationships

Important reminder: Candidate knowledge extracted by a model should not enter the database directly. It still needs rule validation, source tagging, confidence scoring, and human review.

Step 4: Entity disambiguation and fusion

This critical step is often underestimated.

Different systems may use different names for the same object:

IBM = International Business Machines = 国际商业机器公司

The same name can also refer to different objects:

"苹果" → 水果？苹果公司？内部项目？
"张伟" → 销售员工？客户？供应商？

Poor handling leads to:

  • Incorrect merges that bind unrelated facts together
  • Incorrect splits that fragment knowledge about one object

Entity disambiguation and fusion are therefore central to graph quality.

Step 5: Integrate applications and iterate

Building the graph is only the beginning. Connect it to real applications: search, question answering, recommendations, risk control, and data governance.

Then continuously improve it using feedback:

  • What did users click?
  • Was the answer accepted?
  • Which relationships are frequently missing?
  • Which facts have expired?
  • Which entities were created twice?

This feedback drives iterative improvement.

7. Knowledge-graph applications

Knowledge graphs suit scenarios with complex relationships, a need for explanations, and multiple data sources.

Search

When Google introduced Knowledge Graph in 2012, it used the memorable phrase:

Things, not strings—understanding things, rather than just strings.

When you search for a person, place, film, or company, the engine can return structured profiles, related entities, and historical events alongside webpages. Knowledge graphs make this possible.

Recommendation systems

E-commerce recommendations go beyond “people who bought A also bought B.” A knowledge graph can understand:

  • Which category a product belongs to
  • Relationships between brands
  • Users' preferences in different situations
  • Compatibility between accessories and devices

These relationships make recommendations easier to explain and trust.

Financial risk control

A risk graph connects users, accounts, devices, bank cards, phone numbers, IP addresses, merchants, and transactions.

It excels at discovering fraud rings hidden across multiple hops: accounts sharing devices or receiving cards, logging in from the same IP, or funneling funds to one merchant. Graph structures make these patterns easier to identify.

Healthcare and pharmaceuticals

Medical knowledge naturally suits graphs: diseases, symptoms, drugs, genes, examinations, guidelines, and contraindications have explicit relationships.

However, medical graphs impose extremely strict sourcing and review requirements. Automatically generated model output cannot be treated as medical fact.

Enterprise knowledge management

This is a particularly promising new direction.

Enterprise knowledge is scattered across documents, code, tickets, chats, meeting notes, and configuration. Knowledge graphs can connect projects, systems, APIs, people, documents, decisions, and incidents.

When an employee asks a question, the system goes beyond finding similar documents to organizing an answer through the enterprise knowledge network.

Large models and GraphRAG

Large models have opened new applications for knowledge graphs.

Traditional RAG flow: 

文档切块 → 向量检索 → 召回文本 → 大模型生成答案

This works well for single-document questions, but may miss essential context when questions span documents, entities, and multihop relationships.

The GraphRAG approach: 

识别实体和关系
  → 构建图结构
  → 沿着图谱找相关上下文
  → 交给大模型生成答案

Knowledge graphs do not replace large models; they give them a sturdier factual framework.

8. Conclusion

A knowledge graph can be understood simply as:

A machine-readable network of facts and relationships

In depth, however, it involves much more than connecting entities: identity, relationship semantics, ontology constraints, provenance, confidence, permissions, versioning, and application feedback loops all matter.

The real value of a knowledge graph is therefore not drawing data as a network, but making scattered, implicit, hard-to-reuse relationships explicit.

In search, it moves systems from matching strings to understanding entities.

In enterprises, it moves the business from isolated data to relationship insights.

In the large-model era, it helps AI move from generating text to reasoning with structured context.

Deciding whether a scenario needs a knowledge graph

When the essential issue lies in relationships between objects rather than individual records, and answers must explain their sources and paths as well as provide results, knowledge graphs become valuable.

 

Reference link:

https://github.com/husthuke/awesome-knowledge-graph

title: Setting Up a macOS Terminal: Suggestions, Syntax Highlighting, and Themes
html:
Environment: Apple Silicon Mac · zsh · Homebrew

Prerequisites

Make sure Homebrew is installed. If it is not, run:

/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

Step 1: Install Oh My Zsh

sh -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ohmyzsh/ohmyzsh/master/tools/install.sh)"

After installation, the terminal switches to the new zsh configuration and creates ~/.zshrc.

Step 2: Install the Powerlevel10k Theme

git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k.git \
  ${ZSH_CUSTOM:-$HOME/.oh-my-zsh/custom}/themes/powerlevel10k

Edit ~/.zshrc, find the ZSH_THEME line, and change it to:

# 找到这一行
ZSH_THEME="robbyrussell"

# 改为
ZSH_THEME="powerlevel10k/powerlevel10k"

Step 3: Install a Nerd Font

Powerlevel10k needs a font with icon support. Install the Nerd Fonts version of Meslo through Homebrew:

brew install --cask font-meslo-lg-nerd-font

📝 The font installed by this cask appears in the system as MesloLGS Nerd Font, with Regular, Bold, Italic, and Bold Italic variants. Its source differs slightly from the “MesloLGS NF” mentioned in the official P10k documentation, but it is fully compatible with all the icons.

Then select this font in your terminal application's preferences:

  • Terminal.app: Preferences → Profiles → Font → choose MesloLGS Nerd Font
  • iTerm2: Preferences → Profiles → Text → Font → choose MesloLGS Nerd Font

Step 4: Install zsh-autosuggestions

git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-autosuggestions \
  ${ZSH_CUSTOM:-$HOME/.oh-my-zsh/custom}/plugins/zsh-autosuggestions

Step 5: Install zsh-completions

git clone https://github.com/zsh-users/zsh-completions \
  ${ZSH_CUSTOM:-$HOME/.oh-my-zsh/custom}/plugins/zsh-completions

⚠️ Important: After enabling zsh-completions as an OMZ plugin for the first time, you must force a rebuild of the completion cache before it takes effect. Step 8 includes this operation.

Step 6: Install zsh-syntax-highlighting

Install it through Homebrew, rather than in the Oh My Zsh plugin directory:

brew install zsh-syntax-highlighting

Step 7: Configure ~/.zshrc

Replace the entire ~/.zshrc with the following, or use the comments to merge each section into your existing file:

# ── Powerlevel10k 即时提示（必须放最顶部）──────────────────────────
if [[ -r "${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/p10k-instant-prompt-${(%):-%n}.zsh" ]]; then
  source "${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-$HOME/.cache}/p10k-instant-prompt-${(%):-%n}.zsh"
fi

# ── 自定义补全目录加入 fpath（必须在 source oh-my-zsh.sh 之前）─────
# 不要在这里手动调 compinit，OMZ 会自己调一次，避免重复
fpath=("$HOME/.oh-my-zsh/custom/completions" $fpath)

# ── Oh My Zsh 基础配置 ─────────────────────────────────────────────
export ZSH="$HOME/.oh-my-zsh"
ZSH_THEME="powerlevel10k/powerlevel10k"

plugins=(
    git
    zsh-autosuggestions
    zsh-completions
)

source $ZSH/oh-my-zsh.sh

# ── 语法高亮（必须放最末尾）───────────────────────────────────────
# Apple Silicon 下 Homebrew 前缀固定为 /opt/homebrew，写死避免每次启动 fork 一次 brew
source /opt/homebrew/share/zsh-syntax-highlighting/zsh-syntax-highlighting.zsh

# ── Powerlevel10k 用户配置 ────────────────────────────────────────
[[ ! -f ~/.p10k.zsh ]] || source ~/.p10k.zsh

Step 8: Rebuild the Completion Cache and Reload

When enabling zsh-completions for the first time, you must force a rebuild of zcompdump; otherwise, the additional completions will not work:

rm -f ~/.zcompdump*
exec zsh

exec zsh replaces the current shell with a fresh zsh process. This is more thorough than source ~/.zshrc and also lets instant prompt work correctly.

The first load automatically starts the p10k configuration wizard. Follow its prompts:

  1. Check whether font symbols such as diamonds and locks display correctly → choose Yes or No.
  2. Choose a prompt style → Rainbow or Lean is recommended.
  3. Choose a character set → Unicode is recommended.
  4. Select the items you want displayed, such as time, directory, and Git status.

The wizard automatically creates ~/.p10k.zsh.

To run the configuration again:

p10k configure

Step 9: Verify the Result

FeatureHow to check
ThemeThe prompt should display colored icons and the Git branch.
History suggestionsType ls. A gray suggestion should appear to the right; press → to accept it.
Syntax highlightingKnown commands should appear green and unknown commands red.
Tab completionType git che and press Tab to see completion candidates.
Extended completionsType docker comp and press Tab. It should complete to compose, provided by zsh-completions.

title: Publishing Markdown Notes with mdBook and GitHub Pages
html:
All articles from this WeChat account are also organized in the GitHub repository https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/AI-Fullstack-Notes. The repository versions include more complete code examples, supplementary explanations, and subsequent updates. If you find them helpful, star ⭐ the repository to bookmark it, and feel free to report errors or discuss ideas through Issues.

Scenario: You have a collection of Markdown notes and want to organize them into an online “technical book” with navigation and search, automatically published every time you git push. mdBook + GitHub Pages + GitHub Actions can do all this in 30 minutes, completely free.

This article covers:

  • Local installation and initialization
  • Directory structure and SUMMARY.md writing rules
  • book.toml complete configuration guide
  • Customizing appearance (theme colors, fonts, favicon)
  • Automated deployment with GitHub Actions, .gitignore, and Pages settings

1. Prerequisites

ToolVersion requirementDescription
Rust / CargoAny stable releaseUsed to install mdBook through cargo install
Git≥ 2.xVersion control and pushing
GitHub account—Repository hosting + Pages deployment

If you do not want to install Rust, download a precompiled binary from GitHub Releases and put it on your PATH.

2. Install mdBook

Option A: Install through Cargo (Recommended)

cargo install mdbook

Verify after installation:

mdbook --version
# 常见为 v0.5.x（与 CI 里 mdbook-version: "latest" 一致）
# 若需与旧版插件兼容，可固定为 0.4.x，例如：cargo install mdbook --locked --version 0.4.52

Option B: Download a Binary (No Rust Required)

# macOS (Apple Silicon)
curl -L https://github.com/rust-lang/mdBook/releases/latest/download/mdbook-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz \
  | tar xz -C /usr/local/bin

# Linux x86_64
curl -L https://github.com/rust-lang/mdBook/releases/latest/download/mdbook-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz \
  | tar xz -C /usr/local/bin

3. Initialize the Project

3.1 New Project

mdbook init my-notes
cd my-notes

init generates this structure:

my-notes/
├── book.toml        # 核心配置文件
└── src/
    ├── SUMMARY.md   # 目录（mdBook 的"地图"）
    └── chapter_1.md

3.2 Use an Existing Markdown Repository

If you already have a Git repository containing .md files, run this directly at its root:

mdbook init --force .

Then manually adjust the book.toml file's src path (explained in the next section).

Note: mdbook build defaults to the output directory book/ at the repository root. Add the root-level .gitignore entry for book/ early (see Section 9). Do not commit book/ as a submodule; otherwise, it will have no URL in .gitmodules and CI will fail when actions/checkout tries to fetch submodules.

4. Complete book.toml Configuration Guide

book.toml is mdBook's main configuration file, in TOML format. Below is a complete, production-ready configuration with line-by-line comments:

# ── 书籍基本信息 ──────────────────────────────────────────
[book]
title       = "AI-Fullstack-Notes"          # 显示在左上角的书名
description = "全栈工程师的 AI/Agent 学习笔记"
authors     = ["Eva"]
language    = "zh"                           # 界面语言（影响搜索分词）
src         = "."                            # Markdown 源文件根目录
                                             # 默认 "src"；改成 "." 表示仓库根目录即源目录

# ── HTML 输出配置 ─────────────────────────────────────────
[output.html]
site-url = "/AI-Fullstack-Notes/"           # GitHub Pages 子路径，必须与仓库名一致
                                             # 本地预览时注释掉此行，否则资源路径会错

git-repository-url  = "https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/AI-Fullstack-Notes"
# mdBook 0.5+：品牌图标 fa-github 等会触发构建错误 Missing font github，请省略 git-repository-icon。
# git-repository-icon = "fa-github"

# 每个页面底部显示"在 GitHub 上编辑此页"链接
edit-url-template = "https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/AI-Fullstack-Notes/edit/main/{path}"

# 其他常用可选项（按需启用）：
# theme            = "coal"                 # 默认主题：light/rust/coal/navy/ayu
# default-theme    = "light"               # 读者首次打开时的主题
# preferred-dark-theme = "navy"            # 系统暗色模式时使用的主题
# mathjax-support  = true                  # 启用 LaTeX 数学公式
# no-section-label = true                  # 目录标题前不显示章节编号
# additional-css   = ["theme/custom.css"]  # 自定义 CSS
# additional-js    = ["theme/custom.js"]   # 自定义 JS
# search.enable    = true                  # 默认开启全文搜索

A key pitfall: site-url must exactly match your GitHub repository name, including capitalization; otherwise, image and CSS paths will all return 404 after deployment.

5. Rules for Writing SUMMARY.md

SUMMARY.md is the only entry point through which mdBook reads the table of contents. File paths are relative to the src directory (the directory specified by book.toml's src setting).

5.1 Basic Syntax

# 目录

<!-- 前言：不计入章节编号，显示在最顶部 -->
[前言](README.md)

---

# 一级分组标题（纯文本，不可点击）

- [章节标题](path/to/file.md)
  - [子章节](path/to/sub.md)
    - [孙章节](path/to/subsub.md)

# 另一个分组

- [另一章](another.md)

---

<!-- 后记：不计入章节编号 -->
[附录](appendix.md)

5.2 Practical Example (This Project's SUMMARY.md Structure)

# 目录

[前言](README.md)

---

# AI / Agent

- [LangChain 架构浅析](ai/langchain-architecture.md)
- [LangGraph — 通过图结构重新定义 LLM 应用](ai/langgraph-intro.md)
- [RAG 实战：从手写 MVP 到生产级优化](ai/rag-mvp-to-production.md)

# 架构 / 后端

- [高并发架构设计思考](backend/high-concurrency-architecture.md)
- [Nginx 全解析：反向代理与负载均衡](backend/nginx-reverse-proxy-load-balance.md)

# 基础设施 / 运维

- [Docker 基础与 Dockerfile 编写](infra/docker-basics-dockerfile.md)
- [5 分钟用 Docker 自建 Supabase](infra/supabase-docker-self-host.md)

5.3 Quick Reference

RuleDescription
[标题](路径)Only files listed here appear in the book
---Horizontal separator, for visual separation only
# 标题Group heading; not clickable and generates no page
Indentation (2 or 4 spaces)Indicates subchapters; nesting is unlimited
File pathsRelative to the src directory; unlisted .md files are not compiled

6. Local Preview

# 启动本地开发服务器，文件变动自动刷新
mdbook serve --open

# 仅构建，不启动服务器
mdbook build
# 输出目录：./book/

For local previews, if book.toml sets site-url = "/AI-Fullstack-Notes/", visiting http://localhost:3000 shows a blank page. Temporarily comment out that line, or access it through http://localhost:3000/AI-Fullstack-Notes/.

7. Customize the Appearance (Optional)

7.1 Override Theme Variables

Create a theme/ folder at the project root and add custom.css: 

/* theme/custom.css */
:root {
  --sidebar-bg: #1a1a2e;        /* 侧边栏背景色 */
  --sidebar-fg: #e0e0e0;        /* 侧边栏文字色 */
  --links: #4fc3f7;             /* 链接颜色 */
}

Reference it in book.toml:

[output.html]
additional-css = ["theme/custom.css"]

7.2 Add a Favicon

mkdir -p theme
cp your-favicon.png theme/favicon.png
# 或 .ico 格式
cp your-favicon.ico theme/favicon.ico

mdBook automatically recognizes theme/favicon.png or theme/favicon.ico; no extra configuration is needed.

7.3 Enable MathJax (Mathematical Formulas)

[output.html]
mathjax-support = true

Usage:

行内公式：$E = mc^2$

块级公式：
$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-x^2} dx = \sqrt{\pi}
$$

8. Automated Deployment with GitHub Actions

8.1 Directory Structure

your-repo/
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── deploy.yml   ← 新建此文件
├── book.toml
├── SUMMARY.md
├── .gitignore           ← 建议：忽略 book/（见第九节）
└── ...（你的 .md 文件）

8.2 Complete deploy.yml

name: Deploy mdBook to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main          # 只有推送到 main 分支才触发

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write  # 必须：允许 Actions 向仓库写入（gh-pages 分支）

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          submodules: false   # 若误把 book/ 登记成 submodule 且无 .gitmodules，拉子模块会失败；显式关闭更稳妥

      - name: Install mdBook
        uses: peaceiris/actions-mdbook@v2
        with:
          mdbook-version: "latest"   # 可固定版本号，如 "0.4.52"（需与本地/插件兼容时再考虑）

      - name: Build
        run: mdbook build

      - name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
        uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v4
        with:
          github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          publish_dir: ./book        # 只发布构建产物，勿把整个仓库推到 gh-pages
          # force_orphan: true      # 可选：每次用单提交覆盖 gh-pages，清掉历史上误提交的源码/混杂文件

8.3 GitHub Repository Settings

  1. 1. Open the repository → Settings → Pages
  2. 2. For Source, select Deploy from a branch
  3. 3. For Branch, select gh-pages, and for the directory select / (root)
  4. 4. Click Save

Choose the correct Pages source:

  • Do not use main + /docs: it runs Jekyll (logs often show jekyll-build-pages, Source: .../docs). Without a Jekyll project, it reports that the /docs directory does not exist.
  • Do not use main + / (root): GitHub still processes the repository with Jekyll, and the homepage is often README.md, which looks like a “single-page document”, not the mdBook book interface. Online reading must use the static files on gh-pages.
  • Correct: gh-pages + / (root) (the previous section's deploy.yml pushes ./book/ to gh-pages).

After the first git push main, wait for Actions to finish (about 1–2 minutes), then visit:

https://<你的用户名>.github.io/<仓库名>/

8.4 Workflow Explanation

git push main
     │
     ▼
GitHub Actions 触发
     │
     ├─ actions/checkout@v4        # 拉取代码（submodules: false）
     ├─ peaceiris/actions-mdbook@v2 # 安装 mdBook 二进制
     ├─ mdbook build               # 编译 → ./book/
     └─ peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v4
           └─ 将 ./book/ 推送到 gh-pages 分支
                    │
                    ▼
           GitHub Pages 自动部署

9. .gitignore Configuration

The build output directory book/ should be ignored to avoid:

  • Committing large numbers of generated files to main;
  • Accidentally registering book/ as a Git submodule (if the index contains mode 160000 with no .gitmodules, CI reports No url found for submodule path 'book').
# mdBook 构建输出（勿提交；勿误登记为 submodule）
book/

10. Final Project Structure Reference

AI-Fullstack-Notes/
├── .github/
│   └── workflows/
│       └── deploy.yml        # CI/CD 自动部署
├── ai/
│   ├── langchain-architecture.md
│   └── rag-mvp-to-production.md
├── backend/
│   └── high-concurrency-architecture.md
├── infra/
│   └── docker-basics-dockerfile.md
├── projects/
│   └── fastsam-demo-v1.md
├── theme/
│   ├── custom.css            # 可选：自定义样式
│   └── favicon.png           # 可选：网站图标
├── book.toml                 # 核心配置
├── SUMMARY.md                # 目录结构
├── README.md                 # 前言/首页
└── .gitignore                # 排除 book/

Summary

After this process, you have a technical knowledge base with automated publishing, full-text search, dark mode support, free hosting. From then on, edit Markdown on main and git push; Actions runs mdbook build again and updates gh-pages. Readers must access the gh-pages root directory configured in Pages to reach the mdBook site.

title: Understanding MFA and Dynamic Verification Codes Through a Login
html:
You enter your password and click Log In, only for the website to ask you to open your phone's authenticator and enter six digits. You just proved you know the password. Why verify yourself again?

Start with that login screen. If someone else already has your password, how will the server handle their login request?

A password-only system struggles to distinguish you from them. Both submit exactly the same secret, so the server naturally gives the same result. Even a very long password has this problem once it is fully exposed.

MFA adds another check that can still stop the other person at that point.

This article follows the common “account password plus authenticator” flow, explaining an account's journey from enabling protection to everyday login and recovering after losing a device. Algorithm and security requirements are checked against RFCs, NIST, and OWASP materials. The implementations described illustrate the principles; they do not imply that a particular project already includes these features.

What can you verify after a password leaks?

A password proves that you know a secret. The system can also require proof that you control an authenticator bound to the account in advance.

Someone who knows the password then still lacks the second condition. You can open your authenticator to obtain the current code; someone with only the password usually cannot.

These are two different categories of proof, or two “authentication factors.”

Authentication factorWhat it provesCommon examples
Knowledge factorYou know a secretPassword, PIN
Possession factorYou control an authenticator or the secret it containsAuthenticator, security key
Biometric factorYour physical characteristics meet the requirementFingerprint, face

MFA is the umbrella term for multifactor authentication; both 2FA and 3FA are forms of MFA. MFA stands for Multi-Factor Authentication and requires at least two different categories of authentication factors.

The “password plus authenticator code” flow combines knowledge and possession factors, making it 2FA, or two-factor authentication. It already satisfies MFA, so a website can reasonably call it either MFA or 2FA. A third factor is not required.

If a system also requires a fingerprint and correctly combines and verifies a password, hardware security key, and fingerprint, it constitutes 3FA, or three-factor authentication. The distinction is the number of factor categories used; MFA and 2FA are not two separate login technologies.

Three verification steps do not necessarily constitute 3FA. Entering a password, SMS code, and TOTP code looks like three steps, but the last two usually both represent possession. The flow still uses only two categories. Count the categories of proof, not pages or input boxes.

This also explains why “asking one more question” may not help. A security question after a password still tests what you know. There are two steps, but only one factor category. Logging in with only an SMS verification code usually uses just one possession factor; a verification code alone does not mean MFA is enabled.

For this account, we are choosing a password plus an authenticator. The password already exists; next, the website must recognize your authenticator. Otherwise, anyone could open an app that generates numbers—why should the server accept yours?

The setup QR code links your phone to your account

Open the account's security settings and enable an authenticator. The website typically displays a QR code, asks you to scan it, and then asks for the code shown in the app.

This step is called binding or enrollment.

The server first generates a random secret for the account, called a shared key. The QR code carries that key along with the account name, issuer, and algorithm parameters. After scanning it, the authenticator saves this information, giving the phone and server identical copies of the secret. The common otpauth:// format conveys this enrollment information.

Below the QR code, you may also see an option to enter the key manually. This is an alternative when scanning is unavailable.Both the QR code and manual key must remain secret: anyone who obtains their contents may be able to reproduce the same codes.

Why enter a verification code after scanning? Displaying a QR code does not establish that the phone saved the key correctly. You may have scanned the wrong account or closed the page midway. Checking the first code generated by the phone confirms that both sides can calculate from the same information before changing the factor from “pending confirmation” to “enabled.”

The current user's identity must also be verified before binding. Someone who happens to access a device you left logged in should not be able to easily bind their own authenticator. Replacing or disabling MFA later similarly requires reauthentication proportionate to the risk.

The phone now stores the key. Its displayed numbers count down and change at the end of each interval, even without a network connection.

Where do these numbers come from?

How can an offline phone produce numbers the website accepts?

The phone and server agree on an algorithm and independently calculate using the shared key and current time. They do not need to send codes to each other every few dozen seconds.

This mechanism is TOTP, short for Time-Based One-Time Password. A common configuration uses six digits, refreshed every 30 seconds. The number of digits and time interval are configurable; neither value is a universal requirement.

Set formulas aside for now. Imagine dividing time into consecutive intervals. Within the same interval, both parties obtain the same time number and combine it with the same key to calculate the same digits. In the next interval, the number changes, and so does the result.

The algorithm's “time step” is this number.

T = floor((当前 Unix 时间 - 起始时间) / 时间步长度)
TOTP = HOTP(共享密钥 K, 时间步 T)

HOTP in the formula is another one-time-password algorithm. It uses a key and counter, applying HMAC and truncation to produce digits suitable for entry. TOTP builds on it by replacing the event counter with a time step. In real development, use mature libraries and standard test vectors rather than implementing these cryptographic details yourself.

The abbreviations now fall into place. OTP is the general category of one-time-password mechanisms; HOTP and TOTP are specific algorithms. MFA and 2FA describe how many different factors a login combines. We use TOTP for the possession factor and combine it with a password to provide two-factor authentication.

The phone can calculate offline because both its key and clock are local. Accessing the website still requires a network connection, of course.

Clock inaccuracies can cause problems. A phone may run slightly fast or slow, or a user may submit at the final second of a countdown. Servers typically need an explicitly limited time tolerance to verify neighboring time steps. A wider window accepts more possible codes at once, so tolerance cannot grow indefinitely.

Storage differs here as well. To verify TOTP, the server must recalculate with the shared key. It therefore usually encrypts the key and manages the decryption master key separately from the database. An irreversible hash alone cannot support this calculation. Enrollment QR codes, shared keys, and submitted dynamic codes should also stay out of logs.

Only after these preparations does the account have a usable second factor. Log out and log back in to see how it works.

At the next login, the correct password only gets you halfway

You enter your account and password, and the server confirms the password. For an account requiring MFA, it should retain a restricted intermediate state while awaiting code verification.

This temporary state is often called an MFA challenge. It records the account being verified, what is permitted, and when it expires. The browser may use it to submit a code, but not to read business data.

You then see a second page asking you to open your authenticator. After you enter its current digits, the server retrieves the account's shared key, calculates results within the allowed time window, and compares them. Only successful verification establishes a full session with application access.

Between those two checks, the account must not receive full application access. If a full session is issued immediately after password verification and only a frontend code prompt follows, an attacker can skip the page and use that session to call backend APIs directly. The second page exists, but its protection does not.

The server must therefore distinguish two facts. Having MFA enrolled means a factor is available; completing MFA in the current session means this particular login met the requirement. Session refresh must retain the relevant authentication information and expiry, and must not silently promote an incomplete login.

A website usually does not ask for another code every time you open an article. After login, the browser carries session credentials that identify the authenticated login. Changing an authenticator or performing a sensitive operation may require recent reauthentication. Risk signals such as changed devices or login locations can also trigger additional verification.

Authentication still does not confer administrator privileges. The server must separately check what the account may do. An ordinary member who completes MFA can access only authorized data.

The login flow now appears complete, but dynamic codes hide one easily overlooked issue.

Can the same code be used twice before the countdown ends?

Within one time step, the digits displayed on the phone do not change. If the server checks only whether the digits match, two consecutive submissions may both succeed.

That conflicts with the one-time requirement.

TOTP generates numbers that change over time; the server must also remember which time step has already succeeded. After verification, a database transaction and conditional update should mark that step and the current challenge as consumed so later requests cannot succeed again. A common approach stores the most recently accepted time step for the factor and accepts only newer values allowed by policy.

This process must handle concurrency. Two requests can arrive almost simultaneously and both read “unused.” Without atomicity between reading and writing, both might pass. Verification must ensure only one request consumes the challenge and receives a usable session. If the database fails, full privileges must not be granted first.

If the client does not receive the success response, the user may need to restart verification. Safe retry handling is possible, but a consumed code cannot simply become valid again.

Guessing codes is another problem. Six digits provide a limited space, so failed attempts must be restricted. Limiting only an individual challenge is insufficient: an attacker may repeatedly request new challenges. Apply account-level rate limits as well, with source addresses as an additional dimension. Set thresholds according to system risk and actual usage.

At this point, a leaked password alone cannot complete this login flow. But the more effective these restrictions are, the more important reliable recovery becomes when a legitimate user loses their authenticator.

How do you recover an account after losing your phone?

This is why websites often ask you to save recovery codes when enabling MFA.

Recovery codes are pregenerated random backup credentials, each invalidated after successful use. Unlike TOTP, they usually do not change every few dozen seconds. Store them somewhere accessible even after losing the phone. A screenshot kept only on that same phone may disappear along with your backup method.

The server does not need the original recovery codes to recalculate dynamic codes, so it can store hashes of high-entropy recovery codes and their usage state. This differs from TOTP shared keys, which must be decryptable.

Return to the login screen with a lost phone. The password is correct, but TOTP is unavailable, so the user chooses recovery. The system verifies a recovery code under predefined rules, consumes it on success, and guides the user through regaining access or binding a new authenticator.

Define in advance which step the recovery code replaces, whether a password remains required, and which functions become accessible afterward. An administration console could issue a short-lived, restricted recovery session, require enrollment of a new authenticator, and only then restore full access. Revoke the old factor and remaining old recovery codes according to policy, and notify the account holder of the change.

If every authenticator and recovery code is lost, the user must follow a predefined identity-verification process. Support staff cannot disable MFA after improvising a few easily guessed questions, because an attacker could take the same route.

Recovery is therefore part of authentication design. If normal login is strict but recovery checks only an easily compromised email account, attackers may take over through that route. Whether email can support a particular recovery step depends on the complete flow; NIST's out-of-band authentication requirements do not accept email as that type of authentication channel either.

We have now connected enrollment, login, and device-loss handling for an account. One more situation deserves attention. The phone is not lost and the code has not been exposed for long: it was just entered into a fake website immediately after generation. What happens then?

Dynamic codes can also be phished. How can the second factor improve?

An attacker can relay them in real time.

The user enters a password and current code into a fake page; the attacker immediately submits both to the real website. If verification is still valid, login may succeed. TOTP's short lifetime reduces the opportunity for abuse but cannot independently stop immediate exploitation.

Other verification methods are easier to understand once you see which link each changes.

SMS delegates code delivery to telecommunications networks, adding risks such as number transfers and SIM swaps. Push approval removes manual digit entry, but users must recognize legitimate requests, and repeated notifications may lead to accidental approval. Both require carefully designed failure and recovery flows.

FIDO security keys and passkeys use public-key authentication. During registration, the authenticator creates credentials for the service and the server stores the public key. At login, the server issues a challenge, the authenticator signs with the private key, and the server verifies the signature. A correctly implemented WebAuthn flow checks the service identifier and origin, preventing a phishing domain from freely obtaining and using authentication results for the real site.

This provides phishing resistance and changes the user's interaction. They may insert a security key or approve with a device PIN, fingerprint, or face, without copying dynamic digits into a webpage.

Fingerprint verification usually happens locally on the device; the website does not need fingerprint data. When the service correctly requires and verifies user verification, the device credential and local PIN or biometric can jointly provide multifactor authentication. A single fingerprint action can therefore satisfy multiple factors.

This does not contradict the “two inputs” at the start. The authentication method determines the number of factors. Passwordless login means only that the site's password is unused; it does not automatically establish a factor count. Logging in through an email link also offers different protection from a passkey with user verification.

Recovery still matters after choosing passkeys. Credentials may be bound to one device or synchronized through a credential provider. You need to understand how new devices obtain them and how the synchronization account is recovered. With traditional TOTP, keeping the password and code-generating secret in the same password manager is also a tradeoff: it reduces effort, but a complete compromise of that storage system can expose both credentials together.

There is also a shared boundary. After successful login, the browser receives session credentials. If an attacker steals still-valid credentials, they may access the application directly without revisiting the code page. HTTPS, cookie protection, defenses against script injection, and session revocation remain necessary.

Applying this flow to your own project

To add MFA to an existing system, review the journey this account just followed. First decide which accounts must enable it and how existing users will transition, then check the state required at each step.

Account stageWhat the server must storeWhat must be prevented
Preparing enrollmentPending factor, encrypted shared key, and expiryActivation before confirmation
Password acceptedShort-lived challenge, account, purpose, and failure countPremature application access
Dynamic code acceptedConsumed time step, consumed challenge, and session authentication informationReplay and duplicate concurrent success
Everyday accessSession expiry, revocation state, and application permissionsPromotion of unverified sessions or unauthorized access
Lost deviceRecovery-code hashes, consumption state, and recovery permissionsRepeated recovery or bypassed identity verification

Challenge tokens must be sufficiently random, and sensitive database information needs appropriate protection. Operational backups must also account for decryption keys: a database backup without its master key may leave existing TOTP enrollments unrecoverable.

For acceptance testing, walk through the entire flow with a controlled account. Exit halfway through scanning and confirm that the factor stays disabled. After password verification, call a business API directly and confirm access is still denied. Then submit the same code concurrently, confirm only one attempt succeeds, and verify that expired challenges cannot be reused.

Next, simulate an unavailable phone and rebind using a recovery code. Consumed recovery codes must not work again, and revoked authenticators must no longer authenticate. When the database fails or a response is lost, check that the system leaves no improperly usable session.

Finally, log in in the target environment and check certificates, clocks, and mandatory-enrollment policy. Even after the page says “MFA enabled,” test every entry point from logout through account recovery.

References

  • OWASP multifactor authentication implementation guidance
  • NIST authentication and authenticator management guidance
  • RFC 6238: TOTP algorithm and test vectors
  • RFC 4226: HOTP algorithm
  • FIDO Alliance explanation of passkeys

title: From Manual Orchestration to Autonomous Evolution: AI Productivity with OpenClaw
html:
This week marked the start of a new chapter for me as an AI full-stack engineer. I have been immersed in building around the OpenClaw ecosystem: implementing integrations across Feishu, WeChat, and Telegram, designing token-optimization strategies, configuring Skills, and practicing multi-agent collaboration.

After using it, two things stand out as the most practical: Skills and multiple agents. Skills are AI's hands and feet; multiple agents form its organizational structure. Although these may look like configuration choices, they address the same fundamental problem: how to move a language model from simulating human conversation to simulating human work.

The core idea behind Skills and multi-agent systems is turning a model's general-purpose reasoning into engineering productivity. Skills equip AI with senses and limbs. It is no longer just a black box that writes code or poetry; it has tools that use APIs and functions to perceive external systems and perform real business operations. The determinism of those capabilities compensates for the randomness of model generation, making the output more controllable and functional.

When a task becomes too complex for a single tool, multi-agent collaboration becomes a natural choice. The architecture resembles organizational management: divide a large task into specialist areas. Each agent acts as an expert with particular Skills, coordinating and handing off work through state machines or predefined workflows. This division can reduce the intent-recognition confusion that arises when one agent has too many tools. Role-based debate and cross-checking can also substantially reduce hallucinations.

This collaborative system will evolve toward greater autonomy and dynamism. Instead of hard-coding every execution step, a top-level coordinating agent will find, orchestrate, and even learn new Skills in response to real-time needs. The shift from manual orchestration to autonomous evolution is where multi-agent systems can truly realize their potential.

In practice, however, developers may find that the hardest problem is balancing execution cost and efficiency. Frequent interactions among agents create redundant context and can cause token consumption to grow exponentially. That is why so much frontier work focuses on fine-grained memory management and token-saving strategies. Optimizing short- and long-term memory, or passing more compact structured state between agents, is essential to making complex agent systems commercially sustainable.

I had another realization this week. I used to think AI was mostly about calling an API and experimenting. Running a whole system changed that perspective. What OpenClaw showed me was not how impressive one feature could be, but the value of a platform itself. A good platform does more than collect features: it lets everyone in the ecosystem extend and customize it to suit their own needs. Skills are a good example. They do not tell me what to build; they give me tools and let me decide how to put them together. That differs from how I used to approach projects. Previously I asked, “How do I finish this feature?” Now I ask, “How do I build a framework that lets people implement their own features?” That shift has been interesting.

What I learned most this week was not a particular configuration, but how to think in systems. Technical choices require trade-offs. OpenClaw is an ecosystem rather than a single tool, and its approach to Skills and platforms has influenced me. AI changes so quickly that a configuration I learn today may be obsolete in two months. What lasts is the ability to reason about a whole system, make trade-offs through hands-on work, and keep learning by experimenting and starting over. Tools will change; technical judgment and a sense of control over the system are the capabilities that retain their value.

title: OpenSpec: Spec-Driven Development for AI Coding
html:
Introduction

Now that AI coding is part of everyday development, why do requirements that exist only in chat create a hidden delivery risk? And how can spec-driven development tools such as OpenSpec turn drifting AI collaboration into an engineering process that can be reviewed, resumed, and archived?

OpenSpec is not a new code generator or a more complex project-management system.

It adds a lightweight “specification track” to AI coding assistants: align on what to build before coding, document changes during development, and merge incremental specifications into the project's current source of truth afterward. It addresses not whether AI can write code, but whether people and models agree on the goal before coding, and whether the project remembers the change afterward.

This article draws on OpenSpec's official documentation, GitHub project description, and my observations using it in local projects. It shares a practical approach to AI collaboration and represents my personal views.

1. Why Does AI Coding Need a Specification Track?

Over the past year, discussion of AI coding tools has focused on which model is smarter, which IDE integration works best, and how to write prompts that make an Agent get changes right on the first attempt.

These questions matter. But once an AI coding assistant joins a continuously evolving project, the harder questions are:

  • Does it understand this requirement's boundaries?
  • Are its code changes based on current project facts or temporary impressions in chat?
  • If this conversation ends, can the next one resume without losing anything?
  • When several people work simultaneously, who knows why a requirement was designed this way?
  • If production breaks three weeks later, can we recover the original design context?

Traditional development cushions these problems with requirements documents, design reviews, task breakdowns, PR reviews, and test cases. With AI assistants, many teams instead compress those safeguards into a chat:

“Add dark mode.”

“Also follow the system theme.”

“That design was wrong; use localStorage instead.”

“Continue.”

This works smoothly in a demo. In a real project, it gradually becomes context debt.

A chat window is not an engineering source of truth. It is good for communication and exploration, but poor at carrying long-term requirements or serving as a reviewable, reversible, transferable team record.

OpenSpec addresses this gap by moving AI collaboration from temporary chats back into a version-controlled specification workflow inside the repository.

2. What Exactly Is OpenSpec?

OpenSpec is a lightweight Spec-Driven Development (SDD) framework for AI coding assistants. Through a CLI, Slash Commands, and Skills, it puts proposals, specifications, designs, tasks, and archives into the code repository, allowing people and AI to align on what to build before writing code.

In one sentence:

OpenSpec is a specification workbench that moves requirements context from chat into the code repository.

It gives AI's freedom a track to follow rather than simply making AI more “free.”

After initialization, the project contains an openspec/ directory with roughly this structure:

openspec/
├── specs/
│   └── <domain>/
│       └── spec.md
├── changes/
│   └── <change-name>/
│       ├── proposal.md
│       ├── design.md
│       ├── tasks.md
│       └── specs/
│           └── <domain>/
│               └── spec.md
└── config.yaml

Two directories are key:

  • openspec/specs/: The main specification library for the project's current behavior; the requirements-level Source of Truth.
  • openspec/changes/: Active changes, each in its own folder containing a proposal, design, tasks, and specification deltas.

This expresses OpenSpec's basic position:

How the system currently works belongs in specs/; how this change will modify it belongs in changes/.

The separation looks simple, but is crucial for AI collaboration. It distinguishes the system's current state from the current change's intent, so the model need not guess project facts from an ever-longer conversation.

3. How Does OpenSpec Differ from Ordinary Documentation?

Many people first see OpenSpec and wonder whether it simply adds a few Markdown files to a project.

If that were all, a dedicated tool would be unnecessary. Its real value is turning documentation into an executable control plane for AI collaboration.

Common problems with ordinary documentation:

  • Nobody reads it after it is written.
  • Nobody updates it when the design changes.
  • It becomes historical baggage once it diverges from the code.
  • The AI does not know which document to read.
  • Collaborators lack a unified entry point.

OpenSpec embeds documentation into the workflow:

  • /opsx:propose first creates the change proposal and supporting artifacts.
  • /opsx:apply follows tasks.md and checks off progress.
  • /opsx:sync synchronizes delta specifications into the main specifications.
  • /opsx:archive archives the completed change while retaining historical context.

Documentation becomes the input, process, and acceptance criteria for AI work, rather than a side product.

In one sentence:

Ordinary documentation records what we once considered; OpenSpec governs how this change should be understood, implemented, and recorded.

4. Core Concepts: What Does OpenSpec Manage?

To understand OpenSpec, start with four objects: Spec, Change, Artifact, and Delta Spec.

1. Spec: The Source of Truth for Current System Behavior

openspec/specs/ contains specifications describing the behavior the system should currently provide. They are neither implementation plans nor explanations of code structure.

Good specifications focus on externally observable behavior:

  • What does the user do?
  • What should the system return?
  • How should exceptional cases be handled?
  • What are the security, compatibility, performance, and permission requirements?
  • Which behaviors can tests verify?

Avoid writing:

在 UserService.ts 里新增 createUserWithProfile 方法。

Prefer writing:

### Requirement: 用户注册

系统 SHALL 在用户提交合法邮箱和密码后创建账号，并返回登录态。

#### Scenario: 合法注册
- GIVEN 用户输入未注册邮箱和符合规则的密码
- WHEN 用户提交注册表单
- THEN 系统创建账号
- AND 用户进入已登录状态

A Spec governs how the system should behave, not how the programmer intends to write it.

2. Change: An Independent Workspace for One Change

openspec/changes/<change-name>/ is the workspace for a change.

A change typically contains:

  • proposal.md: Why, what, and scope.
  • specs/: Incremental modifications to the main specifications.
  • design.md: Technical approach and key decisions.
  • tasks.md: Implementation task checklist.
  • .openspec.yaml: Optional change metadata.

This resembles a Git branch, except it manages requirements and design differences rather than code differences.

A code branch answers:

What changed in the code?

An OpenSpec change answers:

Why change it, how do we plan to change it, and how should the system behave afterward?

3. Artifact: Turn Vague Ideas into Actionable Outputs

Artifacts are work products within a change.

The default spec-driven process is roughly:

proposal -> specs -> design -> tasks -> implement

The purpose is not ceremony, but breaking a vague requirement into questions at different levels:

  • proposal.md answers why and where the boundaries are.
  • specs/ answers how system behavior changes.
  • design.md answers how to implement it technically.
  • tasks.md answers the order of execution.

When all four questions are crammed into one prompt, the model easily mixes them together. OpenSpec separates them so AI can receive, update, and execute them more reliably.

4. Delta Spec: Describe Only This Change

Delta Spec is a particularly important OpenSpec design.

Instead of rewriting the full specification every time, describe the increment:

  • ADDED Requirements: What behavior is added.
  • MODIFIED Requirements: What existing behavior is modified.
  • REMOVED Requirements: What behavior is removed.

This suits existing projects particularly well. Most real engineering changes a small part of an existing system rather than building a new system from scratch.

The problem with full documents is that readers must perform the diff in their heads.

A Delta Spec tells them directly what the diff is.

5. The OPSX Workflow: From /opsx:propose to /opsx:archive

As of May 22, 2026, OpenSpec's official documentation recommends the new OPSX workflow. The default core profile includes:

  • /opsx:propose
  • /opsx:explore
  • /opsx:apply
  • /opsx:sync
  • /opsx:archive

Enabling the expanded workflow also provides:

  • /opsx:new
  • /opsx:continue
  • /opsx:ff
  • /opsx:verify
  • /opsx:bulk-archive
  • /opsx:onboard

For most teams, mastering the default path is enough to start:

/opsx:propose -> /opsx:apply -> /opsx:sync -> /opsx:archive

1. /opsx:explore: Explore Before the Idea Is Mature

Do not rush to create a formal change while requirements remain vague.

For example:

/opsx:explore 我想给订单列表加一个批量导出能力，但还不确定要导出哪些字段，也不确定权限怎么卡。

At this stage, have the AI:

  • Read existing code and specifications.
  • Clarify business boundaries.
  • Identify potentially affected modules.
  • Compare implementation approaches.
  • Turn a vague idea into a requirement ready for a proposal.

Exploration is not about chatting longer; it prevents the model from changing code before the problem is thought through.

2. /opsx:propose: Formally Create a Change

Once the goal is reasonably clear, create a change:

/opsx:propose 为订单列表添加批量导出 CSV 能力

Based on project context, the AI creates a directory resembling:

openspec/changes/export-orders-csv/
├── proposal.md
├── design.md
├── tasks.md
└── specs/
    └── orders/
        └── spec.md

Review three things carefully here:

  • Is the requirements intent correct?
  • Is the scope too broad?
  • Are non-goals explicit?

Without firm boundaries here, faster implementation only takes you further off course.

3. /opsx:apply: Implement from the Task Checklist

Move to implementation after confirming the proposal:

/opsx:apply export-orders-csv

The AI reads the change's artifacts and follows tasks.md. Each completed item is checked off:

## 1. Export API
- [x] 1.1 增加订单导出接口
- [x] 1.2 校验导出权限
- [ ] 1.3 增加导出字段映射

The key is not having AI automatically finish everything, but keeping each step on a reviewed task track.

If implementation reveals a flawed design, do not push blindly ahead. Update design.md or specs/ first, then continue with /opsx:apply.

4. /opsx:sync: Synchronize Delta Specifications into the Main Specifications

OpenSpec's main specifications live in openspec/specs/, while change-specific deltas live in openspec/changes/<name>/specs/.

To merge a delta spec back into the main specifications, run:

/opsx:sync export-orders-csv

This keeps the source of truth for current system behavior up to date with the change.

Not every team must run sync manually, since archive often prompts for or handles synchronization. Still, this step matters: OpenSpec's full cycle ends not when the code is written, but when the main specifications also reflect the resulting system behavior.

5. /opsx:archive: Archive After Completion

Once the feature is complete and validation passes:

/opsx:archive export-orders-csv

OpenSpec moves the change to the archive directory, for example:

openspec/changes/archive/2026-05-22-export-orders-csv/

Archiving preserves decision history; it is not garbage collection.

Three months later, if you wonder why an order export omitted the cost-price field, the best reference is the original proposal, design, delta spec, and tasks, rather than scattered PR discussion.

6. Where OpenSpec Is Most Useful

Not every change needs OpenSpec. It best suits work whose boundaries are easily lost if managed only through chat.

1. New Features

New features often involve scope, user behavior, interface contracts, error cases, and acceptance tests. Asking AI to code immediately can skip requirements clarification.

OpenSpec first turns the feature into:

  • Intent
  • Scope
  • Requirements
  • Scenarios
  • Design
  • Tasks

Then implementation begins.

2. Modifying Existing Behavior

Changing existing behavior needs specifications even more than adding features.

You must answer not only what is being added, but also:

  • Which old behavior changes?
  • Does the old behavior have compatibility requirements?
  • Which downstream dependencies are affected?
  • Should tests be modified or added?

Delta Spec's MODIFIED Requirements is well suited to expressing such changes.

3. Large Refactors

The biggest refactoring risk is accidentally changing external behavior along with code structure.

OpenSpec fixes external behavior in specifications, telling AI what it must preserve during refactoring. The specification here defines behavioral boundaries, not implementation plans.

4. Cross-Team or Long-Running Tasks

When work spans people, days, or sessions, chat context deteriorates quickly.

The OpenSpec change folder becomes a handoff point:

  • Newcomers read the proposal to learn why.
  • Then the specs to learn how behavior changes.
  • Then the design to learn the technical approach.
  • Finally, the tasks to learn current progress.

This is far more reliable than searching chat history.

5. AI Agent Collaboration

OpenSpec is especially valuable for AI Agents. Their weakness is not inability to execute, but drifting over long sequences of actions.

proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md and delta specs provide external memory and intermediate goals.

This does not freeze the Agent's autonomy; it gives every step a task track it can revisit.

7. OpenSpec and the AI Agent Harness

If an AI coding assistant is a nondeterministic executor, OpenSpec resembles a Harness's source of truth and stage controls.

It provides a specification-level control plane, rather than a runtime sandbox or permission-approval system:

  • Use specs/ to fix current system behavior.
  • Use changes/ to isolate the current change's intent.
  • Use proposal.md to hold the goal and boundaries.
  • Use delta specs to constrain behavioral changes.
  • Use design.md to fix the technical approach.
  • Use tasks.md to govern execution cadence.
  • Use archive to close the delivery cycle and preserve historical traceability.

OpenSpec is not a complete Harness, but is a crucial layer in an AI coding Harness: Spec is Truth.

It addresses the most common context problem in AI collaboration:

Models may forget and chats may end, but the repository's specifications must not disappear.

8. Summary

Engineering in the AI coding era is about more than making models write more code for us.

The deeper question is how to make a model understand the goal before coding, preserve boundaries while coding, and add the change to the project's long-term memory afterward.

This is where OpenSpec's value lies.

It is neither a smarter Agent nor a heavier requirements system. It is a lightweight specification track that turns AI collaboration into an engineering cycle that can be reviewed, resumed, synchronized, and archived.

For individual developers, OpenSpec reduces context loss from forgetting why a change was made in the previous conversation.

For teams, it brings AI-assisted requirements, design, tasks, and historical decisions back into the code repository, allowing reviews to examine intent and behavioral changes before focusing only on code diffs.

For AI Agents, OpenSpec provides an external source of truth. Models can keep executing efficiently without relying solely on temporary chat memory.

More plainly, AI coding's challenge is shifting from generating code to reliably delivering changes. OpenSpec defines changes before they enter code, constrains them during implementation, and ensures the project remembers them afterward.

Appendix: OpenSpec Command Quick Reference

Installation and Initialization

npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest
cd your-project
openspec init

Initialize for Specific Tools

openspec init --tools claude,cursor
openspec init --tools all
openspec init --tools none

Common Slash Commands

/opsx:explore <想法或问题>
/opsx:propose <要构建的能力>
/opsx:apply <change-name>
/opsx:sync <change-name>
/opsx:archive <change-name>

Common CLI Commands

openspec --version
openspec list
openspec show <change-name>
openspec validate <change-name> --strict
openspec status --change <change-name>
openspec list --specs
openspec view
openspec update

Expanded Workflow

openspec config profile
openspec update

After enabling, use these as needed:

/opsx:new
/opsx:continue
/opsx:ff
/opsx:verify
/opsx:bulk-archive
/opsx:onboard
