title: Industry Analysis, Decision Challenges, and Code Acceptance: Three Skills for a Cognitive Exoskeleton
html:
Abstract: Instead of collecting "all-purpose prompts," package frequent thinking processes into a Skill—a reusable expert workflow. This article records three Skills I wrote, their shared methodology, and how anyone can get started.

Skills and Repository Covered in This Article

The complete definitions and source files for these three Skills are open source in my notes repository, for reference and adaptation:

SkillPurpose
Industry X-RayExpert in deep industry analysis
Devil's AdvocateA shadow opponent before major decisions
Skill AcceptorAn acceptance-briefing protocol for AI-generated code

Repository: https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/AI-Fullstack-Notes

Skill files are in the repository's skills/ directory (such as industry-xray-teardown, devils-advocate, and skill-acceptor), matching the names used in this article.

Recently I did something small but, to me, interesting: instead of writing another collection of "all-purpose prompts," I wrote the three AI Skills above.

They seem to serve entirely different purposes: researching industries, challenging decisions, and accepting code. But after writing them, I realized they all point to the same question:

How do we turn AI from a chat tool into an expert counterpart that is truly reusable, capable of delivering work, and collaborative?

This article explores how I wrote these three Skills and the methodology they share.

I. Why Prompts Alone No Longer Satisfy Me

Many people still use AI through one-line requests:

"Analyze this industry for me."
"Tell me whether this decision makes sense."
"Summarize this code for me."

These questions produce answers, of course, but the problem is obvious:inconsistent output. Sometimes AI is insightful, sometimes perfunctory; sometimes well structured, sometimes full of correct but empty statements. Sometimes it helps you judge; sometimes it merely agrees with you.

The reason is simple: you gave it a task, but no working protocol.

The value of a Skill is precisely that it turns a one-off exchange into a reusable expert workflow. A good Skill does more than tell AI who it is. It specifies:

  • When to activate
  • What qualifies as acceptable input
  • Which reasoning steps to follow
  • Which behaviors are prohibited
  • The required final output format
  • How to continue interacting with the user

In other words, a Skill is an operating manual, not a magic incantation.

II. Skill One: An Industry X-ray That Translates Jargon into Plain Language

The first Skill is called Industry X-Ray, positioned as an expert in deep industry analysis.

It solves a common problem: unfamiliar industries can overwhelm us with jargon—SaaS, MCNs, new energy, cross-border commerce, short-form dramas, chips, AI agents. Industry reports are thick, expert interviews opaque, and media coverage piles on concepts. After reading everything, you may remember many terms but still not know how the industry makes money, who earns the big profits, who does the hard work, or who will be disrupted next.

So I designed a very explicit analytical framework for this Skill.

1. Start in Plain Language: What Does This Industry Actually Do?

It must explain the industry's essence in one accessible, perhaps slightly humorous sentence. For example:

SaaS is essentially the software world's "bike sharing": instead of paying a large upfront price to own software, you pay monthly rent and use it whenever you need.

This requirement matters: if the industry's basic reason for existing cannot be explained plainly, everything that follows may be nothing more than jargon.

2. Peel Back Three Layers: The Surface, the Mechanics, and the Foundations

I divide the industry into three layers:

LayerFocus
SurfaceCurrent landscape, leading players, common jargon
MiddleValue chain, money flows, and who earns money the hard way
FoundationFirst principles, core drivers, and variables that could reshuffle the industry

This structure prevents AI from stopping at empty claims like "the industry has great potential" or "competition is fierce." It must answer harder questions: who is upstream and midstream, who pays downstream, where the money comes from, who captures the profits, whether the industry's real foundation is policy, capital, technology, traffic, or human nature, and which future variable could overturn the entire game.

3. Finish by Challenging the User

Another design choice I particularly like:The Skill cannot stop after producing its report. It must ask two scenario-based questions for the user to answer in their own words, such as:

  • Given RMB 5 million, which part of the value chain would you invest in, and why?
  • If a new technology becomes widespread, which type of company fails first?

This may seem unnecessary, but it is crucial: real understanding is not "I followed the explanation"; it is "I can make a judgment in a new situation."AI should be a thinking coach as well as a content generator.

III. Skill Two: A Shadow Opponent That Dismantles Self-Persuasion Before Major Decisions

The second Skill is called Devil's Advocate, which I translate as "shadow opponent." Its temperament is deliberately unappealing:No encouragement, consolation, or emotional reassurance. It does just one thing:

Before a major decision, it coldly plays the clearest-headed opponent in the room.

Perhaps you plan to quit and start a business, spend your savings opening a shop, move cities, make a concentrated investment, or join an early-stage venture. The greatest danger is often not a lack of information, but that we feel the impulse first and then seek reasons to prove ourselves right: classic confirmation bias.

This Skill therefore focuses on just two things: the worst-case scenario through a premortem, and the traps along the execution path through stage-by-stage risks. It closes with two pressure-test questions.

1. Premortem: Put the Worst Case on the Table First

It does not gently ask, "What risks does this plan have?" It starts from an assumption:

It is now one to three years later. Your plan has completely failed, the money is gone, the opportunity cost is enormous, and your reputation may even be damaged.

It then works backward to identify five critical points that caused the failure—a premortem. It forces us to switch from "I will succeed" to "Why will I fail?" and must cover several fatal vulnerabilities:

  • Where cash flow breaks
  • Where capabilities do not match requirements
  • Where the external environment changes abruptly
  • Risks in the team or partnership
  • How the final blow happens

This instantly brings many romantic narratives back to reality.

2. Execution Risks: Defuse Traps Stage by Stage

A catastrophic ending alone is not enough. Many ventures die in the stretch between spending the first money and reaching supposed stability. The Skill therefore follows your plan's actual execution sequence—preparation, launch, ramp-up, or whatever stages fit—and lists each stage's most likely failure points. Wherever possible, it writes "what may happen → what it could turn into," rather than a vague "watch out for risk."

What you receive is not an essay of empty truths, but a risk map aligned with the timeline.

3. End with Hard Questions

It ends not with "Good luck," but with two stress-test questions, such as:

  • If revenue is zero for the first three months, how many months can your cash flow last?
  • If a giant enters tomorrow with heavy subsidies, what concrete defenses do you have besides passion?

If you cannot answer, do not rush to donate your money to reality. I wrote this Skill to make AI willing, at crucial moments, to disagree with me, rather than merely become better at encouragement.

IV. Skill Three: Code Acceptance Without Drowning Humans in AI-generated Code

The third Skill is called Skill Acceptor, and addresses a more engineering-focused situation:How should humans evaluate a large body of code after an AI agent has written it?

This question will grow increasingly important. Code will not become scarcer; it will be generated faster. Previously, the problem was being unable to write it. Now it may be too much code for humans to review. An agent can change more than a dozen files in minutes. Humans who continue reviewing line by line will quickly face cognitive overload.

So Skill Acceptor has a clear goal:

Instead of making humans read undigested low-level boilerplate, have AI produce an architecture-level acceptance briefing.

1. First, Understand the Scope of Changes

It must first answer: where are the main entry points? Which core files were added or modified? Did database schemas change? Were new dependencies introduced? Was global configuration modified? Establish the boundaries first so the risks become visible.

2. Then Filter Out Low-value Code

The rules:Do not explain basic syntax; do not paste large blocks of raw code; do not list files in a mechanical running commentary. What humans need is:

  • What does this code mean for the business?
  • How does the main workflow run, and how does data move?
  • Where are transactions, locks, retries, and fallbacks used?
  • What is returned when something fails?

3. Produce an Acceptance Dashboard

The output resembles a console dashboard: functionality, entry points, a change overview, the core implementation approach, main execution flow, exception and boundary defenses, and code anchors for every key step. For example:

Step 1: An interceptor validates the token and extracts UserId
Step 2: Query inventory and user information in parallel
Step 3: Start a transaction, write the order, and decrement inventory
Step 4: Return 200 while asynchronously sending an MQ message

Every step must include file and function names, so humans can locate crucial code in one click without getting lost in a sea of implementation.

The judgment behind this Skill is:

In the AI era, code review will shift from reading every line toward reviewing architectural intent, business workflows, and boundary defenses.

Humans should focus on higher-level judgment instead of competing with machines on patience.

V. What These Three Skills Share: Turning AI into an Expert with a Process

The scenarios differ, but the underlying structures are similar. My conclusion:A genuinely useful Skill needs at least six elements.

#ElementExplanation
1Define a role, but go beyond itThe role is the skin; the process is the skeleton. Specify how to break things down, what to examine and in what order, what must be asked, and what must not be done.
2Set an entry gate and reject vague inputFor example, Devil's Advocate requires a concrete plan: "I want to start a business" is insufficient; "quit my job and use RMB 500,000 to open an independent cafe in a third-tier city" qualifies.
3Require structured reasoningIndustry X-Ray analyzes industries in three layers; Devil's Advocate uses a premortem plus stage-by-stage execution risks; Skill Acceptor covers change scope, main workflows, and boundary defenses.
4Specify prohibitions to prevent shortcutsFor example: no empty jargon, no mere emotional reassurance, no large code dumps, and no overlooking transactions or exceptions.Constraints often matter more than instructions.
5Fix the output format so results are reusableFormatting is not decoration. It lowers collaboration costs by making output archivable, comparable, and transferable—a work asset.
6Add an interactive feedback loopFinal challenges or acceptance checks force the user to perform an act of thinking. One-way output easily creates an illusion of understanding.

VI. Writing Skills Means Writing Your Own Operating System for Thinking

After writing these three Skills, my strongest impression was:A Skill is more than prompt engineering; it packages a person's way of thinking into a callable module.

  • When writing Industry X-Ray, I was defining how I want to understand an unfamiliar industry.
  • When writing Devil's Advocate, I was defining how I want to counter impulse, optimism, and survivorship bias.
  • When writing Skill Acceptor, I was defining how I want to accept code output in the AI era.

Writing a Skill does more than teach AI how to work. It forces you to clarify what you truly value, your judgment criteria, how you define a good result, which low-quality outputs you dislike, and which thinking practices you want reproduced reliably.

Seen this way, a Skill is a cognitive exoskeleton for a person, not merely a plugin for AI.

VII. How Can Anyone Start Writing Their Own Skills?

If you want to begin, avoid aiming for something all-encompassing immediately. Start with three questions.

1. Which Judgments Do You Make Repeatedly?

Examples include choosing topics, screening resumes, analyzing investments, building customer profiles, reviewing product requirements, organizing meeting notes, reviewing code, and analyzing business models.Anything you do repeatedly that still consumes substantial mental effort is a good candidate for a Skill.

2. What Are Your Standards for a Good Result?

Do not just write "analyze this more deeply." Specify required sections, questions that must be answered, situations that require follow-up, risks that must be listed separately, and outputs that are unacceptable.The more specific you are, the more consistent AI becomes.

3. Whom Should AI Work Like?

Go beyond "an expert" to something more concrete:

  • A sharp-tongued but dependable opponent
  • A teacher who translates jargon into plain language
  • A technical lead focused on architectural intent
  • An exceptionally demanding product reviewer
  • An interviewer skilled at probing motivations

The clearer the role, the clearer the boundaries.

Closing Thoughts

We used to say that people who ask better questions use AI better. The next divide may go beyond question-asking:

Have you turned your frequent thinking processes into reusable Skills?

A prompt addresses one conversation; a Skill addresses a class of problems. Someone who continually packages judgment, experience, and methodology into Skills is doing more than using AI: they are training a set of expert counterparts that understand them increasingly well.

  • When researching an industry, someone strips away the jargon.
  • Before a major decision, someone coldly argues against you.
  • When accepting code, someone translates complex implementation into an architectural briefing.

This does not replace thinking; it helps you uphold a higher standard of thinking. That is what I gained from writing these three Skills. On the surface they are tools; in practice, they are three cognitive extensions I gave myself: one helps me understand a complex world, one counters blind optimism, and one manages code complexity in the AI era.

If AI is an increasingly powerful engine, Skills are the steering wheel, brakes, and dashboard.

  • Without Skills, you are simply chatting with AI.
  • With Skills, you begin building your own working system.

Source files and ongoing updates for all three Skills are available at https://github.com/Eva-Dengyh/AI-Fullstack-Notes

title: Token Budget Management: Dynamic Reserves and Layered Compression
html:
Your LLM has a 200K “credit limit”—but you may actually be able to spend less than half of it.

How Much of Your 200K Window Can You Really Use?

Open a model vendor's documentation and the “200K context window” stands out. The number is reassuring: just keep filling it.

But engineers quickly discover the problem. Let us break it down item by item:

模型硬上限（200K）
├── 系统提示词（System Prompt）          ∼2K–8K
├── 工具/函数定义（Tool Definitions）     ∼5K–134K
├── 安全/隐藏前缀（Hidden Preamble）      ∼数百 token
├── 多模态占位符展开                      ∼不定
├── 对话历史（Conversation History）      ∼动态增长
├── 当前用户输入                          ∼可变
├── 为模型回复预留（Reserve）              ∼4K–20K
└── 思考 token（Thinking/Reasoning）       ∼不可见但计入
─────────────────────────────────────────────
    剩余可用预算                           ？？？

Each item deserves a closer look:

System prompt—the role and behavioral rules you set for the model. A moderately complex Agent system prompt easily exceeds 2,000 tokens. Add safety policies and output-format constraints, and 8,000 tokens is common.

Tool definitions—the easily overlooked hidden heavyweight. Every tool is a JSON Schema: function name, parameters, type constraints, and descriptions all count toward context. Claude Code has 30+ tools; tool definitions alone can consume 55K–134K token. Research suggests that on Claude Opus, the tool-definition portion of each call costs 0.67. Money is spent before your Agent even starts working.

Conversation history—every user message, assistant response, tool call, and tool result accumulates. Twenty turns can easily exceed 50,000 tokens. Every new message also sends the entire history to the model again.

Reserve—without a reserve, replies are hard-truncated: incomplete JSON, half a sentence, unfinished code. You must also avoid the “compression paradox”: compression needs room to write a summary into context, but no room remains even for that summary.

Thinking tokens—reasoning models such as o1 and Claude Opus “think” internally before answering.

Added together, for a real running Agent, a 200K window may offer only 30K–80K of usable budget—less than half.

Three Concepts You Must Understand

Token budget management is more than counting what remains. It needs a simple but precise conceptual framework.

2.1 Budget: How Much This Turn Can Spend

The budget is not 200K; it is what remains after all fixed overhead is subtracted from 200K.

Effective Budget = Context Window − System Overhead − History − Reserve

Treat the budget as an active constraint, not a passive remaining balance. As used tokens approach it, trigger intervention: compression, truncation, or rejection.

2.2 Reserve: Leave Room for the Model's Reply

Imagine writing a long email that hits the character limit at “Tomorrow at three, let us meet at—” and the Send button turns gray. For an LLM, this means:

  • Truncated JSON that fails to parse
  • Incomplete tool-call arguments that fail to execute
  • An abrupt reply ending halfway through a sentence

You must therefore set aside an untouchable portion of the spendable budget. The problem is that a fixed reserve, such as always using 4,096, is too inflexible. A yes/no answer may need 10 tokens; a code refactor may generate 8,000.

A better approach is a dynamic reserve:

reserve = base_reserve + 任务复杂度加成
──────────────────────────────────
是/否判断        → base_reserve × 0.1
简短解释         → base_reserve × 0.3
代码建议         → base_reserve × 1.0（基准）
代码重构/生成    → base_reserve × 2.0
长文档生成       → base_reserve × 3.0

This is exactly like operating-system memory allocation: a process requests memory, and the kernel approves or denies it based on system state.

2.3 Threshold: Act Before Space Runs Out

Claude Code's approach illustrates this best:

UtilizationBehavior
∼85%Show a warning to the user
∼90%Automatically trigger compression
∼95%Block new requests
∼98%The last line of defense for manual compression

The key idea:Warn at 85%; act at 90%. Waiting until 98% may leave too little space even for compression.

This is not a binary enough/not-enough decision, but a gradual response chain that escalates as pressure rises. Lightweight cleanup usually suffices; heavyweight compression is reserved for real emergencies.

Three Practical Problems

3.1 “I Just Divided Character Count by Four”—Your Estimate Will Be Wrong

Different models use different tokenizers. Counts for the same sentence can vary by 10–30%:

Texttiktoken (OpenAI)AnthropicDifference
"How many tokens does this sentence contain?"8 token9 token12.5%

That is just simple English. Chinese is more extreme: one character may require 2–3 tokens. A 2,000-character prompt may be 5,000–6,000 tokens. Dividing character count by four can miss by more than 20%.

A subtler problem is “tokenizer drift”: local counts often differ from the API server's billed count by 5–15%. The sources are locally invisible: JSON structures for role markers, formatted tool schemas inside the request envelope, tokenized multimodal placeholders, and reasoning-model thinking tokens.

3.2 Tool-Result Spikes: Blow the Budget in an Instant

Everything runs smoothly at 60% utilization. Then a search tool returns 50,000 tokens of web content, instantly pushing utilization to 92%.

This is a spike: one result far exceeds expectations and changes the budget state in a single step.

Responses:

Dynamic truncation thresholds: Thresholds should vary with current utilization rather than remain constant.

利用率 < 50% → 慷慨，允许大结果
利用率 50–80% → 保守，截断一半
利用率 > 80% → 告急，只留关键信息

After-the-fact remediation: Claude Code first writes the full result, then snips it afterward. The message chain remains intact—tool calls still pair with tool results—but content is replaced with [Old tool result content cleared]. This reclaims space without damaging semantic structure.

3.3 A Fixed Reserve Is Not Enough

You set reserve = 4096, but a refactoring Agent needs to generate 8,000 tokens of code. The model is capped at 4,096, and the code is cut off halfway through.

A more advanced approach is to let the Agent declare its own reserve requirement through a dedicated tool call specifying required_reserve_tokens: 8000, allowing the system to adjust the current turn's reserve.

Compression: The Question Is How, Not Whether

4.1 Layers: Try Free Options Before Spending Money

When the budget is tight, there are only three choices: stop, truncate, or compress. Compression itself costs money, information, and user waiting time through additional API calls.

Good engineering practice is to move from cheap to expensive, escalating only when needed: 

层级    策略          花费      回收能力    信息损失
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
L1     Snip/Pruning   零 LLM    中等       低（只清内容，保结构）
L2     微压缩         零 LLM    中等       低（基于时间衰减）
L3     主动重组       中等 LLM  高         中
L4     LLM 全文摘要   高 LLM    很高       高

L1 is the most underrated strategy. File contents searched ten turns ago, pages already read, and completed command output have already served their purpose. Clearing them requires no LLM call, preserves message structure, and can reclaim substantial space.

4.2 Circuit Breakers: When Compression Itself Fails

Worse still, compression fails because its prompt is too long, retries, and fails again. Before adding a circuit breaker, Claude Code observed 1,279 sessions with more than 50 consecutive compression failures, wasting about 250,000 API calls per day.

The circuit-breaker logic is simple:Three consecutive failures → open the circuit → skip further compression. One success resets it.

4.3 Compression Is Not the End

Critical context must be reinjected afterward. Claude Code's rules:

压缩后注入上限：
├── 总预算:    50,000 token
├── 单文件最多:  5,000 token
├── 最多恢复:    5 个文件
└── Skills:    25,000 token 总预算

There is also a truePostCompactTokenCount function specifically detecting immediate recompression right after compression.

Larger Windows Make the Problem Worse

A common illusion is that growing context windows from 128K to 200K to 1M will naturally solve the problem.

The opposite is true: larger windows make budget management more important.

5.1 The Cost of Waste Scales Linearly

With a fixed per-token price, filling 200K costs 6.25 times as much as filling 32K. Quality gains are far from linear. The Chroma team found that after inserting about 4,000 tokens—20 retrieved documents—accuracy dropped from 70–75% to 55–60%.Filling more space can make results worse.

5.2 More Context Can Make the Model See Less Clearly

Stanford research found a U-shaped performance curve: models attend strongly to the beginning and end (85–95%) and less to the middle (76–82%). GPT-3.5-Turbo's accuracy on documents buried in the middle fell to 56.1%—worse than giving it nothing.

The root cause is long-range decay in RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding): more distant tokens receive less attention. At 100K tokens, the model must manage roughly ten billion pairwise relationships, severely diluting attention.

5.3 The Cost Curve Is Not Linear

                         成本 ($) 持续线性增长 ↗
                        /
                      /
────────────────────
                      \
                        \  性能 / 准确率先平后降 ↘
                          \

Every additional 1,000 tokens raises cost linearly. Performance first plateaus, indicating redundancy, then declines as information overload starts harming judgment.

That is the essence of budget management: you are managing value for money, not just space.

How Real Projects Do It: Claude Code and Hermes Agent

Enough theory. Let us examine two production-grade systems with very different positioning:


Claude CodeHermes Agent
OriginAnthropic's official CLINous Research's open-source framework
Technology stackTypeScript / BunPython
Model compatibilityFocused on Claude modelsFull compatibility with more than a dozen providers
Core philosophyMaximum optimization within a closed ecosystemGeneral abstractions for open compatibility

6.1 How Do They Determine a Model's Window Size?

Claude Code—five levels of resolution:

Hermes Agent—nine levels of resolution:

In one sentence: Claude Code assumes you are probably in Anthropic's ecosystem and simplifies accordingly. Hermes assumes you could be anywhere, so it must be robust.

6.2 How Do They Count Tokens?

This is the two projects' most fundamental disagreement.

Claude Code—a dual-track approach:

  • Approximate estimates on hot paths: 4 chars/token, 2 chars/token for JSON, and a fixed 2,000 for images
  • An exact API at key decision points (beta.messages.countTokens)
  • But this precision works only in Anthropic's ecosystem; OpenAI and Gemini compatibility layers fall back to estimates

Hermes Agent—estimation only:

  • 4 chars/token throughout
  • A fixed 1,500–1,600 for images
  • But it also counts tool schemas, an often-overlooked overhead that can add 20–30K for tool-heavy Agents

Why Does Hermes Avoid Exact Counting? Supporting over a dozen providers means supporting a different exact-counting API for each. Maintenance is too expensive; lowering the trigger threshold to 50% rather than 90% absorbs estimation error instead.

This is the fundamental engineering choice:

  • Spend effort to eliminate error → exact counts and thresholds near the physical limit (90%)
  • Spend effort to tolerate error → estimates with sufficient safety margin (50%)

6.3 When Does Compression Trigger?

Claude Code—four progressive levels:

200K 窗口下：
∼167K → 警告闪烁（WARNING_BUFFER = 20K）
∼180K → 自动压缩（200K - 20K 预留 - 13K 额外缓冲）
∼197K → 阻塞新请求

Anti-thrashing mechanism:A circuit breaker stops after three consecutive failures.

Hermes Agent—a single 50% threshold:

threshold_tokens = max(context_length × 0.50, 64_000)
tail_token_budget = threshold_tokens × 0.20  # 保留最近 20%

Anti-thrashing mechanism:Suppress compression after two consecutive attempts save less than 10%.

Why Does Hermes Use 50% While Claude Code Uses 90%? Again, the difference is counting: approximation needs a 30–40% error buffer.

6.4 How Are Compression Strategies Layered?

Claude Code 三层：                  Hermes 两层：
┌─ MicroCompact ── 零 LLM          ┌─ Pruning ── 零 LLM
│  清除旧工具输出                    │  去重+单行摘要+截断
├─ Session Memory ── 零 LLM        │
│  用预提取记忆做摘要                └─ LLM 摘要 ── 辅助模型
└─ API 摘要 ── LLM 全文总结           便宜模型做摘要，降级链兜底

Both go from cheap to expensive. Differences:

  • Claude Code has a Session Memory layer, relying on an internal Anthropic experimental feature
  • Hermes uses an auxiliary model: a cheap model such as Gemini Flash summarizes sessions from an expensive main model, saving over 90%

6.5 Details Worth Highlighting

Prompt Cache Sharing: During compression, Claude Code uses forkedAgent to reuse the main thread's cached prefix, raising cache hits from 2% to nearly 100%. Hermes cannot do this because caching behavior differs across providers. This is a classic **optimization exclusive to a closed ecosystem**.

Slot Optimization: Claude Code lowers the default max_tokens from 32K to 8K. The API server reserves inference slots according to max_tokens, while actual p99 output is just 4,911 tokens. At 8K, fewer than 1% of requests are truncated, and those automatically receive a 64K retry. Counterintuitive, but effective.

Session Rotation: After successful compression, Hermes rotates session_id, marking the old session with end_reason=compression and linking the new session as its child. SQLite atomic locks prevent concurrent compression. Claude Code does not need this for a single Agent. Concurrent multi-Agent systems should adopt it.

Trajectory Compressor: Hermes also has a 1,509-line offline compressor that compresses completed Agent histories to 15,250 tokens for training data. This reflects a research organization's distinctive perspective:An Agent's execution history is itself a trainable asset.

Seven Proven Engineering Patterns

Pattern 1: Layer Compression, Free Before Paid

Whether Claude Code's “MicroCompact → SM → API summary” or Hermes's “Pruning → LLM summary,” the principle is to try zero-cost methods first. Clearing old tool outputs usually suffices, with no LLM call needed.

Pattern 2: Align Compression Boundaries with Message Semantics

tool_use and tool_result must remain paired; thinking blocks must not be split, and the most recent user message must remain. Compression follows message semantics, not arbitrary token cutoffs. Both projects emphasize this.

Pattern 3: Preserve the Beginning and End; Compress the Middle

Both LLM attention distribution—primacy and recency effects—and task structure—initial goals and recent context—require this. The amount retained is adjustable, but its position must be at the beginning and end.

Pattern 4: Anti-Thrashing Is Mandatory

Use a circuit breaker or a savings-threshold check. The point is to avoid repeatedly paying for ineffective compression. Claude Code's data: 250,000 wasted calls per day before its circuit breaker.

Pattern 5: Choose Exact or Approximate; Do Not Sit on the Fence

  • Single provider → exact counting, with thresholds near the physical limit
  • Multiple providers → approximate estimates, with sufficient buffer

Demanding both precision and universality is an engineering disaster.

Pattern 6: Separate the Summarization Model

Hermes summarizes Claude Opus or GPT-5 sessions with Gemini Flash or Haiku, potentially saving over 90%.

Pattern 7: Explicit Reinjection After Compression

Compression is more than checking remaining space. Consider that important context must be explicitly restored: files, skills, configuration, and discovered MCP tools.

This article is based on source-code and documentation analysis of:

  • claude-code-best/claude-code (compaction, token-budget, microCompact, autoCompact, and related modules)
  • nousresearch/hermes-agent (context_compressor, model_metadata, conversation_compression, trajectory_compressor, and related modules)
  • Faraday Machines: "40-60% of API Tokens Are Wasted"
  • Stanford TACL 2024: “Lost in the Middle” benchmark
  • ContextBudget (arXiv:2604.01664)

title: Overwhelmed by Information? TrendRadar Finds Useful Signals in the Noise
html:
Does this sound familiar?

You open your phone every morning: 50 trending topics on Weibo, 30 recommended Zhihu articles, a pile of Bilibili notifications, and countless articles forwarded in group chats. After an hour of scrolling, your mind is a blur—you feel you have seen everything and absorbed nothing.

Worse still, the information that actually matters to you—industry developments, news about companies you follow, and relevant technology trends—is buried under celebrity gossip and trending chatter before you can get to it.

This is not your fault. It follows from the business logic of today's information platforms.Their goal is to keep you there longer, not to help you obtain valuable information.

What if you had a personal information assistant?

Imagine this:

Every morning at 8, a message arrives through Feishu, email, or a phone notification. It has already selected what matters to you from a dozen platforms such as Zhihu, Weibo, 36Kr, and Bilibili, with AI analysis attached: “Technology sentiment is optimistic today, with two unusual signals worth watching…”

You never need to open an app, filter things manually, or follow an algorithm's lead.

That is what TrendRadar does.

It is a fully open-source, self-hostable intelligent information radar with a simple core idea:You define what matters; it finds the signal in the noise.

Who is it for?

  • 📈 Investors: Monitor market sentiment, industry developments, and relevant company news in real time
  • ✍️ Content creators: Follow trending topics, find ideas, and catch emerging opportunities for attention
  • 📣 PR and brand professionals: Monitor brand mentions and competitors, and respond promptly to public discussion
  • 🔬 Technology researchers: Follow open-source ecosystems and technology trends while filtering irrelevant information
  • 😩 Everyday users: Avoid the daily information barrage and see only what matters to them

How does it differ from an ordinary news app?


Ordinary news app / RSS readerTrendRadar
Who decides what you see?Platform algorithmsYour own rules + AI
Trend analysis?NoYes, LLM-powered multidimensional analysis
Where is the data?Platform serversYour own machine or cloud storage
Where can it send notifications?In-app notifications9+ channels including Feishu, DingTalk, Telegram, and email
Programmable extensions?Generally noSupports MCP and AI-toolchain integration

Put simply, ordinary information tools offer passive reception, while TrendRadar offers active retrieval.

An example

Suppose you are an investor following the AI industry. You write a sentence in ai_interests.txt:

我关注 AI 创业公司的融资动态、大模型的新产品发布，以及 AI 监管政策的变化

TrendRadar passes that natural-language description to an LLM, which finds items matching your intent among all the trending content collected that day—without manually maintaining keyword lists.

After filtering, it also generates analysis:

Key trends today: Discussion of AI agents is up 40%, and several outlets are covering a new large-model release...

Unusual signals: Discussion of an AI company's share price has spiked over the past two hours, with negative sentiment...

Outlook and suggestions: Watch for policy-related news tomorrow...

It then sends this to your Feishu account or inbox.The whole process is automatic. You only need to read the report.

With that intuition in place, let's look at the technology behind TrendRadar.

Introduction: A structural dilemma in the information age

The internet has brought humanity into an era of information overload. According to IDC data, more than 2.5 quintillion bytes are generated globally every day, most of which are noise to any individual. This is particularly acute for investment analysts, creators, public-opinion monitors, and technology researchers, who must extract high-signal information from vast cross-platform feeds within limited time.

Traditional solutions—RSS readers, aggregators, and manual subscriptions—remain at the aggregation stage, without solving the central problems of filtering and analysis. The deeper dilemma is that platform recommendation algorithms optimize for time spent, rather than users' actual information needs. This is fundamentally a misalignment of incentives.

TrendRadar is an open-source intelligent information radar that turns passive consumption into active retrieval through an end-to-end “aggregate → filter → analyze → deliver” pipeline. This article examines its architecture, core mechanisms, and engineering design in depth.

System positioning and design boundaries

Core problem domain

TrendRadar primarily addresses three problems:

ProblemLimitations of traditional solutionsTrendRadar's approach
Information overloadInefficient manual selection and dependence on recommendationsKeyword engine + AI semantic filtering to define interests proactively
Platform fragmentationSwitching between platforms without a unified viewUnified acquisition layer with one entry point for 11+ platforms
Missing analysisRaw information without trend insightsLLM-driven analysis across five dimensions

Target users

The system is optimized for these scenarios:

  • Quantitative investors: Need low-latency market-sentiment signals and timely data
  • PR and public-opinion monitoring: Need near-real-time tracking of brand mentions and competitor activity
  • Content creators: Follow hot topics and need an aggregated cross-platform popularity view
  • Technology researchers: Follow open-source ecosystems and technology trends, requiring high-quality information with noise removed

System architecture

TrendRadar uses a clear six-layer vertical architecture. Each layer has a single responsibility, with standard interfaces decoupling layers.

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      用户交互层                              │
│  飞书 / 钉钉 / 企业微信 / Telegram / ntfy / Bark / Email     │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↑
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                    输出与分发层                              │
│     NotificationSender (9+ 渠道)  │  HTML Generator         │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↑
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                      AI 处理层                               │
│     LiteLLM Unified Client (100+ LLM 提供商)                 │
│     趋势分析 / 情绪识别 / 异常检测 / 战略建议                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↑
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                    核心处理引擎                              │
│   Analyzer │ FrequencyEngine │ WeightCalculator │ NewDetector│
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↑
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                   调度与控制层                               │
│     Scheduler (timeline.yaml) │ ExecutionDeduplication       │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↑
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                    数据获取层                                │
│     NewsNow API Client (11+ 平台)  │  RSS/Atom Fetcher        │
└─────────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                                      ↓
┌─────────────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────┐
│                      存储层                                  │
│     LocalStorageBackend (SQLite)  │  RemoteStorageBackend    │
│                                   │  (S3 / R2 / OSS / COS)  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Data Acquisition Layer

This layer is the system's data entry point, retrieving raw data from heterogeneous sources and standardizing it.

NewsNow API client wraps 11+ major platforms, including Zhihu, Weibo, Bilibili, Douyin, Baidu trending searches, and 36Kr. Its unified interface hides API differences. Key design points include:

  • Automatic rate-limit handling and retries with exponential backoff
  • URL normalization: removing UTM tracking parameters, standardizing schemes, and normalizing paths
  • Timezone conversion to the user's configured local timezone

RSS/Atom fetcher Built using the feedparser library, it supports custom feeds. Field mappings convert different formats, including RSS 2.0 and Atom 1.0, into the system's unified internal NewsItem data class.

2. Scheduling & Control Layer

The scheduling layer is the system's control plane, coordinating execution timing throughout the workflow.

Scheduler (located in trendradar/core/scheduler.py) reads config/timeline.yaml and converts user-defined schedules into the ResolvedSchedule data class:

@dataclass
class ResolvedSchedule:
    collect: bool    # 当前时间点是否采集数据
    analyze: bool    # 是否触发 AI 分析
    push: bool       # 是否推送通知
    report_mode: str # daily / current / incremental

Execution deduplication uses the period_executions database table to track daily execution records. The once_per_day flag prevents duplicate notifications even if the service restarts within the same time window, which is critical to production stability.

3. Core Processing Engine

The core engine is the system's most complex part, implementing a sequential, multistage data-processing pipeline:

原始数据
   ↓ [1] URL 规范化
   ↓ [2] 全局过滤器（[GLOBAL_FILTER] 排除规则）
   ↓ [3] 关键词匹配（正则 / 纯文本 / AI 语义兴趣）
   ↓ [4] 必需词检查（+前缀词 AND 逻辑）
   ↓ [5] 分组过滤（!前缀词触发组内互斥排除）
   ↓ [6] 权重计算
   ↓ [7] 新内容检测（对比历史数据，标记 🆕）
   ↓ [8] AI 处理（翻译 / 分析 / 摘要）
   ↓ [9] 输出生成（HTML + 多渠道通知）

The weighting model uses a weighted linear combination:

综合权重 = 排名得分 × 0.6 + 频次得分 × 0.3 + 平台热度 × 0.1

The ranking score comes from the original platform ranking. Frequency measures how often the same topic appears across platforms—cross-platform resonance strongly indicates a valuable signal. The platform popularity coefficient is preset based on audience size.

Keyword-filter syntax is thoughtfully designed and supports three filtering modes:

SyntaxMeaningExample
wordOrdinary keyword (OR logic)AI
+wordRequired term (AND logic)+股票
!wordWithin-group exclusion!明星
[GROUP]Group definition[科技]

This syntax lets users define complex filtering rules without writing code, lowering the barrier to use.

AppContext (trendradar/context.py) acts as a dependency-injection container, managing all core services' lifecycles and avoiding global singletons and tight coupling.

4. Storage Layer

The storage layer uses the Strategy Pattern to select an appropriate backend automatically for the deployment environment:

  • LocalStorageBackend: Writes to local SQLite with separate daily databases (output/news/YYYY-MM-DD.db), suitable for a single-machine deployment
  • RemoteStorageBackend: Supports Cloudflare R2, AWS S3, Alibaba Cloud OSS, and Tencent Cloud COS. Its “download existing DB → merge incremental data → upload to cloud” workflow provides persistence for stateless containers

Daily SQLite partitioning balances query performance—historical data is excluded from scans—with management convenience: deleting files removes old data.

5. AI Integration Layer

This layer uses LiteLLM to provide unified access to 100+ LLM providers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and local Ollama. Users can switch the underlying model through configuration without vendor lock-in.

Structured prompts drive five built-in analytical dimensions:

  1. 1. Core trends: Identify dominant narratives and topic clusters in the current feed
  2. 2. Sentiment and controversy: Analyze public sentiment and identify highly contentious topics
  3. 3. Unusual signals: Detect breaking events, black-swan signals, and statistical anomalies
  4. 4. RSS insights: Produce in-depth summaries of feed data
  5. 5. Outlook and strategy: Offer forward-looking suggestions based on current trends

max_news_for_analysis (150 items by default) limits how much data goes into the LLM at once, balancing analytical quality against token cost.

6. Output & Distribution Layer

The system supports nine notification channels, each adapted to its platform's characteristics:

ChannelContent size limitFormatCharacteristics
Feishu29 KBRich-text cardsPreferred for internal enterprise collaboration
DingTalk20 KBMarkdownSuitable for teams
WeCom4 KBMarkdown/textStrict limit; requires content compression
Telegram4 KBHTMLHyperlink support, friendly to individual users
ntfy3.8 KBReverse orderLightweight mobile-friendly notifications
Bark3.6 KBMarkdownNative iOS push experience
Slack4 KBmrkdwnTeam collaboration with channel distribution
EmailUnlimitedHTMLMost complete content, with historical archiving
Webhook4 KBCustom JSONMost flexible; integrates with any system

To handle widely varying channel size limits, the system automatically truncates and summarizes content while preserving the essential information.

Architectural design principles

TrendRadar demonstrates several engineering principles worth learning from:

1. Separation of Concerns (SoC): Each of the six layers has a clear responsibility. Data acquisition excludes business logic, the AI layer ignores data origins, and distribution is independent of data content.

2. Dependency Injection (DI): AppContext serves as an IoC container managing service instances, avoiding scattered global state and hard-coded dependencies while improving testability.

3. Strategy Pattern: Storage backends, filtering modes, and notification channels use strategies selected by runtime configuration. New extensions do not require changing core logic.

4. Pipeline Pattern: Data processing is divided into ordered, composable stages, each feeding its output into the next, simplifying debugging and unit testing.

5. Graceful Degradation: Failed AI analysis falls back to keyword filtering; unavailable remote storage falls back to local SQLite; one failed platform fetch does not disrupt the overall workflow.

6. Idempotent design: Execution deduplication makes operations idempotent within a time window, allowing safe restarts and retries as required for production stability.

7. Configuration-Driven: Declarative configuration defines core behavior instead of imperative code, lowering the barrier to customization and secondary development.

Conclusion

TrendRadar illustrates a shift from information-consumption tools toward information-analysis systems. It integrates retrieval previously scattered across apps into a configurable, extensible, AI-enhanced automated pipeline.

From an engineering perspective, its six-layer architecture, strategy-based storage, dependency-injected service management, and configuration-driven behavior reflect mature practices. For individuals and teams with intensive information needs, it provides highly customizable open-source infrastructure for building their own retrieval workflows.

Information asymmetry is, at heart, a moat around decision quality. TrendRadar aims to make that advantage accessible to more people, which may be its most important contribution.

title: Debugging Missing Umami Events: User-Agent and Traffic Identity
html:
Bug Description

While integrating Umami tracking into a desktop application, I encountered a production issue that is very easy to misdiagnose. Tracking requests appeared to leave the client successfully, and the server returned 200, yet the data never appeared in analytics. Events were missing, sessions were not created, or certain request paths consistently lost data. More confusingly, identical tracking logic persisted data through some call paths, while switching paths—or changing just one User-Agent fragment—immediately changed the outcome.

This deserves a dedicated write-up because it looks like an API problem but often is not. It looks like an unstable SDK, yet requests may already have been classified as low-trust traffic by the identity layer before reaching analytics. Without this diagnostic framework, troubleshooting can circle endlessly through request bodies, event names, site identifiers, the database, and frontend implementation without finding the actual cause.

Some background: Umami is a lightweight, open-source, privacy-focused web analytics system, often used instead of heavier commercial platforms. Integration is usually straightforward: pages or applications report pageviews and events at appropriate times, and the server receives them, attributes them, establishes sessions, and aggregates reports. Because it looks like “add a script and it works,” it is easy to blame tracking code and overlook the identity and traffic-filtering chain requests traverse before reaching the actual analytics logic.

The Essential Problem: The Request Did Not Fail; It Was Not Trusted

The most misleading part was that requests appeared to be sent successfully and the server returned 200, but the analytics system did not treat them as valid human visits.

In other words, this was neither a conventional network error nor invalid API parameter formatting, but a lower-level traffic identity problem.

From first principles, every tracking system ultimately does two things:

  1. 1. Receive a claim: The client says, “I visited a page / triggered an event.”
  2. 2. Decide whether the claim is credible: The server decides whether this is real user behavior or a script, bot, scanner, or forged request.

Engineers usually focus only on step one: Is the body correct? Is the site identifier correct? Did the API report an error? Modern analytics systems, gateways, and WAFs often put more weight on step two:Who you are matters more than what you say.

That was the essence of this issue.

Start with a Minimal Model: What Does a Tracking Request Validate?

At a minimum, a Umami report usually involves several signals:

  • Whether the request path is correct, such as the event ingestion endpoint
  • Whether the body matches the server schema
  • Whether the site identifier is valid
  • Whether Cookie / session context is recognizable
  • Whether request headers resemble a normal browser
  • Whether an upstream gateway or WAF classifies the request as high-risk traffic

It is easy to think of HTTP as a protocol where filling in all fields is enough. In production, it more closely resembles a claim system involving identity judgments.

You submit not just JSON, but a complete client profile:

  • User-Agent
  • Accept
  • Origin
  • Referer
  • TLS fingerprint
  • Header ordering characteristics
  • IP reputation
  • Cookie continuity
  • Request cadence

And User-Agent is often the first and cheapest filter: a readily available, low-cost signal that quickly indicates whether a request resembles a browser.

Therefore, if the UA triggers risk heuristics, even when the API continues to return 200, the analytics pipeline may silently downgrade, ignore, or discard the request, or fail to create a valid session.

This explains the particularly confusing symptoms:

  • Network level: no apparent error;
  • Application level: the API appears successful;
  • Data level: nothing is persisted, or key session identifiers are missing.

User-Agent Is an Identity Claim, Not a Notes Field

User-Agent is a standard HTTP request header, essentially an identity claim string.

It does not directly prove identity, but it affects the server's probabilistic judgment:

“Does this request look like it came from a real browser?”

This distinction is crucial.

The UA is neither a password nor a signature and provides no strong authentication. But it is an important input to risk systems' prior judgments. Its value lies not in absolute truth, but in fitting the normal distribution of real-world experience closely enough.

Why Are Standard Browser UAs More Readily Trusted?

Modern web infrastructure has built extensive empirical models around mainstream browsers.

A typical browser UA contains:

  • A Mozilla/5.0
  • Platform information, such as Macintosh, Windows NT 10.0
  • Rendering-engine information, such as AppleWebKit/537.36
  • A browser version, such as Chrome/132.0.xxx
  • Compatibility fields, such as Safari/537.36

These fields are not security mechanisms, but the internet's long evolution has established a stable distribution. Servers, CDNs, WAFs, and bot-detection libraries naturally place greater trust in frequently seen, statistically stable, mature client profiles.

Conversely, deviations—particularly inserted custom product names, abnormal version numbers, or suspicious placeholders—make requests statistically resemble automated traffic more closely.

Why Custom Shell Identifiers and All-Zero Placeholder Versions Trigger Blocking

This was the central difficulty. Superficially, there were just two extra fields, but to a risk system they represented two different categories of risk signals.

Custom Shell Identifiers: Unknown Fingerprints Raise Heuristic Risk

The problem is not necessarily that a library hardcodes the identifier into a blacklist, but that it disrupts the UA's natural shape.

Think of a UA as a sentence: a standard browser UA has stable grammar and a rich corpus of examples. Inserting a custom shell identifier resembles suddenly inserting an unfamiliar proper noun at an awkward position in otherwise normal English.

A WAF or bot detector may ask:

  • Is this product identifier common in mainstream browser families?
  • Is its position consistent with normal distributions?
  • Does it resemble an automation framework, test container, or private shell application?
  • Does it reduce the posterior probability of a real user's browser?

The issue is therefore not a syntax error, but a distribution anomaly.

The risk system usually does not claim certainty that you are a bot. Its more practical judgment is:

“You do not look typical or trustworthy enough as a browser, so I would rather lower my trust.”

Once trust falls below a threshold, the request may be:

  • Discarded outright;
  • Marked as bot traffic;
  • Excluded from session creation;
  • Given an apparently successful response without being persisted.

All-Zero Placeholder Versions: High-Risk Placeholders Trigger Blacklist-Style Rules

All-zero placeholder versions represent a different risk:a default-placeholder pattern.

0.0.0 almost never represents a properly released client version. It more often appears in:

  • Automation scripts with incorrectly injected version numbers
  • Default values in headless / test containers
  • Rudimentary scrapers or temporary debugging tools
  • Incompletely configured shell programs

From first principles, therefore, 0.0.0 is not merely sparse information; it is dangerous information.

Even with unconventional versioning, real released software rarely identifies itself persistently as 0.0.0. Many anti-scraping rules therefore treat it as a strong machine signal.

This explains why:

  • Custom shell identifiers resemble an unknown-device-fingerprint problem;
  • All-zero placeholder versions resemble a default-script-placeholder problem.

Both can lose data, but their mechanisms operate at different levels.

Why Does It Return 200 Without Persisting Data?

This is the most confusing point for many engineers first encountering risk-filtered data loss.

HTTP Success Does Not Mean Business Success

HTTP 200 tells you only that a service successfully received and processed your request. It does not guarantee:

  • A database write
  • Session creation
  • Inclusion in analytics reports
  • Passing every internal validation stage

Many analytics systems deliberately make such requests appear successful for two reasons:

  1. 1. Avoid exposing specific blocking rules to attackers: An explicit 403 bot detected would make it easier for attackers to iterate quickly;
  2. 2. Keep the public API behavior stable: Frontend SDKs do not flood logs with errors caused by risk-control details.

Silent dropping is therefore very common in anti-bot systems.

The Actual Decision May Happen Before the Analytics Application

A crucial point:The analytics application itself is not necessarily blocking a particular desktop container.

More often, the decision comes from:

  • CDN
  • Nginx rules
  • Cloudflare WAF
  • Libraries such as isbot
  • Custom gateway logic

These may apply UA-based risk filtering before Umami processes the event.

The failure may lie in the identity checks traversed by tracking code, rather than the code itself.

That is why changing the body or site identifier, or even suspecting the database, may never reveal the root cause.

Chrome and Electron are not the blockers in this chain; they are client runtimes sending requests. UA risk judgments are more likely made by ingress infrastructure before Umami: reverse proxies, CDNs, WAFs, or other anti-bot middleware. The “gateway before Umami” is generally not logic inside the Umami application, but rules in your server, reverse proxy, or cloud ingress. Only after passing those layers does Umami's own bot detection or event filtering make a second judgment. A more accurate description is therefore not “Umami blocked Electron,” but “the request was classified as low-trust traffic by ingress infrastructure or the server as it approached or entered Umami's processing pipeline.”

Controlled Testing: Why It Nearly Pinpoints UA as the Root Cause

The strongest part of this investigation was using controlled experiments.

Their engineering value is to break complex systems into testable hypotheses. If everything else remains unchanged and replacing only the UA consistently changes persistence, there is strong causal evidence linking UA to whether data is stored.

The results were:

No.Key UA characteristicsResult
1Gecko) followed directly by Chrome/132..., with no intervening product name and the desktop-container identifier retained✅ Persisted successfully
2Gecko) followed by an all-zero placeholder version, then Chrome + 桌面容器标识❌ Blocked and discarded
3Gecko) followed by a conventional, self-descriptive, non-placeholder client identifier, then Chrome + 桌面容器标识✅ Persisted successfully
4Plain Chrome + Safari, with no desktop-container identifier✅ Persisted successfully
5Another purely standard browser string✅ Persisted successfully
6A minimal string containing only the custom shell identifier and Safari compatibility field❌ Blocked and discarded

These results support several strong conclusions.

Conclusion 1: The Desktop-Container Identifier Is Not the Root Cause

Requests persisted successfully even with the container identifier retained. This directly rules out the crude assumption that the analytics system does not support desktop shell containers.

The real problem is that certain additional UA identifiers undermine the credibility of the entire string.

Conclusion 2: The Custom Shell Identifier Strongly Correlates with Loss

Removing the custom shell identifier restores normal behavior even with the desktop-container compatibility identifier retained. Reducing the UA to an unusual minimal structure containing only the shell identifier and Safari compatibility field consistently fails.

The custom shell identifier is therefore a clear high-risk signal, not harmless metadata.

Conclusion 3: All-Zero Placeholder Versions Match Another Set of Rules

Replacing the shell identifier with an all-zero placeholder still fails, while a conventional, self-descriptive, non-placeholder client identifier succeeds. This means custom product names are not universally fatal:

  • A custom product name may raise risk;
  • But a placeholder version such as 0.0.0 pushes it beyond a higher risk threshold.

This is a typical case of combined multidimensional heuristics: several anomalous signals jointly influence the result, rather than one Boolean rule.

First Principles: Why Looking Like a Browser Matters More Than Being One

This sounds counterintuitive, but closely reflects modern web risk control.

A server usually cannot directly prove that a real person is operating a browser. It collects low-cost signals to estimate a probability:

How likely is this request to be normal user traffic?

The UA is a cheap, high-value feature in that probabilistic system.

Risk Systems Evaluate Distributions, Not Labels

You may really be a desktop shell application or an internally developed client, but the risk model does not know your business context. It knows only client distributions historically seen at scale on the internet.

It does not ask:

  • “Are you a trusted internal application?”

It asks:

  • “Do you resemble ordinary traffic from real browsers?”

That is why the solution is not proving a custom shell identifier legitimate, but shaping outbound requests into a browser profile consistent with mainstream internet distributions.

Analytics Systems Aim to Filter Noise, Not Accept Everything

From an analytics system's perspective, mistakenly accepting bot traffic is often worse than dropping a small amount of edge-case traffic, because bots contaminate aggregate metrics:

  • UV
  • Session
  • Bounce Rate
  • Retention
  • Conversion Funnel

The system therefore prefers caution over readily accepting unusual UAs.

In other words, mistakenly blocking a few atypical clients is a cost many analytics and risk systems accept.

This explains why retrying will not cure the issue, and why an error-free API response cannot prove that everything is fine.

The Final Fix: Unify Outbound Identity Rather Than Tracking Semantics

Since the root cause was an abnormal outbound identity profile, the solution was not further payload changes, but:

Make all Umami-bound requests present the same trustworthy browser UA, verified to persist successfully, at the egress layer.

We used outbound sanitization and alignment across both paths.

The idea was straightforward:

  • Leave the analytics server's logic alone;
  • Do not rely on relaxed gateway rules;
  • Remove high-risk characteristics before requests leave the client;
  • Make page and script paths present the same external identity.

This is a typical engineering fix that corrects system boundary conditions with minimal changes.

Why Align Both Paths?

The page-originated path receives targeted sanitization at the desktop network egress, applying only to the target analytics service's unified event-ingestion endpoint. The script path does not rely on desktop interception; it directly reuses the same outbound UA constant already verified to persist successfully.

This is crucial. Fixing only the page path leaves a subtle inconsistency:

  • Page tracking persists correctly;
  • Script tracking continues to disappear unpredictably;
  • Analytics ends up measuring the same feature differently depending on its entry point.

The script runtime / command-line client must therefore switch to the same outbound UA constant too.

Summary

The root cause of this Umami data loss was neither unsent requests nor malformed bodies. Abnormal outbound User-Agent characteristics triggered risk controls, causing an upstream gateway or risk pipeline to classify the requests as machine traffic. Targeted UA sanitization at desktop network egress, combined with the same verified standard UA in the script path, aligned identity across the tracking pipeline and eliminated the misleading silent-loss problem where the API returns 200 but the data never reaches storage.
